At every nonzero finite-rate path, take a sufficiently small open neighborhood whose endpoints stay in $[\epsilon,K]$. Formula (Q.0.1l.17), continuity of $\Phi$, and the reference LDP lower bound give the lower bound $-I_\kappa(z)$. If an open set contains zero, use the exact probability

$$
P_n(Z_n\equiv0)=\exp(-n\delta_n T),\qquad
\frac1n\log P_n(Z_n\equiv0)=-\delta_nT\longrightarrow0.
\tag{Q.0.1l.19}
$$

This supplies the missing lower bound without falsely applying a continuous-tilt theorem at zero.

For a closed set $F\subset E$ excluding zero, there exists $\epsilon>0$ such that $z(T)\ge\epsilon$ on $F$. Indeed otherwise monotonicity would give $\|z\|_\infty=z(T)\to0$, contradicting closedness. On the closed truncation $F\cap\{z(T)\le K\}$, (Q.0.1l.17) and the reference LDP yield

$$
\limsup_n n^{-1}\log P_n(F\cap\{Z_n(T)\le K\})
\le -\inf_{F\cap\{z(T)\le K\}}[J(z)-\Phi(z)+\kappa].
\tag{Q.0.1l.20}
$$

To see this bounded-tilt upper step without a hidden compactness premise, partition the bounded range of $\Phi$ into finitely many closed intervals of length $\eta$; each intersection with the closed truncation is closed. Apply the reference closed upper bound on each piece and then let $\eta\downarrow0$. Uniformity of (Q.0.1l.17) absorbs its error. The finite union changes no speed-$n$ exponent.

There is also the direct source tail bound, by thinning domination with intensity $nC$, where $C=M+1$: for $K>CT$,

$$
\limsup_n n^{-1}\log P_n(Z_n(T)>K)
\le-[K\log(K/(CT))-K+CT]\longrightarrow-\infty.
\tag{Q.0.1l.21}
$$

Splitting $F$ at $K$ in (Q.0.1l.20) and sending $K\to\infty$ proves its full closed upper bound. If $F$ contains zero, the bound is the trivial probability bound, because the rate is nonnegative, as shown next. Sets outside $E$ cause no issue: the laws are supported on the closed set $E$.

For an absolutely continuous $z\in E$, the monotone change of variables, first with bounded truncations of $\log b$, gives

$$
\int_0^T\dot z(t)\log b(z(t))dt=B(z(T)).
\tag{Q.0.1l.22}
$$

The integral over the initial zero interval is defined as zero, since $\dot z=0$ almost everywhere there. Integrability follows from $\int_0^{z(T)}|\log b(u)|du<\infty$; the positive part is bounded by a constant times $z(T)$. Thus (Q.0.1l.22) is a finite real number and no $\infty-\infty$ cancellation occurs. Since the negative part of $v\log v$ is bounded, (Q.0.1l.18) becomes

$$
I_\kappa(z)=\kappa\mathbf1_{\{z(T)>0\}}+
\int_0^T\left[\dot z\log\frac{\dot z}{b(z)}-\dot z+b(z)\right]dt.
\tag{Q.0.1l.23}
$$

This identity remains valid when the entropy integral is infinite. It proves nonnegativity and the claimed local-action expression before stopping.

The rate is lower semicontinuous: $J$ is lower semicontinuous, $\Phi$ continuous, and $\kappa\mathbf1_{\{z(T)>0\}}$ lower semicontinuous on $E$, since $\kappa\ge0$. For goodness put $c=\max(0,\log M)$, so $B(y)\le cy$. Then

$$
I_\kappa(z)\ge J(z)-cz(T)-T.
\tag{Q.0.1l.24}
$$

The entropy dual bound with $\theta=c+1$ gives $J(z)\ge(c+1)z(T)-T(e^{c+1}-1)$, hence

$$
I_\kappa(z)\ge z(T)-Te^{c+1}.
\tag{Q.0.1l.25}
$$

A common $I_\kappa$-sublevel has bounded endpoints and, by the previous inequality, bounded $J$. It is a closed subset of a uniformly compact $J$-sublevel, proving goodness in both topologies.

When $\kappa=\infty$,

$$
P_n(Z_n\not\equiv0)=1-e^{-n\delta_nT}\le n\delta_nT,
\qquad \limsup_n n^{-1}\log P_n(Z_n\not\equiv0)=-\infty.
\tag{Q.0.1l.26}
$$

Together with (Q.0.1l.19), this directly proves the good LDP with only zero of finite rate, for every open and closed set. There is no need to subtract an infinite coefficient in (Q.0.1l.17).

**E. Clipping, the moving lattice endpoint, and the stopped rate.**

The pointwise clipping map $C_a(z)(t)=\min(z(t),a)$ is $J_1$-continuous: any time changes witnessing $z_n\to z$ also witness $C_a(z_n)\to C_a(z)$, because clipping is 1-Lipschitz. The contraction principle therefore gives a good LDP for $C_aZ_n$, with rate

$$
\widehat I^a_\kappa(x)=\inf\{I_\kappa(z): C_a z=x\}.
\tag{Q.0.1l.27}
$$

On the same birth-history construction, $X_n=C_{a_n}Z_n$ exactly, since clipping stops the first $m_n$ births and ignores all subsequent births. Moreover

$$
\|C_{a_n}Z_n-C_aZ_n\|_\infty\le|a_n-a|\longrightarrow0.
\tag{Q.0.1l.28}
$$

They are deterministically exponentially equivalent at speed $n$. This handles arbitrary convergence of $a_n$; no $O(1/n)$ endpoint approximation is assumed. All chains take values in $[0,a]$ under the stated $a_n\le a$ convention.

It remains to identify (Q.0.1l.27), rather than just state a contraction formula. A finite-rate preimage is absolutely continuous and nondecreasing, so its clip is in $\mathcal A_a$. If $x(T)<a$, the only preimage in $E$ is $z=x$, and (Q.0.1l.23) gives (Q.0.1l.3). If $x$ reaches $a$ at $s\le T$, every finite-rate preimage agrees with $x$ on $[0,s]$. It pays the same entrance charge and the same action up to $s$, followed by a nonnegative action. This gives the lower bound in (Q.0.1l.3). It is attained by the absolutely continuous preimage

$$
z(t)=x(t)\quad(t\le s),\qquad
z(t)=a+M(t-s)\quad(t\ge s).
\tag{Q.0.1l.29}
$$

For $z\ge a$, the extended rate equals $M$, so the post-hit path has velocity $M=b(z)$, and its local cost is exactly zero. Thus (Q.0.1l.27) is precisely (Q.0.1l.3). This argument also covers $s=T$, and the zero preimage is unique for the zero output. For $\kappa=\infty$, contraction leaves only zero of finite rate. The compact sublevels obtained in the contraction are continuous and uniformly compact, since clipping is uniformly continuous on the uniformly compact unstopped sublevels.

**F. Continuous interpolation and normalization.**

With the interpolation in the theorem, between successive jump vertices the step path is constant and the interpolated path lies between that value and its next value. After the last jump both are constant. Therefore

$$
\|\overline X_n-X_n\|_\infty\le 1/n
\tag{Q.0.1l.30}
$$

almost surely (jump times exactly at zero or $T$ have probability zero and may be defined arbitrarily). Exponential equivalence transfers the same $J_1$ LDP to $\overline X_n$. The subspace $C([0,T],[0,a])$ is $J_1$-closed, and its induced $J_1$ topology is exactly its uniform topology. Because the interpolated laws are supported there, the restricted LDP is the asserted good uniform-topology LDP. The same reasoning applies to any stated deterministic $o(1)$ continuous interpolation.

Finally, all rates are nonnegative and $I^a_\kappa(0)=0$, so their infimum is zero, consistent with probability normalization. Under the assumed divergent $\int_0^a1/\lambda$, zero is the only zero-action path even for $\kappa=0$: equality in the entropy density would force $\dot x=\lambda(x)$ before stopping. A nondecreasing solution departing from zero would require finite elapsed time at least $\int_\epsilon^bdu/\lambda(u)$ to reach any $b>0$, which diverges as $\epsilon\downarrow0$. This is impossible. No local Lipschitz assumption or unproved ODE uniqueness at zero is used. ∎

<a id="remark-q01l1-stopped-source-scope-and-independent-hitting-probabilities"></a>**Remark Q.0.1l.1 (Stopped-source scope and independent hitting probabilities).**

1. This is a full path-space LDP, not merely an endpoint or hitting-time contraction, for precisely the one-way monotone boundary-degenerate source above. The proof uses that each positive level is visited once. It does not extend to repeated visits, opposite jump directions, interior zero sets, or nonmonotone rate functions without new estimates.
2. At a fixed positive endpoint $a$, minimizing (Q.0.1l.3) over arrival by $T$ recovers the variational value $\kappa+J_\lambda(T)$ of Theorem Q.0.1g. An exact event such as endpoint equality need not have nonempty interior, so the probability equality in Theorem Q.0.1g should retain its independent holding-time proof; the present LDP is not used to infer a boundary-event exponent from an unverified continuity-set condition.
3. The infinite deterministic travel-time assumption is needed here to retain the accepted source class and to prove uniqueness of the zero-cost path. The path-LDP proof itself only uses positivity away from zero, bounded monotone extension, and log-integrability. No relaxation is part of this registered theorem.
4. Definition Q.0.1a currently requires a local integral rate. When $\kappa>0$, the additional entrance charge is not the displayed limiting local Hamiltonian's integral conjugate. This theorem therefore discharges the exact good path-law subpredicate, but does not by itself instantiate all of Definition Q.0.1a unchanged. At $\kappa=0$, the theorem supplies the purely local stopped action rate if the nominated source contract is separately met; the local density must still use the absorbing-boundary convention. For $\kappa>0$, it supplies a checked entrance correction and obstruction to the unchanged purely local form, not a redefinition or silent extension of PU's action notion. For every $\kappa$, Theorem Q.0.1b requires its own interior/closure infimum condition, and Corollary Q.0.1c requires the historywise reconstruction.
5. The theorem is a dimensionless path-law result for this registered source. An additive finite-ledger $\Gamma$ limit, physical ND–RID realization, Appendix-U/Y boundary map, structural-operation identity and charged-bath implementation retain their separate source requirements. The dimensionless entrance coefficient $\kappa$ is unrelated to the action-calibration scale $\kappa_A$. The zero-floor accessibility obstruction remains valid.

### Q.0.2 The Discrete Predictive Cost Functional

The MPU network executes cyclical predictive operations, each cycle implementing the Fundamental Predictive Loop (Definition 4):

$$\text{Predict} \to \text{Verify} \to \text{Update}$$

On the registered binary-support branch, the structural ledger value is exactly
$$
\varepsilon_0=\ln|\{0,1\}|=\ln2
$$
by Proposition 5, Definition 28, Definition J.1, and Theorem J.1. This is a log-cardinality theorem and is independent of the event distribution. If a reusable implementation additionally resets the prediction register under Theorem 31's thermodynamic hypotheses, its separate physical ledger obeys
$$
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{reset}}
=H_q(P\mid R)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{diss}}
\ge H_q(P\mid R),
\qquad
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{diss}}\ge0.
$$
A positive uniform heat floor inferred from this entropy bound requires an independent positive lower bound on $H_q(P\mid R)$; structural log-cardinality alone implies neither heat nor mechanical action.

<a id="definition-q01-dimensionless-discrete-predictive-ledger"></a>**Definition Q.0.1 (Dimensionless Discrete Predictive Ledger).** For a trajectory with finitely many registered steps, let
$$
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{disc}}:=\sum_{i=1}^N\ell_i
$$
be a declared dimensionless additive ledger. The values $\ell_i$ must be supplied by the relevant structural, stochastic-rate, or thermodynamic implementation record; they are not all identified with bath heat or total entropy production. Given an independent action scale $\kappa_A>0$, define
$$
\mathcal S_{\mathrm{disc}}:=\kappa_A\mathcal L_{\mathrm{disc}}.
$$

<a id="proposition-q01-conditional-structural-count"></a>**Proposition Q.0.1 (Conditional Structural Count).** If a branch assigns exactly one binary structural label to each of $N_{\mathrm{ops}}$ registered steps and no other contribution to this ledger, then
$$
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{disc}}=N_{\mathrm{ops}}\ln2.
$$
This is an alphabet-counting identity, not a universal physical-action, heat, or entropy-production lower bound. ∎

<a id="remark-q01a-ledger-separation"></a>**Remark Q.0.1a (Ledger Separation).** Registered reset heat obeys Theorem J.1 and depends on $H_q(P\mid R)$. A large-deviation rate functional and a mechanical action require their own bridge. The calibration $\kappa_A=\hbar$ is never inferred from $\ln2$.

### Q.0.3 The Continuum Limit via Γ-Convergence

A continuum action can be assigned to the discrete predictive ledger on a branch with an independently established $\Gamma$-limit and action-scale calibration. Theorem D.6 of Appendix D gives convergence of minima and minimizing subsequences under its liminf, recovery, equicoercivity, and properness hypotheses; Section O.7.1 of Appendix O treats the spatial sector under its additional continuum-identification hypotheses.

<a id="theorem-q01-calibrated-continuum-action-limit"></a>**Theorem Q.0.1 (Calibrated Continuum-Action Limit).** Let $\kappa_A>0$ be an independently supplied action scale. Assume the declared topology, equicoercivity, liminf inequality, and recovery sequences establish
$$
\mathcal L_h\xrightarrow{\Gamma}\mathcal L
$$
for a dimensionless discrete ledger. Then
$$
\mathcal S_h:=\kappa_A\mathcal L_h
\xrightarrow{\Gamma}
\mathcal S:=\kappa_A\mathcal L.
$$
The $\Gamma$-limit fixes the functional only relative to $\kappa_A$; it does not derive $\kappa_A=\hbar$. ∎

<a id="corollary-q01-conditional-action-entropy-calibration"></a>**Corollary Q.0.1 (Conditional Action--Entropy Calibration).** If $\kappa_A=\hbar$ is independently calibrated and a recovery sequence carries the additive history ledger, then
$$
\mathcal S[\phi]
=\hbar\lim_{h\to0}\sum_{i\in\phi_h}\varepsilon_i^{(h)}.
$$
This is a calibrated representation, not a derivation of $\hbar$. ∎

<a id="definition-q01a-predictive-large-deviation-branch"></a>**Definition Q.0.1a (Predictive Large-Deviation Branch).** A predictive large-deviation branch is a family of finite ND-RID/PCE stochastic dynamics
$$
X^\eta_t,
\qquad
\eta>0,
$$
on a compact retained state space, with small effective noise parameter $\eta$, satisfying a good path-space large-deviation principle: for every admissible path set $\mathcal A$,
$$
-\inf_{\gamma\in\mathcal A^\circ} I_{\mathrm{PU}}[\gamma]
\le
\liminf_{\eta\downarrow0}
\eta\log\mathbb P_\eta(X^\eta_{[0,T]}\in\mathcal A)
\le
\limsup_{\eta\downarrow0}
\eta\log\mathbb P_\eta(X^\eta_{[0,T]}\in\mathcal A)
\le
-\inf_{\gamma\in\overline{\mathcal A}} I_{\mathrm{PU}}[\gamma].
\tag{Q.0.1a.1}
$$
The rate functional has local form
$$
I_{\mathrm{PU}}[\gamma]
=
\int_0^T
L_{\mathrm{PU}}(\gamma(t),\dot\gamma(t))\,dt
\tag{Q.0.1a.2}
$$
for absolutely continuous retained paths and is $+\infty$ otherwise. The physical action of the same retained path is
$$
\mathcal S_{\mathrm{PU}}[\gamma]
=
\kappa_A I_{\mathrm{PU}}[\gamma],
\tag{Q.0.1a.3}
$$

<a id="theorem-q01b-predictive-large-deviation-variational-principle"></a>**Theorem Q.0.1b (Predictive Large-Deviation Variational Principle).** On a predictive large-deviation branch, the dominant rare transition from a closed retained basin $A$ to a closed retained basin $B$ over the time window $[0,T]$ is governed by the finite-time transition cost
$$
\mathcal I_{A\to B}
=
\inf_{\gamma(0)\in A,\ \gamma(T)\in B}
I_{\mathrm{PU}}[\gamma].
\tag{Q.0.1b.1}
$$
Let $\mathcal T_{A\to B}$ be a transition tube satisfying
$$
\inf_{\gamma\in\mathcal T_{A\to B}^{\circ}}I_{\mathrm{PU}}[\gamma]
=
\inf_{\gamma\in\overline{\mathcal T}_{A\to B}}I_{\mathrm{PU}}[\gamma]
=
\mathcal I_{A\to B}.
$$
Then
$$
\lim_{\eta\downarrow0}
\eta\log
\mathbb P_\eta(X^\eta_{[0,T]}\in\mathcal T_{A\to B})
=
-\mathcal I_{A\to B}.
\tag{Q.0.1b.2}
$$
On the accepted action-calibration branch,
$$
\frac{\mathcal S_{A\to B}^{\min}}{\kappa_A}
=
\mathcal I_{A\to B}.
\tag{Q.0.1b.3}
$$

*Proof.* Apply the path-space large-deviation lower bound to the tube interior and the upper bound to its closure. The three-way infimum hypothesis makes the two exponential bounds equal to $-\mathcal I_{A\to B}$, proving (Q.0.1b.2). Multiplication of the minimizing rate functional by the accepted action scale $\kappa_A$ proves (Q.0.1b.3). ∎

<a id="corollary-q01c-conditional-branch-action-reconstruction"></a>**Corollary Q.0.1c (Conditional Branch-Action Reconstruction).** Let a retained branch satisfy Definition Q.0.1a, and suppose an accepted reconstruction identifies the branch's dimensionless action $\mathcal S_{\mathrm{br}}/\kappa_A$ historywise with $I_{\mathrm{PU}}$ on the same admissible transition class and boundary data. Their global infima then agree. If a transition tube also satisfies the interior-and-closure infimum condition of Theorem Q.0.1b, its probability exponent equals that common infimum with a minus sign. In particular, an Appendix-U or Appendix-Y transition exponent belongs to this common large-deviation ledger only when both the reconstruction and the transition-tube condition are certified for its retained paths. Stationarity alone does not identify a dominant transition exponent.

*Proof.* Definition Q.0.1a supplies the path-space large-deviation principle. Historywise equality on the same admissible class gives equality of the global infima. The transition-tube hypothesis then supplies the matching lower and upper bounds in Theorem Q.0.1b. A stationary history that does not attain the global infimum is not selected by that conclusion. Without the historywise reconstruction, two action functionals need not be the same rate functional and no consolidation follows. ∎

<a id="theorem-q01d-uniformly-elliptic-nd-rid-diffusion-rate-and-reconstruction-residual"></a>**Theorem Q.0.1d (Uniformly Elliptic ND--RID Diffusion Rate and Reconstruction Residual).** Let the retained state space be the flat torus $\mathbb T^d$, let $b:\mathbb T^d\to\mathbb R^d$ be Lipschitz, and let $\sigma$ be an invertible constant matrix with $a=\sigma\sigma^T$. Fix $x_0\in\mathbb T^d$. For $\eta>0$, define the retained stochastic dynamics
$$
dX_t^\eta=b(X_t^\eta)dt+\sqrt{2\eta}\,\sigma\,dW_t,
\qquad X_0^\eta=x_0,
\qquad
\mathcal G_\eta f=b\cdot\nabla f+\eta\,a:D^2f.
\tag{Q.0.1d.1}
$$
Its nonlinear generator satisfies
$$
\eta e^{-f/\eta}\mathcal G_\eta e^{f/\eta}
=b\cdot\nabla f+(\nabla f)^Ta\nabla f+\eta\,a:D^2f
\longrightarrow
H(x,\nabla f),
\tag{Q.0.1d.2}
$$
where $H(x,p)=b(x)\cdot p+p^Tap$. The path laws obey a good large-deviation principle on $C([0,T],\mathbb T^d)$ with rate
$$
I_{\mathrm{PU}}[\gamma]
=\frac14\int_0^T
(\dot\gamma-b(\gamma))^Ta^{-1}(\dot\gamma-b(\gamma))\,dt
\tag{Q.0.1d.3}
$$
for absolutely continuous paths with $\gamma(0)=x_0$ and $+\infty$ otherwise.

For any continuous claimed branch density $L_{\mathrm{br}}$ on a compact path domain
$$
K_V:=\{(x,v):x\in\mathbb T^d, |v|\le V\},
$$
define the registered reconstruction residual
$$
r_{\mathrm{br}}(x,v)
:=L_{\mathrm{br}}(x,v)
-\frac14(v-b(x))^Ta^{-1}(v-b(x)).
\tag{Q.0.1d.4}
$$
If $\|r_{\mathrm{br}}\|_{L^\infty(K_V)}\le\epsilon$, then every admissible path with $|\dot\gamma|\le V$ satisfies
$$
\left|
\int_0^TL_{\mathrm{br}}(\gamma,\dot\gamma)dt
-I_{\mathrm{PU}}[\gamma]
\right|
\le T\epsilon,
\tag{Q.0.1d.5}
$$
and, on every nonempty fixed-boundary admissible class for which both infima are finite, the corresponding infima differ by at most $T\epsilon$. In particular, $r_{\mathrm{br}}=0$ on $K_V$ is a sufficient certificate for exact historywise reconstruction on the displayed admissible path class. No converse from equality of the fixed-$x_0$ path functionals to pointwise equality of densities is asserted.

*Proof.* Direct differentiation of $e^{f/\eta}$ gives (Q.0.1d.2). The Legendre transform of $H(x,p)$ is
$$
\sup_p\{p\cdot v-H(x,p)\}
=\frac14(v-b(x))^Ta^{-1}(v-b(x)),
$$
because the maximizer is $p=\tfrac12a^{-1}(v-b)$. To justify the path-law claim, periodically lift $b$ to $\mathbb R^d$ and choose one lift of $x_0$. The lifted drift is bounded and globally Lipschitz; the constant matrix $\sqrt2\,\sigma$ is Lipschitz and uniformly nondegenerate. Chiarini and Fischer (2014, Theorem 2 and Example 1) give a good finite-time path LDP for the Euclidean lifted SDE with speed $1/\eta$ and controlled rate $\tfrac12\int_0^T|u(t)|^2dt$ under $\dot\phi=b(\phi)+\sqrt2\,\sigma u$. Invertibility of $\sigma$ gives $u=(\sqrt2\,\sigma)^{-1}(\dot\phi-b(\phi))$ and the $1/4$ factor in (Q.0.1d.3). Projection of Euclidean paths to $C([0,T],\mathbb T^d)$ is continuous in the uniform topology, so the contraction principle gives a good torus-path LDP. Every torus path beginning at $x_0$ has a unique continuous lift beginning at the chosen Euclidean lift, making the contracted rate exactly (Q.0.1d.3), with $+\infty$ off the absolutely continuous class. Integrating the pointwise residual bound proves (Q.0.1d.5); a vanishing pointwise residual makes the two path functionals equal. Taking infima preserves the same uniform error. ∎

<a id="lemma-q01x-poisson-path-reference-in-j_1-and-uniform-interpolation"></a>**Lemma Q.0.1x (Poisson Path Reference in $J_1$ and Uniform Interpolation).** Fix $T>0$. Let $Q_n$ be the law of $Y_n(t)=N(nt)/n$, with $N$ a rate-one Poisson process. Put
$$
\ell_1(v)=v\log v-v+1\quad(v\ge0),\qquad 0\log0=0,
$$
and let $\mathcal A$ consist of nondecreasing absolutely continuous paths $\phi:[0,T]\to[0,\infty)$ with $\phi(0)=0$. Then $Q_n$ has a good speed-$n$ large-deviation principle on $D([0,T],[0,\infty))$ with the $J_1$ topology and rate
$$
J(\phi)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\int_0^T\ell_1(\dot\phi(t))\,dt,&\phi\in\mathcal A,\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}
\tag{Q.0.1x.1}
$$
Its sublevels are uniformly compact. Join $(0,0)$ and the actual post-jump vertices $(t_j,j/n)$ by straight segments, then hold the last value through $T$; the no-jump interpolation is zero. These continuous interpolations have the same good principle on $C([0,T],[0,\infty))$ in the uniform topology.

*Proof.* On a finite time partition the increments are independent, with Poisson means $n\Delta t_i$, and
$$
\frac1n\log\mathbb E\exp\!\left(n\sum_i\theta_i\Delta Y_{n,i}\right)
=\sum_i\Delta t_i(e^{\theta_i}-1).
\tag{Q.0.1x.2}
$$
Stirling's formula for lattice probabilities, the exact zero-increment probability $e^{-n\Delta t_i}$, and exponential Chernoff tails give the finite-dimensional rate $\sum_i\Delta t_i\ell_1(u_i/\Delta t_i)$, including zero increments. For nested dyadic partitions of mesh $h=T/2^r$, let $P_hY_n$ be the polygon through the sampled values. Its rate on nondecreasing mesh polygons is
$$
J_h(z)=\sum_i h\ell_1\!\left(\frac{z((i+1)h)-z(ih)}h\right).
$$
Monotonicity gives $\|Y_n-P_hY_n\|_\infty\le\max_i\Delta_iY_n$. For $\varepsilon>h$, the union and Poisson Chernoff bounds therefore give
$$
\limsup_n\frac1n\log Q_n\{\|Y_n-P_hY_n\|_\infty>\varepsilon\}
\le-\varepsilon\log(\varepsilon/h)+\varepsilon-h\longrightarrow-\infty
\quad(h\downarrow0).
\tag{Q.0.1x.3}
$$
The finite partition count has zero speed-$n$ contribution, and uniform distance bounds $J_1$ distance.

If $J_h(z_h)\le R$, superlinear growth of $\ell_1$ makes the nonnegative polygon slopes uniformly integrable and bounds their total mass. The polygons are thus uniformly bounded and equicontinuous. A uniformly convergent subsequence has an absolutely continuous limit, and the convex integral is lower semicontinuous. Explicitly,
$$
\int_0^T\ell_1(v)\,dt
=\sup_{f\in C([0,T])}\left\{\int_0^Tfv\,dt-\int_0^T(e^f-1)\,dt\right\}.
\tag{Q.0.1x.4}
$$
Conversely $P_h\phi\to\phi$ uniformly and Jensen's inequality gives $J_h(P_h\phi)\le J(\phi)$. These facts identify the limiting rate and its uniformly compact sublevels. For an open neighborhood of a finite-cost path, choose a sufficiently fine polygon in that neighborhood and make the error exponent in (Q.0.1x.3) smaller than $-J(\phi)-1$; the finite-dimensional lower bound minus the error probability gives the path lower bound. For closed $F$, use
$$
Q_n(F)\le Q_n(P_hY_n\in F^\varepsilon)
 +Q_n(d_{J_1}(Y_n,P_hY_n)>\varepsilon),
$$
where $F^\varepsilon$ is the closed metric enlargement. Bounded approximate polygon costs have a convergent subsequence whose limit lies in $F$ as $h,\varepsilon\downarrow0$; unbounded costs give exponent $-\infty$. This proves the full closed upper bound. The vertex interpolation preserves the endpoint and differs from $Y_n$ by at most $1/n$. Its distance to $P_hY_n$ is bounded by the preceding polygon error plus $1/n$. The identical approximation, compactness and recovery argument in the uniform topology proves its $C$-space assertion. $\square$

<a id="theorem-q01y-finite-real-traps-arithmetic-charges-and-complete-subsequential-classification"></a>**Theorem Q.0.1y (Finite Real Traps, Arithmetic Charges and Complete Subsequential Classification).** Fix $\kappa,T>0$, a finite set $Z=\{z_1<\cdots<z_r\}\subset[0,\infty)$, exponents $\alpha_i>0$ and a positive continuous function $g$. Assume
$$
\lambda(x)=g(x)\prod_{i=1}^r|x-z_i|^{\alpha_i}
\quad\text{is bounded on }[0,\infty).
\tag{Q.0.1y.1}
$$
The empty product is allowed. Start $X_n$ at zero and give the jump $k/n\to(k+1)/n$ rate $na_n(k/n)$, where $a_n=\lambda+e^{-\kappa n}$. These chains are nonexplosive. Define the nearest nonnegative lattice sites, with upward ties, and their charges by
$$
q_{n,i}=\frac{\lfloor nz_i+1/2\rfloor}{n},\qquad
c_{n,i}=\max\left\{0,-\frac1n\log a_n(q_{n,i})\right\}\in[0,\kappa].
\tag{Q.0.1y.2}
$$
The sites are distinct for all sufficiently large $n$. For $a>0,v\ge0$, write $\ell(v,a)=v\log(v/a)-v+a$, with $\ell(0,a)=a$, $\ell(0,0)=0$, $\ell(v,0)=+\infty$ for $v>0$, and $\ell(v,a)=+\infty$ for $v<0$. On $\mathcal A$ of Lemma Q.0.1x put
$$
S(\phi)=\int_0^T\ell(\dot\phi(t),\lambda(\phi(t)))\,dt.
$$
Along every infinite subsequence on which $c_n\to c$, the laws of $X_n$ have a good speed-$n$ $J_1$ path principle with rate
$$
I_c(\phi)=\begin{cases}
S(\phi)+\displaystyle\sum_i c_i\mathbf1_{\{\phi(T)>z_i\}},&\phi\in\mathcal A,\\
+\infty,&\text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\tag{Q.0.1y.3}
$$
Sublevels are uniformly compact. The endpoint-preserving vertex interpolation has the same principle in uniform $C$ space. An infinite subsequence has a speed-$n$ path principle with a lower semicontinuous rate **if and only if** its charge vectors converge. Consequently the full sequence has a principle exactly when $c_n$ converges, and its subsequential rates are exactly $I_c$ for the cluster vectors $c$ of $c_n$. Distinct vectors give distinct rates.

For $b>0$ with $b\notin Z$ and $\tau_{n,b}=\inf\{t:X_n(t)\ge b\}$, every convergent-charge subsequence also satisfies
$$
\lim-\frac1n\log\mathbb P(\tau_{n,b}\le T)
=\sum_{z_i<b}c_i+\sup_{\eta\ge0}\{B_b(\eta)-\eta T\},\qquad
B_b(\eta)=\int_0^b\log\!\left(1+\frac\eta{\lambda(x)}\right)dx,
\quad B_b(0)=0.
\tag{Q.0.1y.4}
$$

*Proof: uniform moving-prefix estimate.* Set $C(y)=\int_0^y\log\lambda(x)\,dx$. It is finite and continuous on bounded intervals. For every finite $K$,
$$
\sup_{0\le j\le\lfloor nK\rfloor}
\left|\frac1n\sum_{k<j}\log a_n(k/n)-C(j/n)
 +\sum_i c_{n,i}\mathbf1_{\{j/n>q_{n,i}\}}\right|\longrightarrow0.
\tag{Q.0.1y.5}
$$
To prove this, work on a compact interval containing the endpoint cutoff and the needed zero neighborhoods. Remove the one nearest site for each zero. Every retained site is at distance at least $1/(2n)$ from every zero, including an unchosen tied site. With $A_0=\sum_i\alpha_i$ and the compact minimum $g_{\min}>0$,
$$
\lambda(k/n)\ge g_{\min}(2n)^{-A_0},\qquad
0\le\log a_n(k/n)-\log\lambda(k/n)
\le g_{\min}^{-1}(2n)^{A_0}e^{-\kappa n}.
$$
Thus the floor contributes a uniformly vanishing normalized prefix error on retained sites. The continuous term $\log g$ has uniform partial Riemann convergence; removing finitely many samples costs $O(1/n)$. For $\log|x-z_i|$, the cell attached to the removed site lies within $3/(2n)$ of $z_i$ and has absolute integral $O(\log n/n)$. The finitely many adjacent cells have that same bound, since their retained sample distances are between $1/(2n)$ and $O(1/n)$. On remaining cells monotone integral comparisons telescope on each side of the zero, again giving $O(\log n/n)$ uniformly over every prefix. Removing sites chosen for other zeros costs $O(1/n)$ because distinct zeros are separated. Truncated neighborhoods obey the same estimate. Each removed sample present in a prefix contributes exactly $-d_{n,i}$, where $d_{n,i}=-n^{-1}\log a_n(q_{n,i})$. Its difference from $c_{n,i}$ is at most $n^{-1}\log\max\{1,\|\lambda\|_\infty+1\}$, proving (Q.0.1y.5). No Diophantine lower bound on a removed distance was used. Its indicator is at the moving $q_{n,i}$: arrival at that site does not yet include its outgoing rate.

*Proof: exact likelihood and lower bound.* On the closed space $\mathcal E$ of nonnegative nondecreasing càdlàg paths starting at zero, let
$$
\Phi(x)=C(x(T))-\int_0^T[\lambda(x(t))-1]dt.
$$
It is $J_1$-continuous and bounded on endpoint cutoffs: endpoints converge, path values converge at continuity times, and bounded continuous $\lambda$ permits dominated convergence. Relative to the Poisson law in Lemma Q.0.1x, a history with $j=nx(T)$ has the normalized likelihood, including final survival,
$$
\frac1n\log\frac{dP_n}{dQ_n}(x)
=\frac1n\sum_{k<j}\log a_n(k/n)
 -\int_0^T[\lambda(x(t))+e^{-\kappa n}-1]dt
=\Phi(x)-\sum_i c_{n,i}\mathbf1_{\{x(T)>q_{n,i}\}}+o_K(1)
\tag{Q.0.1y.6}
$$
uniformly when $x(T)\le K$. A positive endpoint away from $Z$ has a neighborhood on which its charge converges uniformly to the constant strict-terminal sum. Continuity of $\Phi$ and the reference lower bound give the lower bound there. The zero path uses its exact no-jump probability $\exp[-n(\lambda(0)+e^{-\kappa n})T]$, with exponent $T\lambda(0)$. At a positive terminal zero, use $a\phi$ with $a\uparrow1$, its endpoint below that zero and above all smaller zeros. It has exactly the required strict-terminal charge, and
$$
J(a\phi)=a\int_0^T\dot\phi\log\dot\phi\,dt
 +a\log(a)\phi(T)-a\phi(T)+T\longrightarrow J(\phi),
\tag{Q.0.1y.7}
$$
while $\Phi(a\phi)\to\Phi(\phi)$. This supplies recovery even when the path waits at its terminal zero.

*Proof: full closed upper bound.* For fixed $\varepsilon>0$ and large $n$, $q_{n,i}<z_i+\varepsilon$, so positivity of the charges gives
$$
\sum_i c_{n,i}\mathbf1_{\{x(T)>q_{n,i}\}}
\ge P_\varepsilon(x(T))-\sum_i|c_{n,i}-c_i|,
\qquad P_\varepsilon(y)=\sum_i c_i\mathbf1_{\{y>z_i+\varepsilon\}}.
\tag{Q.0.1y.8}
$$
The shifted penalty is lower semicontinuous. For closed $F\subset\mathcal E$, divide endpoint space into its finitely many constant-penalty regions and the bounded range of $\Phi$ into arbitrarily narrow closed strips. Take the closure of each piece and apply the reference closed upper bound. The penalty can only decrease on the closure boundary, giving
$$
\limsup_n\frac1n\log P_n(F\cap\{X_n(T)\le K\})
\le-\inf_{\substack{\phi\in F\\\phi(T)\le K}}
 [J(\phi)-\Phi(\phi)+P_\varepsilon(\phi(T))].
\tag{Q.0.1y.9}
$$
The infima converge as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ to the infimum with $P(y)=\sum_i c_i\mathbf1_{\{y>z_i\}}$. Indeed bounded approximate costs imply bounded $J$ on the cutoff; reference compactness gives a limiting path in $F$. Every strictly crossed limiting zero is eventually crossed with the $\varepsilon$ margin. Lower semicontinuity of $J$ and continuity of $\Phi$ give the required liminf. The reverse comparison follows from $P_\varepsilon\le P$; the same compactness argument excludes bounded approximate costs when the limiting infimum is infinite. With $M=\|\lambda\|_\infty+1$, Poisson domination gives, for $K>MT$,
$$
\limsup_n\frac1n\log P_n(X_n(T)>K)
\le-K\log\frac K{MT}+K-MT\longrightarrow-\infty.
\tag{Q.0.1y.10}
$$
This removes the cutoff. Reference exponential tightness transfers on cutoffs by the upper likelihood bound, and the same endpoint tail handles their complement.

*Proof: action, goodness and topology.* For $\phi\in\mathcal A$, bounded truncation and local absolute integrability of $\log\lambda$ give the monotone change of variables
$$
\int_0^T\dot\phi(t)\log\lambda(\phi(t))dt=C(\phi(T)).
\tag{Q.0.1y.11}
$$
The derivative vanishes almost everywhere on every fixed zero-level set. Thus $J-\Phi=S$ as extended integrals; $\Phi$ is finite at a finite endpoint, so there is no undefined cancellation. Finite $J$ and finite $S$ are equivalent on $\mathcal A$. Put $M_0=\max(1,\|\lambda\|_\infty)$. The estimates
$$
\Phi(\phi)\le\phi(T)\log M_0+T,\qquad
J(\phi)\ge\phi(T)\log\frac{\phi(T)}T-\phi(T)+T
$$
force bounded endpoints, then bounded $J$, on $I_c$ sublevels. Lower semicontinuity and reference compactness prove uniform compactness. The vertex interpolation in Lemma Q.0.1x preserves the terminal count and is within $1/n$ of the step path. On cutoffs its $\Phi$ changes by $o(1)$ while its charges agree exactly; the uniform reference argument therefore proves the stated $C$-space principle.

*Proof: complete subsequence criterion.* The charge vectors lie in the compact cube $[0,\kappa]^r$. Distinct vectors $c,d$ have a first differing coordinate $j$. Take a positive $b$ after $z_j$ and before the next zero, or beyond the last zero. The linear path $bt/T$ has finite action and
$$
I_c(bt/T)-I_d(bt/T)=\sum_{i\le j}(c_i-d_i)=c_j-d_j\ne0.
$$
If charge vectors on a subsequence do not converge, two different cluster vectors give two further subsequences with these distinct good rates. A hypothetical path principle on the original subsequence would be inherited by both; uniqueness of a lower semicontinuous rate on the metric path space contradicts the difference. Convergence suffices by the preceding proof. The empty-vector case is automatic.

*Proof: direct hitting law.* Put $L_n=\lceil nb\rceil$. Independent exponential holding times give, for $\eta>0$,
$$
Z_n(\eta)=\mathbb E e^{-n\eta\tau_{n,b}}
=\prod_{k<L_n}\frac{a_n(k/n)}{a_n(k/n)+\eta},\qquad
-\frac1n\log Z_n(\eta)\longrightarrow\sum_{z_i<b}c_i+B_b(\eta).
\tag{Q.0.1y.12}
$$
Here $b\notin Z$ fixes every prefix indicator eventually; the denominator has ordinary continuous Riemann convergence. Local logarithmic integrability makes $B_b$ finite and continuous at zero. Its derivative $t_b(\eta)=\int_0^b(\lambda+\eta)^{-1}dx$ decreases continuously and strictly from $t_0\in(0,\infty]$ to zero. When $T<t_0$, the unique maximizer solves $t_b(\eta_T)=T$; for $T\ge t_0$ the supremum is zero. Chernoff gives one exponent bound. For the other, change the holding rates to $n(a_n+\eta)$. Their sum has mean tending to $t_b(\eta)$, variance at most $L_n/(n^2\eta^2)=O(1/n)$, and original-to-tilted density $Z_n(\eta)e^{n\eta\tau}$. For $T<t_0$ choose $t_b(\eta)=s<T$, localize near $s$, then take $s\uparrow T$. For $T\ge t_0<\infty$, every positive tilt has mean strictly below $T$; take $n$ first, then $\eta\downarrow0$, using $B_b(\eta)\to0$ and $\eta t_b(\eta)\le\eta t_0\to0$. This includes $T=t_0$ and proves (Q.0.1y.4) directly. $\square$

<a id="corollary-q01y1-algebraic-admission-parity-and-an-irrational-counterexample"></a>**Corollary Q.0.1y.1 (Algebraic Admission, Parity and an Irrational Counterexample).** For rational $z=p/q$ in lowest terms, indices divisible by $q$ have charge $\kappa$; on nonadmitted indices $|k/n-z|\ge1/(qn)$, so the charge tends to zero. For an algebraic irrational zero with integer minimal polynomial $P$ of degree $d$, $n^dP(k/n)$ is a nonzero integer. On a compact interval, the mean-value bound $|P(k/n)|\le C|k/n-z|$ therefore gives a polynomial lower separation and charge tending to zero. The finite congruence classes modulo the least common multiple of rational denominators give the exact admitted-zero rates. The same argument works with polynomial lattice separation in place of algebraicity.

In particular, take $\lambda(x)=x^2(x-1/2)^2$ for $x\le1$ and $\lambda(x)=1/4$ for $x>1$. The even and odd subsequences have respectively
$$
I_{\mathrm{even}}=S+\kappa\mathbf1_{\{\phi(T)>0\}}
 +\kappa\mathbf1_{\{\phi(T)>1/2\}},\qquad
I_{\mathrm{odd}}=S+\kappa\mathbf1_{\{\phi(T)>0\}}.
\tag{Q.0.1y.13}
$$
For $b\in(1/2,1)$ their hitting exponents are $2\kappa+J_b(T)$ and $\kappa+J_b(T)$. Here $t_0=\infty$, so the positive optimizer exists uniquely for every $T>0$ and $J_b(T)>0$. Nonzero grid rates on $[0,1]$ are at least $1/(64n^2)$, and the prefix error is $O(\log n/n)+O(n^2e^{-\kappa n})$. Arrival at $1/2$ on an even grid does not incur the second charge; departure does.

For genuinely different irrational charges, set $a_1=1$, $a_{j+1}=10^{2a_j}$, $Q_j=10^{a_j}$ and
$$
z=\sum_{j\ge1}10^{-a_j},\qquad p_j=Q_j\sum_{i\le j}10^{-a_i}\in\mathbb Z.
$$
Then $0<z<1/2$ and
$$
10^{-Q_j^2}\le z-p_j/Q_j\le2\,10^{-Q_j^2}.
\tag{Q.0.1y.14}
$$
The infinitely many nonzero decimal digits with unbounded intervening gaps make $z$ irrational; the bound beats every fixed rational-power approximation. Take $\lambda=x^2(x-z)^2$ on $[0,1]$, continued constantly as $(1-z)^2$ after $1$. It satisfies (Q.0.1y.1), with $g=1$ up to $1$ and $g=(1-z)^2/[x^2(x-z)^2]$ thereafter. On $n=Q_j$ the nearest interior rate is at most $C10^{-2Q_j^2}$, negligible against the floor, so its charge tends to $\kappa$. On $n=Q_j+1$,
$$
nz=p_j+z+Q_j(z-p_j/Q_j)=p_j+z+o(1),
\qquad n|z-p_j/n|\longrightarrow z.
$$
Its nearest rate is bounded above and below by positive multiples of $n^{-2}$, so that charge tends to zero. The initial charge remains $\kappa$. Thus the two subsequences have rates $S+\kappa\mathbf1_{\{\phi(T)>0\}}+\kappa\mathbf1_{\{\phi(T)>z\}}$ and $S+\kappa\mathbf1_{\{\phi(T)>0\}}$, and their hitting exponents beyond $z$ differ by $\kappa$. Both have the same limiting Hamiltonian $H(x,p)=\lambda(x)(e^p-1)$, since the floor vanishes in the smooth-test nonlinear generator limit. They have no common full-sequence path principle by Theorem Q.0.1y. This construction concerns asymptotic laws, with no finite-size numerical premise. $\square$

<a id="theorem-q01z-finite-logarithmic-defect-measures-and-non-power-traps"></a>**Theorem Q.0.1z (Finite Logarithmic Defect Measures and Non-Power Traps).** Let $\lambda:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be bounded and continuous with a finite zero set $Z=\{z_1<\cdots<z_r\}$, possibly empty, and locally integrable $|\log\lambda|$. Define $a_n$, $X_n$, $\mathcal A$ and $S$ as in Theorem Q.0.1y, without assuming its power factorization. Fix $M\ge\max(1,\|\lambda\|_\infty+1)$ and suppose, on an infinite subsequence, that the positive measures
$$
\mu_n=\frac1n\sum_{k\ge0}\log\frac M{a_n(k/n)}\,\delta_{k/n}
\quad\text{converge vaguely to a locally finite }\mu.
\tag{Q.0.1z.1}
$$
It suffices to have weak convergence of restrictions to one $[0,L]$ with $L>\max Z$ and $\lambda(L)>0$; for empty $Z$, any $L>0$ suffices. A bound on $\mu_n([0,L])$ gives a further weakly convergent subsequence, but such a bound is an additional hypothesis. Necessarily, with $f=\log(M/\lambda)$ off $Z$,
$$
\mu=f(x)\,dx+\sum_i c_i\delta_{z_i},\qquad 0\le c_i<\infty.
\tag{Q.0.1z.2}
$$
These atoms are independent of $M$ and may exceed $\kappa$. Along the given subsequence, the good $J_1$ path rate, its uniform-interpolation version and the direct hitting law for $b>0$, $b\notin Z$, are exactly (Q.0.1y.3) and (Q.0.1y.4) with these $c_i$.

*Proof: defect and moving cumulative endpoints.* Away from $Z$, the log weights converge locally uniformly to $f$, so the limit equals $f\,dx$ there. For $R>0$, the cap $f_R=\min(f,R)$, extended by $R$ at each zero, is continuous and
$$
\log\frac M{a_n}\ge f_R-\log\!\left(1+\frac{e^{-\kappa n}e^R}{M}\right).
\tag{Q.0.1z.3}
$$
This follows by factoring out $\lambda$ when $\lambda\ge Me^{-R}$ and comparing with $Me^{-R}+e^{-\kappa n}$ otherwise. Test against nonnegative compactly supported continuous functions and pass through Riemann and vague convergence, then $R\uparrow\infty$. Thus $\mu\ge f\,dx$. Its difference is a nonnegative measure on finite $Z$, giving (Q.0.1z.2). Changing $M$ adds the same constant multiple of Lebesgue measure to the limit and its density, leaving the atoms fixed. Positivity outside the cutoff gives ordinary local Riemann convergence and no boundary atom there.

Set $F(y)=\int_0^y f(x)dx$ and $C(y)=y\log M-F(y)$. At a lattice endpoint $y=j/n$,
$$
\frac1n\sum_{k<j}\log a_n(k/n)=y\log M-\mu_n([0,y)).
\tag{Q.0.1z.4}
$$
This half-open interval counts departures. On a compact interval of positive endpoints avoiding $Z$, monotonicity and a finite continuity mesh make the cumulative convergence uniform:
$$
\mu_n([0,y))\longrightarrow F(y)+\sum_{z_i<y}c_i.
\tag{Q.0.1z.5}
$$
In the relative half-line, $0$ is not a boundary obstruction for $[0,y]$ at a positive continuity endpoint; an origin atom is retained. At arbitrary endpoints, the needed substitute is the one-sided bound: for fixed $K,\varepsilon>0$ there is $e_n\to0$ such that
$$
\mu_n([0,y))\ge F(y)+\sum_i c_i\mathbf1_{\{y>z_i+\varepsilon\}}
 -\omega_F(\varepsilon)-e_n\quad(0\le y\le K),
\tag{Q.0.1z.6}
$$
where $\omega_F$ is the modulus of continuity on $[0,K]$. Choose finitely many continuity points, with sufficiently small gaps, so that for each $y\ge\varepsilon$ one lies in $[y-\varepsilon,y-\varepsilon/2]$. Refine near zero if necessary. Then $[0,s]\subset[0,y)$, all shifted atoms lie below $s$, and $F(s)\ge F(y)-\omega_F(\varepsilon)$. Weak convergence on this finite mesh and positivity prove the bound. For $y<\varepsilon$, no shifted atom is active and positivity with $F(y)\le\omega_F(\varepsilon)$ suffices.

*Proof: path and hitting estimates.* Lemma Q.0.1x supplies the reference. Use the same $\Phi$ and exact normalized likelihood in (Q.0.1y.6), with the exact prefix (Q.0.1z.4). Uniform convergence (Q.0.1z.5) gives its local lower bound at positive endpoints outside $Z$. The zero path again has exponent $T\lambda(0)$ even if its origin atom is larger than $\kappa$. Scaling $a\phi$ from below, with (Q.0.1y.7), recovers positive terminal zeros and their strict-terminal charge. By (Q.0.1z.6), on the endpoint cutoff the log likelihood is at most
$$
\Phi(x)-\sum_i c_i\mathbf1_{\{x(T)>z_i+\varepsilon\}}
 +\omega_F(\varepsilon)+o(1).
\tag{Q.0.1z.7}
$$
The finite endpoint-region and closed-$\Phi$-strip argument in the proof of (Q.0.1y.9) gives, for closed $H\subset\mathcal E$,
$$
\limsup_n\frac1n\log P_n(H\cap\{X_n(T)\le K\})
\le\omega_F(\varepsilon)-\inf_{\substack{\phi\in H\\\phi(T)\le K}}
 \left[J(\phi)-\Phi(\phi)+\sum_i c_i\mathbf1_{\{\phi(T)>z_i+\varepsilon\}}\right].
$$
Bounded approximate costs imply bounded $J$, hence a compact limiting path. Every strictly crossed zero is eventually charged; letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ gives the strict-terminal infimum. The endpoint tail (Q.0.1y.10) removes $K$ and transfers exponential tightness. Local absolute log-integrability gives (Q.0.1y.11) by truncation, so $J-\Phi=S$ without infinite cancellation. The same Jensen bounds prove goodness and uniform compactness. Exact endpoint preservation and a cutoff $o(1)$ change of $\Phi$ give the interpolation assertion.

For hitting, the exact product (Q.0.1y.12) still applies. Equation (Q.0.1z.5) at $\lceil nb\rceil/n\to b$ identifies its numerator, and the positive-tilt denominator has ordinary Riemann convergence. Thus its limit is $\sum_{z_i<b}c_i+B_b(\eta)$. The tilted mean, variance and density in the proof of Theorem Q.0.1y apply unchanged. Taking positive tilts first also handles $T=t_0<\infty$. This proves the direct exponent, without a hitting-map contraction. $\square$

<a id="example-q01z1-a-finite-defect-larger-than-the-exponential-floor"></a>**Example Q.0.1z.1 (A Finite Defect Larger Than the Exponential Floor).** Fix $n_1\ge10$ and $n_{j+1}=2^{n_j^2}$. Put $a_j=1/n_j$, $w_j=n_j^{-4}$, $H_j=2\kappa n_j$, $\psi(u)=\max(1-|u|,0)$, and
$$
B(x)=\sum_{j\ge1}H_j\psi\!\left(\frac{x-a_j}{w_j}\right),\qquad
\lambda(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x=0,\\x^2e^{-B(x)},&0<x\le1,\\1,&x>1.\end{cases}
\tag{Q.0.1z.8}
$$
The supports are disjoint, contained in $(0,1)$ and locally finite away from zero. Since $0\le\lambda(x)\le x^2$, the rate is bounded and continuous, with sole zero $0$, and
$$
\int_0^1|\log\lambda(x)|dx=2+2\kappa\sum_j n_j^{-3}<\infty.
\tag{Q.0.1z.9}
$$
Outside the supports $\lambda=x^2$, forcing exponent $2$ in any putative positive continuous power factorization at zero; at their centers $\lambda(a_j)/a_j^2=e^{-2\kappa n_j}\to0$, contradicting such a factor.

Its log measures converge to $f\,dx+2\kappa\delta_0$ on $n=n_j$, and to $f\,dx+\kappa\delta_0$ on $n=n_j+1$. To verify this, compare with the base rate $\lambda_0=x^2$ on $[0,1]$, continued as $1$. Removing the exact zero sample and using monotone log Riemann sums gives its limit $f_0\,dx+\kappa\delta_0$; nonzero samples have rate at least $n^{-2}$ and negligible floor error. On notch supports the log difference is
$$
D_n(x)=\log\frac{x^2+e^{-\kappa n}}{x^2e^{-B(x)}+e^{-\kappa n}},\qquad0\le D_n\le B.
$$
For $j=1$ the previous-notch family is empty. For $j\ge2$ and previous notches $i<j$, $x\ge1/(2n_{j-1})$ and $B\le2\kappa n_{j-1}$, giving
$$
|D_n-B|\le4n_{j-1}^2e^{2\kappa n_{j-1}-\kappa n}\longrightarrow0
$$
on both schedules. The variation of the previous-notch sum is $2\sum_{i<j}H_i$; its prefix Riemann discrepancy is at most that variation divided by $n$, tending to zero. Its integrals converge in $L^1$ to $B$, so it contributes $B\,dx$ without an atom. At $n=n_j$ the current support contains exactly $a_j$, and
$$
\frac1{n_j}D_{n_j}(a_j)
=\frac1{n_j}\log\frac{n_j^{-2}+e^{-\kappa n_j}}
 {n_j^{-2}e^{-2\kappa n_j}+e^{-\kappa n_j}}\longrightarrow\kappa.
$$
This site tends to zero. At $n=n_j+1$, its closest positive site is separated from $a_j$ by $1/[n_j(n_j+1)]>w_j$, so the current notch is missed. All future supports lie below $1/(2n_j)$ and exclude zero, hence contain no sampled site on either schedule; their continuum integrals tend to zero. These previous/current/future comparisons also hold against compactly supported continuous tests and prove the two measure limits. Theorem Q.0.1z therefore gives distinct good path rates, differing by $\kappa$ on every nonzero finite-action path, and hitting exponents to any $b>0$ differing by $\kappa$. Uniqueness rules out a common full-sequence path principle. The atom $2\kappa$ comes from two outgoing sites collapsing onto one continuum zero, and exceeds the single-site charge in Theorem Q.0.1y. $\square$

Theorems Q.0.1y–z concern finite-zero one-direction pure-birth sources. Their departure charges and logarithmic-measure hypothesis identify the microscopic information needed in addition to a limiting local Hamiltonian. Theorem Q.0.1r treats its separate fixed-sector marked-history accessibility class; neither theorem identifies an arbitrary multidirectional physical source, an infinite barrier or a fixed-endpoint obstacle recovery.

<a id="theorem-q01e-degenerate-torus-diffusions-and-jump-generator-hamiltonians"></a>**Theorem Q.0.1e (Degenerate Torus Diffusions and Jump-Generator Hamiltonians).**

1. *Degenerate constant noise.* Keep the torus $\mathbb T^d$, the Lipschitz drift $b$ and the starting point $x_0$ of Theorem Q.0.1d, let $\sigma\in\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ be an arbitrary constant matrix, possibly of rank below $d$, let $W$ be an $m$-dimensional Brownian motion, and put $a:=\sigma\sigma^T$ with Moore--Penrose inverse $a^+$. The laws of
   $$
   dX_t^\eta=b(X_t^\eta)dt+\sqrt{2\eta}\,\sigma\,dW_t,
   \qquad X_0^\eta=x_0,
   \tag{Q.0.1e.1}
   $$
   satisfy a good large-deviation principle on $C([0,T],\mathbb T^d)$ with speed $1/\eta$ and rate
   $$
   I_{\mathrm{PU}}[\gamma]
   =\frac14\int_0^T
   (\dot\gamma-b(\gamma))^Ta^+(\dot\gamma-b(\gamma))\,dt
   \tag{Q.0.1e.2}
   $$
   when $\gamma$ is absolutely continuous, $\gamma(0)=x_0$ and $\dot\gamma(t)-b(\gamma(t))\in\operatorname{ran}a$ for almost every $t$, and $I_{\mathrm{PU}}[\gamma]=+\infty$ otherwise. The nonlinear-generator identity (Q.0.1d.2) holds unchanged, and the Legendre transform of $H(x,p)=b(x)\cdot p+p^Tap$ equals $\frac14(v-b(x))^Ta^+(v-b(x))$ where $v-b(x)\in\operatorname{ran}a$ and $+\infty$ elsewhere. Along every finite-cost path the velocity component in $\ker a$ equals that of the drift, and (Q.0.1d.3) is the invertible case $a^+=a^{-1}$.
2. *Jump generators.* Let $Z\subset\mathbb R^d\setminus\{0\}$ be finite and let $\lambda_\zeta:\mathbb T^d\to[0,\infty)$, $\zeta\in Z$, be continuous. For
   $$
   \mathcal G_\eta^Jf(x)
   :=\frac1\eta\sum_{\zeta\in Z}\lambda_\zeta(x)\bigl[f(x+\eta\zeta)-f(x)\bigr]
   \tag{Q.0.1e.3}
   $$
   and every $f\in C^1(\mathbb T^d)$, uniformly in $x$,
   $$
   \eta e^{-f/\eta}\mathcal G_\eta^Je^{f/\eta}
   \longrightarrow H_J(x,\nabla f),
   \qquad
   H_J(x,p):=\sum_{\zeta\in Z}\lambda_\zeta(x)\bigl(e^{p\cdot\zeta}-1\bigr).
   \tag{Q.0.1e.4}
   $$
   The limiting Hamiltonian $H_J(x,\cdot)$ determines the rates $(\lambda_\zeta(x))_{\zeta\in Z}$ uniquely. Its Legendre transform $L_J(x,v):=\sup_p\{p\cdot v-H_J(x,p)\}$ is convex and nonnegative, vanishes exactly at the mean drift $v=\sum_\zeta\lambda_\zeta(x)\zeta$, and is finite exactly on the convex cone generated by $Z_x:=\{\zeta:\lambda_\zeta(x)>0\}$, where
   $$
   L_J(x,v)\le\sum_{\zeta\in Z_x}\lambda_\zeta(x)\,\theta\!\left(\frac{\mu_\zeta}{\lambda_\zeta(x)}\right),
   \qquad
   \theta(r):=r\ln r-r+1,\quad\theta(0):=1,
   \tag{Q.0.1e.5}
   $$
   for every decomposition $v=\sum_{\zeta\in Z_x}\mu_\zeta\zeta$ with $\mu_\zeta\ge0$.
3. *Second-order generator data do not fix the rate.* For $d=1$, $Z=\{1,-1\}$ and constant $\lambda_{\pm1}=\lambda>0$, the generator (Q.0.1e.3) satisfies $\mathcal G_\eta^Jf=\eta\lambda f''+O(\eta^3)$ for smooth $f$, which has the drift and diffusion coefficients of (Q.0.1d.1) with $b=0$ and $a=\lambda$. The lifted endpoint laws on $\mathbb R$ started at $0$ satisfy large-deviation principles with speed $1/\eta$ and rates $TL_J(x/T)$ for the jump process and $TL_D(x/T)$ for the diffusion, where
   $$
   L_J(v)=v\operatorname{arsinh}\frac{v}{2\lambda}-\sqrt{v^2+4\lambda^2}+2\lambda
   <L_D(v)=\frac{v^2}{4\lambda}
   \qquad(v\ne0).
   \tag{Q.0.1e.6}
   $$
   Hence the two branches assign different exponents to $\{X_T^\eta\ge x\}$ for every $x>0$.

*Proof.* Item 1. Periodically lift $b$ to a bounded globally Lipschitz field $\tilde b$ with constant $L_b$, lift $x_0$ to $\tilde x_0$, and let $\Psi(w)$ be the unique solution of $\phi(t)=\tilde x_0+\int_0^t\tilde b(\phi(s))\,ds+\sigma w(t)$ for $w\in C_0([0,T];\mathbb R^m)$. Gronwall's inequality gives $\|\Psi(w_1)-\Psi(w_2)\|_\infty\le\|\sigma\|e^{L_bT}\|w_1-w_2\|_\infty$, and the lifted solution of (Q.0.1e.1) is $\Psi(\sqrt{2\eta}W)$ pathwise. Schilder's theorem (Dembo and Zeitouni 1998, Theorem 5.2.3) gives the laws of $\sqrt{2\eta}W$ a good principle with speed $1/(2\eta)$ and rate $\frac12\int_0^T|\dot w|^2dt$ on absolutely continuous $w$ with square-integrable derivative, and $+\infty$ otherwise; at speed $1/\eta$ the rate is $\frac14\int_0^T|\dot w|^2dt$. The contraction principle (Dembo and Zeitouni 1998, Theorem 4.2.1) for the continuous map $\pi\circ\Psi$, with $\pi$ the torus projection, gives a good principle with rate $\inf\{\frac14\int_0^T|\dot w|^2dt:\pi\Psi(w)=\gamma\}$. A torus path from $x_0$ has a unique continuous lift $\tilde\gamma$ from $\tilde x_0$, and $\pi\Psi(w)=\gamma$ exactly when $\sigma w(t)=\tilde\gamma(t)-\tilde x_0-\int_0^t\tilde b(\tilde\gamma)\,ds$. If this holds for a finite-energy $w$, then $\tilde\gamma$ is absolutely continuous and $r:=\dot{\tilde\gamma}-\tilde b(\tilde\gamma)=\sigma\dot w\in\operatorname{ran}\sigma=\operatorname{ran}a$ almost everywhere; the least-norm solution of $\sigma u=r$ is $\sigma^+r$ and $(\sigma^+)^T\sigma^+=(\sigma\sigma^T)^+=a^+$, so $|\dot w|^2\ge r^Ta^+r$. Conversely, if $r\in\operatorname{ran}a$ almost everywhere with $\int_0^Tr^Ta^+r\,dt<\infty$, then $\dot w:=\sigma^+r$ is square integrable and $\sigma\sigma^+r=r$, because $\sigma\sigma^+$ is the orthogonal projection onto $\operatorname{ran}\sigma$, so the bound is attained. If $\tilde\gamma$ is not absolutely continuous or $r\notin\operatorname{ran}a$ on a set of positive measure, no finite-energy $w$ exists. This proves (Q.0.1e.2). The computation of (Q.0.1d.2) does not use invertibility. If $v-b\notin\operatorname{ran}a$, its nonzero component $q\in\ker a=(\operatorname{ran}a)^\perp$ gives $p\cdot(v-b)-p^Tap=t|q|^2\to\infty$ along $p=tq$; if $v-b=r\in\operatorname{ran}a$, the concave quadratic is maximized at $p=\frac12a^+r$, where $aa^+r=r$ and $a^+aa^+=a^+$ give the value $\frac14r^Ta^+r$.

Item 2. By the mean-value theorem $(f(x+\eta\zeta)-f(x))/\eta=\zeta\cdot\nabla f(x+\vartheta\eta\zeta)$ for some $\vartheta\in(0,1)$, which converges uniformly to $\zeta\cdot\nabla f(x)$ by uniform continuity of $\nabla f$ on the compact torus; the rates are bounded and the exponential is uniformly continuous on bounded sets, which proves (Q.0.1e.4). Choose $q$ with the numbers $c_\zeta:=q\cdot\zeta$ nonzero and pairwise distinct; then $H_J(x,tq)=\sum_\zeta\lambda_\zeta(x)e^{tc_\zeta}-\sum_\zeta\lambda_\zeta(x)$, and linear independence of $1$ and the exponentials $e^{tc_\zeta}$ determines every $\lambda_\zeta(x)$. The Legendre transform is a supremum of affine functions and hence convex, and $p=0$ gives $L_J\ge0$. Since $H_J(x,\cdot)$ is convex, differentiable and vanishes at $0$, $L_J(x,v)=0$ exactly when $v$ is its gradient at $0$, namely $\sum_\zeta\lambda_\zeta(x)\zeta$. If $v=\sum_{\zeta\in Z_x}\mu_\zeta\zeta$ with $\mu_\zeta\ge0$, the termwise bound $\mu_\zeta s-\lambda_\zeta(e^s-1)\le\lambda_\zeta\theta(\mu_\zeta/\lambda_\zeta)$ for all real $s$ gives (Q.0.1e.5). If $v$ lies outside the finitely generated, hence closed, cone, Farkas' lemma gives $q$ with $q\cdot\zeta\le0$ on $Z_x$ and $q\cdot v>0$, and $p=tq$ gives $L_J(x,v)\ge tq\cdot v\to\infty$.

Item 3. Taylor expansion of $f(x\pm\eta)$ to fourth order gives the generator expansion. The lifted jump endpoint is $\eta(N_+-N_-)$ with independent Poisson counts of mean $\lambda T/\eta$, so $\eta\ln\mathbb E\exp(pX_T^\eta/\eta)=\lambda T(e^p+e^{-p}-2)$ for every $\eta$; the diffusion endpoint is centered Gaussian with variance $2\eta\lambda T$, giving $\lambda Tp^2$. Both limits are finite and differentiable, so the Gärtner--Ellis theorem (Dembo and Zeitouni 1998, Theorem 2.3.6) gives the two principles with the Legendre transforms $TL_J(x/T)$ and $TL_D(x/T)$ of $TH_J$ and $TH_D$, where $H_J(p)=2\lambda(\cosh p-1)$ and $H_D(p)=\lambda p^2$. Solving $v=2\lambda\sinh p$ gives $p=\operatorname{arsinh}(v/(2\lambda))$ and the closed form of $L_J$. Since $\cosh p-1>p^2/2$ for $p\ne0$, $H_J>H_D$ off $0$; for $v\ne0$ the maximizer $p_v$ of $pv-H_J(p)$ is nonzero, so $L_J(v)=p_vv-H_J(p_v)<p_vv-H_D(p_v)\le L_D(v)$. Both rates are continuous and strictly increasing on $[0,\infty)$, so the infima over $(x,\infty)$ and $[x,\infty)$ coincide and the half-line exponent is $-TL(x/T)$ in each case. ∎

<a id="theorem-q01g-exact-boundary-entrance-cost-for-vanishing-floor-birth-sources"></a>**Theorem Q.0.1g (Exact Boundary-Entrance Cost for Vanishing-Floor Birth Sources).** Let $a>0$ and let $\lambda:[0,a]\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous and nondecreasing, with
$$
\lambda(0)=0,\qquad \lambda(x)>0\quad(0<x\le a),\qquad
\int_0^a|\log\lambda(x)|\,dx<\infty,\qquad
\int_0^a\frac{dx}{\lambda(x)}=\infty.
\tag{Q.0.1g.1}
$$
Let $m_n\ge1$ be integers with $m_n/n\le a$ and $m_n/n\to a$, and let $\delta_n>0$ tend to zero with $-n^{-1}\log\delta_n\to\kappa\in[0,\infty]$. Start the finite pure-birth chain $X_n$ at zero, give its jump from $k/n$ to $(k+1)/n$ rate $n[\lambda(k/n)+\delta_n]$ for $0\le k<m_n$, and absorb it at $m_n/n$. Write $\tau_n$ for its absorption time. Then, for every fixed $T>0$,
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}-\frac1n\log\mathbb P(\tau_n\le T)
=\kappa+J_\lambda(T),\qquad
J_\lambda(T):=\sup_{\theta\ge0}\left\{A_\lambda(\theta)-\theta T\right\},
\quad
A_\lambda(\theta):=\int_0^a\log\left(1+\frac\theta{\lambda(x)}\right)dx.
\tag{Q.0.1g.2}
$$
Here $A_\lambda(0):=0$ and the right side is $+\infty$ when $\kappa=\infty$. There is a unique maximizer $\theta_T>0$, characterized by
$$
\int_0^a\frac{dx}{\lambda(x)+\theta_T}=T,
\qquad J_\lambda(T)=A_\lambda(\theta_T)-\theta_T T>0.
\tag{Q.0.1g.3}
$$
No monotonicity or prescribed rate of decay of the sequence $\delta_n$ is required. In particular the theorem includes $m_n=\lfloor an\rfloor$, after discarding any initial zero values.

The local Hamiltonian $H(x,p)=\lambda(x)(e^p-1)$ has conjugate
$$
L(x,v)=v\log\frac v{\lambda(x)}-v+\lambda(x)\quad(x>0,v\ge0),
\qquad L(x,v)=+\infty\quad(x>0,v<0),
\tag{Q.0.1g.4}
$$
with $0\log0=0$, and $L(0,0)=0$, $L(0,v)=+\infty$ for $v\ne0$. Among absolutely continuous paths in $[0,a]$ from zero to $a$ in time $T$, the minimum of $\int_0^T L(x,\dot x)dt$ is exactly $J_\lambda(T)$. Its unique minimizer is the inverse of the strictly increasing function
$$
F_{\theta_T}(u):=\int_0^u\frac{dx}{\lambda(x)+\theta_T},
\qquad x(t)=F_{\theta_T}^{-1}(t),\qquad
\dot x=\lambda(x)+\theta_T.
\tag{Q.0.1g.5}
$$
Thus the transition exponent has the additional initial entrance cost $\kappa$, which is absent from the limiting local Hamiltonian and its integrated conjugate. This is an exact hitting-probability theorem, not a full path-space large-deviation principle.

*Proof.* Put $\lambda_{n,k}:=\lambda(k/n)+\delta_n$. The holding times $E_{n,k}$ are independent exponentials of rates $n\lambda_{n,k}$ and $\tau_n=\sum_{k=0}^{m_n-1}E_{n,k}$. Consequently, for $\theta>0$,
$$
Z_n(\theta):=\mathbb E e^{-n\theta\tau_n}
=\prod_{k=0}^{m_n-1}\frac{\lambda_{n,k}}{\lambda_{n,k}+\theta},
\qquad A_n(\theta):=-\frac1n\log Z_n(\theta)
=\frac1n\sum_{k=0}^{m_n-1}\log\left(1+\frac\theta{\lambda_{n,k}}\right).
\tag{Q.0.1g.6}
$$
The zero-state term is $n^{-1}\log(1+\theta/\delta_n)=-n^{-1}\log\delta_n+n^{-1}\log(\delta_n+\theta)\to\kappa$.

For the remaining terms put $f_\delta(x):=\log(1+\theta/(\lambda(x)+\delta))$. The function $f_0$ is decreasing and integrable: where $\lambda\le1$, it is bounded by $\log(1+\theta)+|\log\lambda|$, and where $\lambda\ge1$, by $\log(1+\theta)$. On $[\varepsilon,a]$, $f_{\delta_n}\to f_0$ uniformly. Near zero, comparison of right endpoints with preceding cells gives
$$
\frac1n\sum_{1\le k\le n\varepsilon} f_{\delta_n}(k/n)
\le\frac1n\sum_{1\le k\le n\varepsilon} f_0(k/n)
\le\int_0^\varepsilon f_0(x)dx\longrightarrow0
\quad(\varepsilon\downarrow0).
\tag{Q.0.1g.7}
$$
Ordinary Riemann convergence away from zero, including the moving endpoint $m_n/n\to a$, therefore proves $A_n(\theta)\to\kappa+A_\lambda(\theta)$ when $\kappa<\infty$.

For $\theta>0$, bounded differentiation on compact positive $\theta$ intervals gives $A_\lambda'(\theta)=t(\theta):=\int_0^a(\lambda(x)+\theta)^{-1}dx$. This is continuous and strictly decreasing, tending to infinity at zero by (Q.0.1g.1) and monotone convergence, and to zero at infinity since $t(\theta)\le a/\theta$. Also $A_\lambda(\theta)\to0$ as $\theta\downarrow0$, by domination by the integrable integrand at $\theta=1$. Thus $A_\lambda(\theta)-\theta T$ has the unique positive maximizer (Q.0.1g.3), and its maximum is positive.

On $\{\tau_n\le T\}$, $e^{-n\theta\tau_n}\ge e^{-n\theta T}$, so
$$
\mathbb P(\tau_n\le T)\le e^{-n[A_n(\theta)-\theta T]}.
\tag{Q.0.1g.8}
$$
For finite $\kappa$, taking a liminf of the negative normalized logarithm and optimizing over $\theta>0$ gives the lower bound $\kappa+J_\lambda(T)$ on that exponent.

For the reverse bound, define $Q_{n,\theta}$ by making the independent holding times exponential with rates $n(\lambda_{n,k}+\theta)$. Direct comparison of their densities gives
$$
\frac{d\mathbb P}{dQ_{n,\theta}}
=Z_n(\theta)e^{n\theta\tau_n},\qquad
\mu_n(\theta):=\mathbb E_Q\tau_n
=\frac1n\sum_{k=0}^{m_n-1}\frac1{\lambda_{n,k}+\theta}\longrightarrow t(\theta),
\qquad
v_n(\theta):=\operatorname{Var}_Q\tau_n
=\frac1{n^2}\sum_{k=0}^{m_n-1}\frac1{(\lambda_{n,k}+\theta)^2}
\le\frac{m_n}{n^2\theta^2}\longrightarrow0.
\tag{Q.0.1g.9}
$$
The mean convergence is a bounded Riemann sum. Fix $s\in(0,T)$, choose $\theta_s$ with $t(\theta_s)=s$, and fix $0<\varepsilon<\min\{s,T-s\}$. Chebyshev's inequality gives $Q_{n,\theta_s}(s-\varepsilon\le\tau_n\le s+\varepsilon)\to1$. Restricting the density integral to this event yields
$$
\mathbb P(\tau_n\le T)
\ge e^{-nA_n(\theta_s)+n\theta_s(s-\varepsilon)}
Q_{n,\theta_s}(s-\varepsilon\le\tau_n\le s+\varepsilon).
\tag{Q.0.1g.10}
$$
First take $n\to\infty$ with $s,\varepsilon$ fixed, then $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, then $s\uparrow T$. Continuity of the inverse of $t$ gives the upper exponent bound $\kappa+J_\lambda(T)$. This proves (Q.0.1g.2) for finite $\kappa$ without exchanging the noise-floor and small-jump limits. If $\kappa=\infty$, the first holding time alone gives $\mathbb P(\tau_n\le T)\le1-e^{-n\delta_nT}\le n\delta_nT$, proving divergence of the exponent. Although $Z_n(0)=1$, the positive-$\theta$ limit of $-n^{-1}\log Z_n$ includes $\kappa$; no differentiability theorem at $\theta=0$ is being invoked.

For the action assertion, finite action forces $\dot x\ge0$ almost everywhere. At fixed $\theta=\theta_T$, let $p_M(x):=\min\{M,\log(1+\theta/\lambda(x))\}$, with $p_M(0):=M$. This is bounded and continuous and $H(x,p_M(x))\le\theta$. Fenchel's inequality and the chain rule for its continuously differentiable primitive give
$$
\int_0^T L(x,\dot x)dt\ge\int_0^a p_M(u)du-\theta T.
\tag{Q.0.1g.11}
$$
Monotone convergence proves the lower bound $J_\lambda(T)$. The inverse in (Q.0.1g.5) exists and is $C^1$ because $F_\theta'=1/(\lambda+\theta)>0$. For its path, Fenchel equality holds for $t>0$, and substitution $dt=dx/(\lambda+\theta)$ gives
$$
\int_0^T L(x,\dot x)dt
=\int_0^a\left[\log\left(1+\frac\theta{\lambda(x)}\right)-\frac\theta{\lambda(x)+\theta}\right]dx
=A_\lambda(\theta)-\theta T.
\tag{Q.0.1g.12}
$$
This is finite by log-integrability; an infinite density at the single initial time does not affect the integral.

For uniqueness, a nondecreasing continuous path has an initial zero interval $[0,w]$ and is positive afterward. On $[w+\varepsilon,T]$ put $p(x)=\log(1+\theta/\lambda(x))$ and $D=L-p\dot x+\theta\ge0$. This gap vanishes exactly when $\dot x=\lambda(x)+\theta$. The bounded-primitive chain rule on that interval, followed by $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, gives
$$
I(x)=J_\lambda(T)+\theta w+\int_{(w,T)}D\,dt.
\tag{Q.0.1g.13}
$$
Here the initial zero segment has zero action, and monotone convergence handles $D$. Equality forces $w=0$ and $D=0$ almost everywhere. Differentiating $F_\theta(x(t))$ then proves (Q.0.1g.5) uniquely. This separated strictly positive scalar equation needs only the stated continuity, not local Lipschitz regularity. Finally $J_\lambda'(s)=-\theta_s<0$, so permitting first arrival at any $s\le T$ has minimum $J_\lambda(T)$. The post-arrival cost for the stopped source is zero; the interior density $L(a,0)=\lambda(a)$ must not be charged after absorption. ∎

<a id="example-q01g1-quadratic-boundary-rate-and-closed-form-cost"></a>**Example Q.0.1g.1 (Quadratic Boundary Rate and Closed-Form Cost).** For $\lambda(x)=x^2$, all hypotheses of (Q.0.1g.1) hold. The conclusion also holds for arbitrary positive integers $m_n$ with $m_n/n\to a$, without the restriction $m_n/n\le a$, using the same quadratic rate beyond $a$: the moving-endpoint Riemann argument has only a vanishing bounded terminal contribution. Direct integration gives
$$
A_a(\theta)=a\log\left(1+\frac\theta{a^2}\right)+2\sqrt\theta\arctan\frac a{\sqrt\theta},
\qquad
T=\frac1{\sqrt\theta}\arctan\frac a{\sqrt\theta},
\qquad
J_a(T)=a\log\left(1+\frac\theta{a^2}\right)+\theta T.
\tag{Q.0.1g.14}
$$
The optimizer is $x(t)=\sqrt\theta\tan(\sqrt\theta t)$, with no pole on $[0,T]$ by the endpoint equation. At $a=T=1$, $\theta\simeq0.7401738843949671$ and $J_a(T)\simeq1.2941589261887052$. The entrance contribution remains exactly $\kappa$ for every allowed schedule.

The source can be embedded before stopping in a smooth periodic nominated generator: choose a circle coordinate chart containing a neighborhood of $[0,a]$, a smooth nonnegative periodic $\lambda$ equal to $x^2$ there, and rates $n[\lambda(x)+\delta_n]$ for jumps of size $1/n$. For all sufficiently large $n$, stopping at the $m_n$-th jump gives precisely the finite chain above. Smoothness is asserted for the unstopped source, not for its absorbing boundary. ∎

<a id="example-q01g2-the-same-sine-squared-source-as-the-accessibility-obstruction"></a>**Example Q.0.1g.2 (The Same Sine-Squared Source as the Accessibility Obstruction).** For $\lambda(x)=\sin^2x$ on $[0,a]$ with $0<a<\pi/2$, the rate is increasing, $\log\lambda(x)=2\log x+O(x^2)$ is integrable, and $\int_0^a\csc^2x\,dx=\infty$. Thus Theorem Q.0.1g applies to the smooth periodic one-direction birth source with jump size $1/n$ and rate $n[\sin^2x+\delta_n]$, stopped at $\lfloor an\rfloor/n$. Substitution $u=\tan x$ makes its exact time equation
$$
T=\frac1{\sqrt{\theta(1+\theta)}}
\arctan\left(\sqrt{\frac{1+\theta}{\theta}}\tan a\right).
\tag{Q.0.1g.15}
$$
The exponent is $\kappa+J_{\sin^2}(T)$ with $J$ given by (Q.0.1g.2). At exactly zero floor the source is absorbed at zero and its hitting probability is identically zero, while the displayed formal action minimum is finite. Thus the new theorem quantitatively extends, rather than removes, the initial-accessibility obstruction. ∎

<a id="corollary-q01g3-order-of-limits-and-explicit-finite-size-certificates"></a>**Corollary Q.0.1g.3 (Order of Limits and Explicit Finite-Size Certificates).** For a fixed positive floor $\delta$, let
$$
J_{\lambda,\delta}(T):=\sup_{\theta\ge0}
\left\{\int_0^a\log\left(1+\frac\theta{\lambda(x)+\delta}\right)dx-\theta T\right\}.
\tag{Q.0.1g.16}
$$
Then $\lim_n-n^{-1}\log\mathbb P_\delta(\tau_n\le T)=J_{\lambda,\delta}(T)$ and $J_{\lambda,\delta}(T)\uparrow J_\lambda(T)$ as $\delta\downarrow0$. Taking $n\to\infty$ before removing the floor therefore yields $J_\lambda(T)$; joint schedules can instead yield $\kappa+J_\lambda(T)$. Removing the floor first at fixed $n$ gives zero hitting probability and infinite exponent.

For every finite $n$ and $\theta>0$, the quantities in (Q.0.1g.6) and (Q.0.1g.9) give the exact bounds
$$
A_n(\theta)-\theta T\le-\frac1n\log\mathbb P(\tau_n\le T)
\le A_n(\theta)-\theta(\mu_n(\theta)-\varepsilon)
-\frac1n\log\left(1-\frac{v_n(\theta)}{\varepsilon^2}\right),
\tag{Q.0.1g.17}
$$
where the upper bound requires $0<\varepsilon<\mu_n(\theta)$, $\mu_n(\theta)+\varepsilon\le T$, and $v_n(\theta)<\varepsilon^2$.

*Proof.* With fixed $\delta$, the product/tilt proof above applies using the nonsingular rate $\lambda+\delta$. If $T<\int_0^a(\lambda+\delta)^{-1}dx$, the optimizer is positive and the same proof applies directly. If $T$ exceeds that travel time, un-tilted mean/variance concentration makes the exponent zero. At equality, tilt to means strictly below $T$ and send the tilt parameter to zero; its bound tends to zero, which is also the trivial lower bound on a negative probability logarithm. As $\delta\downarrow0$ the integrands increase, giving $J_{\lambda,\delta}\le J_\lambda$ and monotonicity; evaluation at the fixed optimizer $\theta_T$ and dominated convergence give the matching limiting lower bound. At fixed $n$, $\mathbb P_\delta(\tau_n\le T)\le n\delta T\to0$. Finally (Q.0.1g.8) proves the left inequality of (Q.0.1g.17); restricting the exact tilted density ratio to $|\tau_n-\mu_n|\le\varepsilon$ and applying Chebyshev proves the right one. ∎

All costs in this theorem are dimensionless. The entrance coefficient $\kappa$ is distinct from the independently calibrated action scale $\kappa_A$. The result proves this exact stopped hitting exponent and formal local-action minimum. It does not itself prove a full path-space large-deviation principle, a historywise action reconstruction, an ND–RID physical source or an Appendix-U/Y map. Uses in Definition Q.0.1a, Theorem Q.0.1b or Corollary Q.0.1c retain their stated path-law, transition-tube and reconstruction hypotheses. No identification with reset heat, mechanical action or $\hbar$ follows.

<a id="remark-q01c1-conditional-reset-power-viability-inequality"></a>**Remark Q.0.1c.1 (Conditional Reset-Power Viability Inequality).** Choose a finite window of duration $\tau>0$ and one bath temperature $T>0$. For each of finitely many reset classes $j$, prescribe a deterministic count $n_j\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ of completed resets and require the complete Definition 28 contract on every admitted reset history, finite mean heats, and an additive conditional-expectation ledger. For reset $l$ in class $j$, put
$$
h_{jl}:=\mathbb E\!\left[H_{q_{jl}}(P_{jl}\mid R_{jl})\right],
\qquad
r_j:=\frac{n_j}{\tau},
\qquad
H_j:=\frac1{n_j}\sum_{l=1}^{n_j}h_{jl}
$$
when $n_j>0$, and set $H_j=0$ when $n_j=0$. The expectation averages the actual conditional reset laws over their registered histories. Define
$$
\nu:=\sum_jr_j,\qquad
\overline{H_q(P\mid R)}:=\nu^{-1}\sum_jr_jH_j
$$
when $\nu>0$, and define the normalized mean bath-heat rate by
$$
\dot{\mathcal L}_{\mathrm{reset}}
:=\frac1{k_BT\tau}\sum_j\sum_{l=1}^{n_j}\mathbb E Q_{\mathrm{bath},jl}.
$$
All entropies are in nats. Sequential conditional Landauer gives
$$
\dot{\mathcal L}_{\mathrm{reset}}\ge\sum_jr_jH_j
=\nu\,\overline{H_q(P\mid R)}
$$
for $\nu>0$. For the input-power comparison, independently require a complete, nonoverlapping mean-energy balance on the same window,
$$
E_{\mathrm{in}}
=\sum_{j,l}\mathbb E Q_{\mathrm{bath},jl}
+E_{\mathrm{loss}}+\Delta E_{\mathrm{store}},
\qquad E_{\mathrm{loss}}\ge0,\quad\Delta E_{\mathrm{store}}\ge0,
$$
where $E_{\mathrm{loss}}$ counts the other exports and $\Delta E_{\mathrm{store}}$ is the retained energy change, excluding energy already assigned to the bath or other exports. Set $R_{\mathrm{in}}:=E_{\mathrm{in}}/(k_BT\tau)$ and $R_{\mathrm{loss}}:=E_{\mathrm{loss}}/(k_BT\tau)$. These rates have units of inverse time, and
$$
R_{\mathrm{in}}\ge\dot{\mathcal L}_{\mathrm{reset}}+R_{\mathrm{loss}}.
$$
This comparison uses the additional no-drawdown energy premise; it does not follow from conditional Landauer alone.

*Proof.* Conditional Landauer and the tower property give $\mathbb E Q_{\mathrm{bath},jl}\ge k_BT h_{jl}$. Finite summation and division by $k_BT\tau>0$ prove the reset-rate bound. Dividing the separate energy balance by the same factor and using $\Delta E_{\mathrm{store}}\ge0$ proves the input-rate inequality. If $\nu=0$, every $n_j=0$ and the completed-reset sum is empty, so $\dot{\mathcal L}_{\mathrm{reset}}=0$; apparatus overhead still belongs to its own energy entry. Any limiting rate statement additionally requires convergence of these window averages and preservation of their heat and energy balances. ∎

The specialization $\nu\ln2$ requires every registered binary record to be conditionally uniform on its admitted histories. The structural value $\varepsilon_0=\ln2$ alone determines no maintenance power.

This is a necessary finite-resource viability condition for code-maintaining aggregates.

### Q.0.4 Action-Scale Calibration

<a id="convention-q02x-action-scale-calibration"></a>**Convention Q.0.2x (Action-Scale Calibration).** The continuum action carries an independent positive scale $\kappa_A$ with units of action per dimensionless ledger unit. The identification $\kappa_A=\hbar$ is a calibration condition against quantum phase data, not a consequence of counting or dimensional analysis.

<a id="corollary-q02-dimensional-role"></a>**Corollary Q.0.2 (Dimensional Role).** On a calibrated branch,
$$
\mathcal S=\kappa_A\mathcal L.
$$
If comparison with experiment selects $\kappa_A=\hbar$, then the familiar phase factor $e^{i\mathcal S/\hbar}$ is recovered. ∎

<a id="corollary-q02b-conditional-per-cycle-action"></a>**Corollary Q.0.2b (Conditional Per-Cycle Action).** If one registered structural cycle contributes $\ln2$ to $\mathcal L$, then its calibrated action contribution is $\kappa_A\ln2$. This is not a universal minimum physical action. ∎

<a id="remark-q01-status"></a>**Remark Q.0.1 (Status).** Neither $\ln2$ nor the variational limit fixes the empirical value of $\kappa_A$.

<a id="theorem-q02e-local-coherent-phase-calibration-and-geometric-phase-separation"></a>**Theorem Q.0.2e (Local Coherent-Phase Calibration and Geometric-Phase Separation).** On the independent reference carrier $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ref}}=\operatorname{span}\{|0\rangle,|1\rangle\}$, implement, for every registered control value $\ell\in\mathbb R$,
$$
U_{\mathrm{ref}}(\ell)
=|0\rangle\!\langle0|+e^{i\ell}|1\rangle\!\langle1|.
\tag{Q.0.2e.1}
$$
Prepare $|+_x\rangle=(|0\rangle+|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ and use the normalized projective readouts in the $x$ and $y$ bases, where $|+_y\rangle=(|0\rangle+i|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$. Their positive-outcome probabilities are
$$
p_x^+(\ell)=\frac{1+\cos\ell}{2},
\qquad
p_y^+(\ell)=\frac{1+\sin\ell}{2}.
\tag{Q.0.2e.1a}
$$
Thus the pair of normalized responses identifies $e^{i\ell}$ exactly and fixes the reference phase without using the PU ledger.

Suppose the same control family has a registered dimensionless PU ledger $\mathcal L(\ell)=\ell$ and candidate action $\mathcal S(\ell)=\kappa_A\ell$ with $\kappa_A>0$, and that its quantum action rule represents the relative phase by
$$
U_A(\ell)
=|0\rangle\!\langle0|
+e^{i\kappa_A\ell/\hbar}|1\rangle\!\langle1|.
\tag{Q.0.2e.2}
$$
Equality of the two coherent channels on any open interval about zero holds exactly when
$$
\kappa_A=\hbar.
\tag{Q.0.2e.3}
$$

In particular, after (Q.0.2e.3), the registered event value $\ell=N\ln2$ has relative phase $e^{iN\ln2}$ for every $N\in\mathbb Z$. For a registered closed scalar transport branch at leading adiabatic and semiclassical order, assume that the phase factors are $e^{i\mathcal S/\hbar}$, $e^{i\gamma_{\mathrm B}}$, $e^{-i\pi\mu/2}$ and $e^{i\Theta_{\partial}}$, with a common gauge and endpoint convention and each contribution counted once. Their product has leading transport phase
$$
\Theta_{\mathrm{sc}}
=\frac{\mathcal S}{\hbar}
+\gamma_{\mathrm B}
-\frac\pi2\mu
+\Theta_{\partial}
\pmod{2\pi},
\tag{Q.0.2e.4}
$$
where $\gamma_{\mathrm B}\in\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)$ is the Berry phase of a smooth isolated nondegenerate eigenline, with holonomy $e^{i\gamma_{\mathrm B}}$, $\mu\in\mathbb Z$ is the oriented Maslov index in the $e^{i\mathcal S/\hbar}$ convention, and $\Theta_{\partial}$ is the registered scalar boundary/spin phase on the same branch. On variations of $\ell$ that preserve the eigenline loop and connection, caustic class and boundary/spin data, the last three leading terms are constant. This does not establish constancy or vanishing of omitted finite-speed or higher semiclassical phase corrections; any claim about the exact transported phase requires a separate bound or a certificate that those corrections vanish. The exact calibration (Q.0.2e.3) follows from the independent coherent-channel equality, without using this approximation.

*Proof.* Direct Born-rule evaluation gives (Q.0.2e.1a); its two centered probabilities are $(\cos\ell,\sin\ell)$ and therefore recover the reference phase modulo $2\pi$. Both unitaries fix $|0\rangle$ and hence cannot differ by a nontrivial global phase. Equality gives $e^{i\ell}=e^{i(\kappa_A/\hbar)\ell}$ on an open interval. Differentiation at $\ell=0$ gives $1=\kappa_A/\hbar$. Conversely, (Q.0.2e.3) makes (Q.0.2e.1)--(Q.0.2e.2) identical. On the stated adiabatic eigenline branch, the Berry holonomy is $e^{i\gamma_{\mathrm B}}$ (Berry 1984; Simon 1983). For the scalar semiclassical convention, passage through a caustic of oriented multiplicity $m$ multiplies the leading amplitude by $e^{-i\pi m/2}$; reversing the crossing reverses $m$ (Keller 1958, equations 14–15). Multiplication of the registered scalar factors yields (Q.0.2e.4) modulo $2\pi$. Preserving their defining data makes the three nonaction terms locally constant at that order. This scalar product identity supplies no estimate for the omitted phase corrections. ∎

<a id="proposition-q02f-finite-calibration-records-that-identify-kappa_a"></a>**Proposition Q.0.2f (Finite Calibration Records That Identify $\kappa_A$).** In the setting of Theorem Q.0.2e, let $\Lambda\subset\mathbb R$ be a registered set of control values, let $\langle\Lambda\rangle$ be the additive subgroup of $\mathbb R$ that it generates, and put
$$
K(\Lambda)
:=\{\kappa_A>0:\ U_A(\ell)=U_{\mathrm{ref}}(\ell)\ \text{for every }\ell\in\Lambda\}.
\tag{Q.0.2f.1}
$$
By (Q.0.2e.1a), $\kappa_A\in K(\Lambda)$ exactly when the two channels have equal normalized $x/y$ response pairs at every $\ell\in\Lambda$. Then:

1. If $\langle\Lambda\rangle=\{0\}$, then $K(\Lambda)=(0,\infty)$.
2. If $\langle\Lambda\rangle=\ell_0\mathbb Z$ with $\ell_0>0$, then $K(\Lambda)=\{\hbar(1+2\pi m/\ell_0):m\in\mathbb Z,\ m>-\ell_0/(2\pi)\}$, an infinite discrete set.
3. If $\langle\Lambda\rangle$ is not cyclic, then $K(\Lambda)=\{\hbar\}$. For finite $\Lambda$ this holds exactly when $\Lambda$ contains two nonzero values with irrational ratio.

Consequently no single control value identifies $\kappa_A$, while any two values with irrational ratio do. On the event lattice $\Lambda=\{N\ln2:N\ge1\}$, item 2 gives
$$
K(\Lambda)=\{\hbar(1+m\beta_L):m\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\},
\qquad
\beta_L=\frac{2\pi}{\ln2},
\tag{Q.0.2f.2}
$$
with $\beta_L$ the reciprocal Landauer angle of Section Q.0.7.1, so event-count responses leave infinitely many action scales. Adjoining the single control value $2\pi$ gives the two-value record $\{\ln2,2\pi\}$, for which $K=\{\hbar\}$.

*Proof.* Both unitaries fix $|0\rangle$, so they agree at $\ell$ exactly when $e^{i\ell}=e^{i\kappa_A\ell/\hbar}$, that is, $c\ell\in2\pi\mathbb Z$ with $c:=\kappa_A/\hbar-1$. The set $\{\ell:c\ell\in2\pi\mathbb Z\}$ is an additive subgroup of $\mathbb R$, so the condition on $\Lambda$ is equivalent to the condition on $\langle\Lambda\rangle$. Item 1 is immediate. In item 2 the condition reads $c\ell_0\in2\pi\mathbb Z$, and positivity of $\kappa_A$ is $1+2\pi m/\ell_0>0$. Every additive subgroup of $\mathbb R$ is cyclic or dense; in item 3, $c\ne0$ would make $c\langle\Lambda\rangle$ a dense subset of the discrete set $2\pi\mathbb Z$, so $c=0$. A finitely generated subgroup whose nonzero generators have pairwise rational ratios lies in $\ell_1\mathbb Q$ for one generator $\ell_1$ and is cyclic, while two values with irrational ratio cannot lie in one cyclic group. For the event lattice $\langle\Lambda\rangle=\ln2\,\mathbb Z$, and $m>-\ln2/(2\pi)$ means $m\ge0$. Finally $2\pi/\ln2$ is irrational by Lemma Q.0.7b. ∎

<a id="theorem-q02g"></a>

<a id="theorem-q02g-canonical-free-source-action-likelihood-phase-bridge"></a>**Theorem Q.0.2g (Canonical Free-Source Action–Likelihood–Phase Bridge).** The registered finite-source family below gives a channel-identification bridge beyond the finite logarithmic module of Theorem M.6.6c. Its complete normalized Gaussian comparison laws, quadratic momentum dynamics and paid positive finite inverse-free echo implement the full field/probe/reference phase channel with calibrated relative action equal to $\hbar$ times the raw ledger. It supplies the canonical normal limit, shear and Gaussian geometry, exact endpoint/Gouy and typed Berry/Maslov records, independently normalized observables and complete finite source/control/invoice/error contracts. The mass, duration, Gaussian widths and reference-arm energy are calibrations chosen for this source, and $\hbar$ enters as an independently calibrated unit.

*Proof and complete source record.*

#### 1. Source contract and finite canonical family

Fix independently calibrated mass $m>0$, action unit $\hbar>0$ and positive duration $t$. Put

$$
a=t/(2m\hbar),\quad p_{*} = \sqrt{\ln(2)/a}.
$$

These quantities carry physical units of mass, momentum, action and time. At source grade $n\ge 0$ let

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\delta_n=2^{-n},\quad J_n=2^{2n},\quad h_n=p_{*} \delta_n, \\
&p_j=j h_n,\quad -J_n\le j\le J_n, \\
&d_n=2J_n+1,\quad b_n=\lceil\log_2 d_n\rceil,\quad D_n=2^{b_n}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The declared physical momentum register has the $d_{n}$ active levels $|j\rangle$, embedded in a $D_n$-level binary appliance. Its remaining padding levels are supplied, retained and priced; all matrices below are completed on them. Admitted input states are arbitrary normal states on the active field and two-state probe, including arbitrary external-reference entanglement. A finite $|j\rangle$ is an ordinary normalized finite state.

Install the self-adjoint momentum observable

$$
\begin{aligned}
P_n&= \sum_j p_j |j\rangle\langle j|, \\
