## 2. Common Fourier embedding and the required free tail

Identify each finite lattice Hilbert space isometrically with the trigonometric polynomials on the side-$\ell$ torus whose labels lie in the usual centered Brillouin cube $K_{M}$. Let $I_{M}$ denote this interpolation isometry and extend embedded finite operators by zero on the orthogonal complement. A fixed smooth sampled vector $J_M\psi$ becomes $I_MJ_M\psi$, which converges to $\psi$ in $L^2$. This is the ordinary Fourier alias sum: sufficiently many decaying Fourier coefficients make its tail and aliases summable by Cauchy-Schwarz. It is uniform for families with uniformly bounded sufficiently high Sobolev norms, as supplied by the earlier consistency proof. It is NOT an isometry claim for sampling arbitrary $L^2$ functions.

At the flat background, $B_{M}$ is diagonal in momentum labels. Its two nonzero singular values per charge/label are $a/s_Q(p)$, where $p=(2\pi k-QLe_0)/M$ modulo $2\pi$ and $s_{Q}$ is the overlap singular value. Let $k$ be the centered integer representative. The torus metric inequality gives

$$
M |p_{\mathrm{principal}}| \ge 2\pi |k|-|QL|.
$$

Since $\max|QL|=9\ln 2<2\pi$, for $|k|\ge 2$ the right-hand side is at least $\pi|k|$. If the Wilson scalar $W<0$, the established bound $s\ge|p_{\mathrm{principal}}|/(4\pi)$ gives $a/s\le 4\ell/|k|$. If $W\ge 0$, $s\ge\sqrt{2}$, hence $a/s\le\ell/(\sqrt{2}M)\le\ell/(\sqrt{2}|k|)$, because $|k|\le M$ in the four-dimensional centered cube. For the finitely many $|k|<2$, the established $s_M\ge d_*/(4\pi M)$ gives $a/s\le 4\pi\ell/d_*$.

Therefore one cutoff-independent constant, for example

$$
C_B=\max(6\ell,12\pi\ell/d_*),
$$

satisfies $a/s_Q(p)\le C_B/(1+|k|)$ for every $M\ge3$ and every label. The continuum inverse has the same bound. This is the explicit ultraviolet estimate missing from strong fixed-test convergence.

For the Fourier projection $P_{N}$ onto $|k|\le N$, $N\ge4$, shell counting gives

$$
\lVert B_M(I-P_N)\rVert_5^5,\lVert B(I-P_N)\rVert_5^5\le 6400C_B^5/N.
$$

Here the ten flavours and two chiral singular values are included. One conservative count uses max-norm shells, with $(2m+1)^4-(2m-1)^4=64m^3+16m\le 80m^3$; $|k|>N$ implies $m>N/2$ and the remaining sum is bounded by a multiple of $\sum m^{-2}$. The displayed constant deliberately over-reserves that bound.

On each fixed finite set of momenta, the explicit free symbol converges to $K(0)^{-1}P_+$, including its full matrix orientation. Hence

$$
\lVert B_M-B\rVert_5\le\epsilon_B(M,N)+2(6400C_B^5/N)^{1/5},
$$

where $\epsilon_B(M,N)=\lVert(B_M-B)P_N\rVert_5$ is a finite, explicitly evaluable Fourier-symbol sum and tends to zero for each fixed $N$. This is genuine $S_5$ convergence with a two-cutoff error bound.

For later use, the same symbol estimate gives, for $j=1,2,3,4$,

$$
\lVert B_M\rVert_j^j\le 20C_B^j[1+80\sum_{m=1}^{\lceil M/2\rceil}m^3/(1+m)^j].
$$

Thus these quantities are $O(M^3)$, $O(M^2)$, $O(M)$, $O(1+\log M)$, respectively. They are not uniformly trace-class or uniformly $S_4$. Those divergences must be carried in the nonlinear analysis.

## 3. S5 convergence of the actual relative operator

The common-disk sign estimate gives $\lVert U_M(z)\rVert\le C_U$ uniformly in $M$ and $|z|\le\rho$; one can take $C_U=144F\rho/[\ell(1-0.00144)]$. The continuum $\lVert zV\rVert$ is bounded by the same conservative constant.

For each fixed smooth spinor $\psi$, the accepted complex consistency theorem applied to $D_M(z)$ and $D_M(0)$ gives

$$
I_M U_M(z)J_M \psi \to zV \psi
$$

in $L^2$, uniformly on $|z|\le\rho$. Sampling/interpolation errors are controlled by the uniformly smooth coefficient family. For a fixed trigonometric polynomial, $J_{M}$ and the Fourier coordinates agree once $M$ is large. Density and the uniform operator bound then give strong convergence of embedded $U_M(z)$ to $zV$, uniformly on each fixed vector over this disk. No ultraviolet norm convergence is claimed.

Now split the product using a fixed finite Fourier projection $P_{N}$:

$$
\lVert U_MB_M-zVB\rVert_5 \le C_U\lVert B_M-B\rVert_5 +\lVert(U_M-zV)BP_N\rVert_5 +2C_U\lVert B(I-P_N)\rVert_5.
$$

The middle term tends uniformly to zero because $BP_{N}$ has finite rank and smooth Fourier columns. For a quantitative bound it is at most its Hilbert-Schmidt norm, obtained by summing the finitely many squared consistency/interpolation errors on those columns; call this explicitly bounded finite quantity $\epsilon_U(M,N)$. It is $O(a)$ for fixed $N$ with constants from the already established stencil estimates and Fourier alias bounds. The other two terms are controlled by section 2.

Thus, after compression to H_+,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sup_{|z|\le \rho} \lVert R_M(z)-zT_+\rVert_5 \\
&\le C_U \epsilon_B(M,N)+\epsilon_U(M,N)+4 C_U(6400 C_B^5/N)^{1/5} \\
&=:\delta_5(M,N).
\end{aligned}
$$

First choose N to control the displayed tail, then M to control the finite-symbol/stencil quantities. This proves uniform S5 convergence constructively. All norms here are on the common Fourier Hilbert spaces; a changing-dimensional matrix norm is not silently equated to an infinite-dimensional one.

## 4. The regularized trace-log part converges

The actual relative-log lemma gives $\lVert R_M(z)\rVert<1/4$ on the disk. The same smallness holds for $zT_+$ by its continuum inverse/multiplication bound. The $S_5$ norms are uniformly bounded by section 3. Define

$$

Its series converges normally and starts at degree at least five because $R_M(0)=0$. Let $B_5$ bound the $S_5$ norms of $R_{M}$ and $zT_+$, and let $\kappa<1$ bound their operator norms. Indeed each term contains the S5 difference, four other S5 factors and n-5 operator-norm factors; the n terms cancel the denominator n. The preceding $\delta_{5}$ bound therefore controls this regularized part uniformly.

This is only part of the ordinary actual trace-log. The four lower powers cannot be dropped until their nonlinear Taylor remainders have been estimated.

## 5. Nonlinear vertex suppression with the divergent lower ideals retained

Use the auxiliary Wilson-sign disk $|z|\le rM$, $r=1/(10000F)$, established in the analytic-frame lemma. No matter inverse on that large disk is needed. On it $\lVert D_M(z)-D_M(0)\rVert$ is bounded by a cutoff-independent constant $A_*=0.0144/(1-0.0144)$. Cauchy's coefficient bound yields

$$
\begin{aligned}
D_M(z)-D_M(0)&=\sum_{k\ge 1} z^k D_{k,M}, \\
\lVert D_{k,M}\rVert&\le A_{*}/(rM)^k.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the coefficients of $U_{M}$ satisfy

$$
\lVert U_{k,M}\rVert\le A_*r^{-k}M^{1-k}/\ell.
$$

This is the actual nonlinear overlap-vertex estimate. It is not an assumption that the lattice action is linear in z.

For $j$ in $\{1,2,3,4\}$, write $Q_{j,M}(z)=\operatorname{Tr}R_M(z)^j$. The coefficient of $z^n$, $n\ge j$, is a sum over $\binom{n-1}{j-1}$ ordered compositions $k_1+\dots+k_j=n$. Each factor is a bounded $U_{k_i,M}$ times $B_{M}$, compressed to $H_+$. Schatten Holder in $S_{j}$, including the $j=1$ trace-class case, gives

$$
\lvert[z^n]Q_{j,M}\rvert \le\binom{n-1}{j-1}(A_*/\ell)^jr^{-n}M^{j-n}\lVert B_M\rVert_j^j.
$$

The growth estimates in section 2 now give a uniform coefficient bound of the form

$$
\lvert[z^n]Q_{j,M}\rvert\le C_j\binom{n-1}{j-1}r^{-n}M^{4-n}(1+\log M),
$$

where for $j\le 3$ the logarithm can be omitted. This retains exactly the ultraviolet growth which a bare operator-norm argument would miss.

Let $T_4$ denote the Taylor polynomial through degree four at zero. For $|z|\le\rho$, sum the $n\ge5$ coefficients. Since $\rho/(rM)<1/2$ for every $M\ge3$, the binomial-series tail is bounded by a constant depending only on $j$ and $\rho/r$. Consequently

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sup_{|z|\le \rho} |Q_{j,M}(z)-T_4 Q_{j,M}(z)| \\
&\le C'_j (1+\log M)/M.
\end{aligned}
$$

The bound is explicit via the displayed shell sum and geometric/binomial series; no cancellation between charges is required. This proves suppression of the nonlinear contribution of the lower trace powers ABOVE fourth order. Their degree $\le 4$ coefficients need not converge and remain retained actual finite subtractions.

## 6. The actual chart determinant now matches the relative target

The accepted exact phase formula is

$$
L_M(z)=\operatorname{Tr} \operatorname{Log}(I+R_M(z))-(1/2)\operatorname{Tr} \operatorname{Log} G_M(z),\quad L_M(0)=0.

F_M&=H_M+\sum_{j=1}^4 (-1)^{j+1}[Q_{j,M}-T_4 Q_{j,M}]/j \\
&\quad -(1/2)[\operatorname{Tr} \operatorname{Log} G_M-T_4 \operatorname{Tr} \operatorname{Log} G_M].
\end{aligned}
$$

The Gram lemma, or its large-disk Taylor coefficient bound, gives an $O(1/M)$ bound for the last bracket on the common disk. Combining sections 3–5 proves

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sup_{|z|\le \rho} |F_M(z)-\log Z_5(z)| \\
&\le [B_5^4/(1-\kappa)] \delta_5(M,N) \\
&\quad + C_{\mathrm{nl}}(1+\log M)/M + C_{\mathrm{Gram}}/M.

The constants and finite error terms are supplied by the preceding formulas. Taking N then M proves uniform convergence. On any smaller disk, Cauchy's formula gives convergence of every fixed derivative, in particular the previously missing fifth logarithmic derivative. This is a theorem about the actual overlap measure convention, including its analytic frame phase, not just a continuum Fourier regulator substituted in its place.

Exponentiation yields the exact finite subtracted relative response

The baseline $Z_M(0)$, the four actual Taylor coefficients, high-mode factors and all phase choices remain recorded. The limiting relative phase is fixed by the common log branch and $Z_5(0)=1$. No statement is made that $Z_{M}$ itself has a finite nonzero absolute continuum limit or that the original normalized determinant instrument stops collapsing without these explicit factors.

## 6. Controlled convergence on the common smooth test class

Write $L(t)=\partial_u+B(t)$, $L_N(t)=\partial_u+B_N(t)$ on periodic $u$. $$

Extending finite outputs by inclusion gives

\lVert L_N^{-1}P_Nh-L^{-1}h\rVert\le(1+v/\delta)\lVert(1-P_N)\psi\rVert.

## 8. Concrete Shale test; what it obstructs and what it does not

At the flat background let P_-(n) be the negative spectral projection of alpha·(2 $\pi$ n-Q L e0). A nonconstant smooth gauge multiplier g has Fourier coefficient $g_{k}\ne 0$ for some $k\ne 0$. The commutator matrix has entries

$$
[P_-,g]_{n+k,n}=g_k [P_-(n+k)-P_-(n)].
$$

On an angular cone not parallel to $k$, the squared two-spin matrix norm of this difference is bounded below by $c/|n|^2$ for sufficiently large $n$: differentiating $(I-\alpha\cdot p/|p|)/2$ yields its nonzero transverse derivative, with uniform $O(|n|^{-2})$ remainder in the projection difference. The cone contains order $R^3$ lattice points in a dyadic shell $R\le|n|\le 2R$. The shell contribution to the Hilbert--Schmidt sum is therefore at least $c'R$, and diverges. Choose, for example, $g_Q=\exp(iQ\epsilon\sin(2\pi y_1))$ with a nonzero first Fourier coefficient; this is a genuinely periodic small gauge function within the stated class.

Hence the common flat-sea Fock representation cannot implement all these gauge multipliers by unitaries satisfying the CAR field intertwiner. The Shale--Stinespring criterion is verified in Deckert and Merkl (2015, Theorem 1.2). The explicit Fourier divergence here is for this torus and does not depend on transplanting their massive noncompact theorem. Ten direct-summed flavours do not cancel a sum of squared Hilbert--Schmidt norms.

This is not an obstruction to the single abstract CAR algebra, its positive state family, finite source resets, or intertwiners between appropriately transported sea fibers. It forbids a specific unsupported common-vacuum implementation. A stronger assertion that any two distinct bump controls have disjoint thermal representations is not required and not proved here. A physical protocol continuously changing an infinite sea would need its own implementation; the present protocol instead prepares each finite trial at its nominated control.

No price is zero. Tariff coefficients are fixed positive rationals (integers); N-dependent inventory, description length, clock duration, trial count and reserve may grow. Each reserved service is prepaid even when a failure makes it unused. Ancillary idleness has a positive holding price even when its idle Hamiltonian is degenerate.

## 2. Unambiguous preparation-error convention

In section 4 take $\eta$ to mean the FULL trace-norm error

$$
\eta=\lVert \rho_{\mathrm{actual}}-\rho_{\mathrm{target}}\rVert_1.
$$

Then $|\operatorname{Tr}[(\rho_{\mathrm{actual}}-\rho_{\mathrm{target}})X_N]|\le\Lambda_N\eta$ and the parity expectation error is $\le\eta$. This factor of two must be included before using the ratio-error formula. Statistical, calibration, pulse-approximation and readout errors are then added to their appropriate numerator/denominator budgets; the denominator condition remains total $\epsilon_d<d_0/2$.

The default $J=(2m+1)n$ reserves no replacement trials. Every scheduled outcome is recorded and used. If a calibration certificate fails, a required outcome is missing, or verification fails, the default report is an unsuccessful run, with the full reservation invoice and records retained. The stated Hoeffding guarantee applies to the completed, certified independent-trial protocol; it is not inferred for a subsequence selected by successful measurement outcomes.

An optional larger reservation $J=(2m+1)n+J_{\mathrm{spare}}$ must nominate the nonnegative integer $J_{\mathrm{spare}}$ and its scheduling before execution, update $T_{\mathrm{ret}}$ and every stock/invoice, and use replacements only for failures detected before the affected quantum preparation/measurement and independent of its unseen outcome. Any outcome-dependent or postmeasurement missing-record failure makes the run unsuccessful rather than permitting biased deletion/replacement. This preserves the declared independent source sampling law.

The positive lower bound $d_N(t)\ge\bar{d}$ concerns the exact source mean. It does not guarantee that a particular finite empirical parity mean is nonzero or large enough for safe division. The finite-record exporter is therefore defined on EVERY record as follows.

1. Perform all existing completeness, calibration and failure checks. If any fails, retain the full records/invoice and report an unsuccessful estimate.
2. Compute the empirical parity mean $\hat{d}$ from the complete reserved parity trials.
3. If $\hat{d}<\bar{d}/2$, do not divide. Retain every numerator/parity outcome and all resource records; report an unsuccessful estimate with the denominator-guard flag.
4. If $\hat{d}\ge\bar{d}/2$, compute the declared normalized numerator-component estimates using this $\hat{d}$ and return them with their specified confidence/error certificate.

No outcome is deleted; there is no outcome-selected replacement, automatic retry or conditioning of the reported confidence guarantee on passing this gate. A later separately authorized fresh run would be a different fully invoiced experiment, not a repair of these records.

On the simultaneous good-error event used in the existing proof, $|\hat{d}-d_N|\le\epsilon\le\bar{d}/4$, so $\hat{d}\ge3\bar{d}/4>\bar{d}/2$. Thus the good event always passes the guard, and with probability at least $1-\alpha$ the complete experiment returns estimates satisfying the stated component error bound. Outside that event it may return an unsuccessful estimate or estimates without guaranteed realized accuracy, exactly as allowed by the unconditional confidence statement. The guard makes the exporter total without strengthening or changing the statistical theorem.

The probability statement takes the following form:

- For the certified, failure-free independent sampling law, the probability of returning estimates with all specified component errors within $\zeta$ is at least $1-\alpha$. The simultaneous good-error event implies the denominator guard passes.
- If an additional abort/failure process is allowed with no probability bound, no positive lower bound on successful return is asserted. The universal error-control statement is $P(\text{a returned estimate is inaccurate})\le\alpha$, provided the retained trial outcomes obey the certified underlying independent sampling law and the protocol does not substitute a postselected trial population. Returning nothing cannot count as accuracy or success.
- If the probability of the additional abort process is certified at most $\beta$, then $P(\text{successful return with all specified errors within }\zeta)\ge 1-\alpha-\beta$, by the union bound. The lower bound may be replaced by zero when negative. No independence between the abort event and the sampling-error event is required for this union bound.

The universal statement bounds the joint event 'return AND inaccurate'; it is NOT the conditional probability of inaccuracy given return. The latter can be larger after outcome-dependent abortion. We never condition the Hoeffding proof on completion or on passing the denominator guard.

These bounds presuppose certified source/readout error limits on the data-generating trials. An arbitrary undetected physical corruption of the sampling law is outside that certificate. Detected failure leads to the already specified whole-run abort, retained records and full invoice; it does not authorize selective data removal or outcome-selected replacement.

Following the computational-basis detector measurement, the already inventoried detector-dilation ancilla is retained in the outcome basis state $|z\rangle$. The displayed section 5 CP map is the marginal after suppressing this explicitly retained dilation register from the notation, not an instruction to discard it from the source boundary or invoice.

## 2. Scalar-kernel theorem at finite regulator

identically for every Grassmann O, including neutral tests. Consequently every fixed-order parameter derivative, every finite linear combination, product of normalized output numbers and covariance-derived Wick minor is identical wherever defined. The trace over Hplus is one half the ordinary four-spin trace for this product. The gamma5 part vanishes: the only possible antisymmetric expression has two identical transverse p vectors. Direct Clifford multiplication gives the real even kernel

$$
J_q(u)=q^2 \sum_{k_0,k_1,k_3 \in \mathbb{Z}} 2\{G'_\omega(u)^2+(\omega^2-2p_1^2)G_\omega(u)^2\}.
$$

The complete answer is

$$
B(f,g)=\sum_{q\in Q,\ \text{twice}} \int_0^1 dy \int_0^1 dz\, f(y)g(z) J_q(y-z).
$$

No absolute value of a determinant was substituted. The specified separated quadratic response is real; this says nothing about a general-background phase or higher-order odd/chiral terms.

## 3. Absolute convergence and a computable tail

Recenter $k_0$ at its nearest toron integer, so $p_0=2\pi n_0+\alpha_q$ with $|\alpha_q|\le\pi$. For the shell $m=\max(|n_0|,|k_1|,|k_3|)\ge 1$,

$$
\begin{gathered}
\omega\ge w_m=2\pi(m-1/2), \\
\text{number of shell points}=24m^2+2.
\end{gathered}
$$

If $d\ge\delta>0$, the image/exponential formulas imply

$$
\begin{gathered}
\lvert G\rvert\le\exp(-\omega\delta)/[\omega(1-\exp(-\omega))], \\
\lvert G'\rvert\le\exp(-\omega\delta)/[1-\exp(-\omega)].
\end{gathered}
$$

Consequently each summand of $J_{q}$ has absolute value at most

$4q^2\exp(-2\omega\delta)/(1-\exp(-\omega))^2$.

After retaining all recentered shells $m\le N$, the full ten-flavour kernel error is bounded by

$$
E_N(\delta)=1760 \sum_{m>N} (24m^2+2) \exp[-4\pi \delta(m-1/2)]/[1-\exp(-2\pi(m-1/2))]^2.
$$

Here sum $q^{2}=440$, including multiplicity. Multiplying $E_{N}$ by ||f||L1 ||g||L1 bounds the response error. The sum is bounded by an elementary geometric-polynomial tail, or evaluated with a further such tail certificate. It is uniform in y,z on separated supports. The finitely many $m=0$ modes are nonsingular because every $\alpha_{q}$ is nonzero.

This also justifies the trace: multiplication f S g has a smooth kernel because the supports have positive separation. Its transverse Fourier components and every derivative decay exponentially; its one-dimensional kernels are smooth on the support product. Smooth periodic kernels are trace class, as can be proved by integrating their Fourier coefficients by parts more than four times in each variable. Composing with bounded S preserves trace class. The displayed diagonal integral and sum therefore equal the operator trace, not just a conditionally ordered diagram.

## 4. An explicit strictly nonzero separated-support theorem

Choose nonzero nonnegative smooth $f$ supported in $(0.24,0.26)$ and $g$ in $(0.74,0.76)$. Their circular separation satisfies $0.48\le d\le 0.5$. Both obey the source-circle condition.

For each charge the recentered $m=0$ mode has $p_1=p_3=0$ and contributes nonnegatively. For $q=-9$, $\alpha$ has magnitude $2\pi-9\ln 2<0.05$. For every $d$ in this interval its contribution is at least

$$
81/[2 \sinh(\alpha/2)^2]>64000.
$$

There are two $q=-9$ flavours. For every remaining $m\ge 1$ mode, the preceding absolute bound gives, after division by $q^{2}$, a total less than 6:

$$
\sum_{m\ge 1} (24m^2+2)\, 4 \exp[-0.96\cdot 2\pi(m-1/2)]/[1-\exp(-2\pi(m-1/2))]^2 < 6.
$$

This strict bound needs no floating-point premise: use $\pi>3.14$, $\exp(-3.14)<0.044$, $\exp(-0.96\times 3.14)<0.05$ and $\exp(-1.92\times 3.14)<0.0025$. The sum is at most

$$
[4\cdot 0.05/(1-0.044)^2] \sum_{m\ge 1}(24m^2+2)(0.0025)^{m-1}<6,
$$

using $\sum m^2r^{m-1}=(1+r)/(1-r)^3$. The elementary exponential inequalities can equally be certified by their positive Taylor series. Also $\sinh(.025)<.02501$ proves the 64000 bound.

Thus the full kernel is greater than $128000-440\times 6=125360$ on this support product, and

$$
B(f,g)>125360\,(\int f)(\int g)>0.
$$

This is a rigorous continuum finite nonlocal susceptibility, amplified here by the inherited near-resonant $q=-9$ toron. It is not a large-cutoff extrapolation. The numerical constants are deliberately loose.

## 5. Exact point-splitting contact decomposition

The shell estimate, now with $\delta=d$ tending to zero, proves $|J(u)|\le C(1+d^{-3})$ for the total kernel $J=\sum J_q$: $\sum m^{2}\exp(-cmd)=O(d^{-3})$. Constants are finite for the fixed inherited toron. No asymptotic heat-kernel coefficient is assumed.

For arbitrary smooth $f,g$ define $h(u)=\int f(y)g(y-u)\,dy$ and $h_e(u)=[h(u)+h(-u)]/2$. Let $\chi$ be an even smooth periodic function equal to 1 near zero and supported in $|u|<1/4$, using $u$ in $[-1/2,1/2]$. Then

$$
h_e(u)-\chi(u)[h(0)+(u^2/2)h''(0)]=O(u^4).
$$

Define the explicitly finite extension

$$
B_\chi(f,g)=\int_{-1/2}^{1/2} J(u)\{h_e(u)-\chi(u)[h(0)+(u^2/2)h''(0)]\}\,du.
$$

The omitted $|u|<\epsilon$ integral is bounded by $C'\epsilon^{2}$ times an explicit fourth-derivative norm of $h$, for sufficiently small $\epsilon$. Combining this with the transverse tail gives a convergent two-stage certified evaluation: first fix $\epsilon$, truncate transverse modes with $E_N(\epsilon)$, then bound the small-$u$ remainder.

The EXACT point-split expression decomposes as

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_{|u|>\epsilon} J(u)h_e(u)\,du \\
&= B_\chi(f,g)+A_\epsilon h(0)+D_\epsilon h''(0)+O(\epsilon^2),
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
A_\epsilon&=\int_{|u|>\epsilon} J(u)\chi(u)\,du, \\
D_\epsilon&=(1/2)\int_{|u|>\epsilon} J(u)\chi(u)u^2\,du.
\end{aligned}
$$

These have rigorous upper growth bounds $A_\epsilon=O(\epsilon^{-2})$, $D_\epsilon=O(\log(1/\epsilon))$; these are bounds, not assertions of nonzero divergent coefficients. Since $h(0)=\int fg$ and $h''(0)=-\int f'g'$, the contact terms are local in these profiles. Changing $\chi$ changes only these two local bilinear terms. Additional finite constants $a\,h(0)+b\,h''(0)$ specify an explicit extension scheme.

This constructs a local-contact/finite-remainder decomposition for THIS continuum point-splitting prescription, including its finite nonlocal piece. It does not prove the masslike contact term is gauge admissible. Full local gauge Ward restoration must exclude/fix any inadmissible contact term and match the curvature term with physical normalization conditions. A profile-only point-splitting prescription is not automatically a full gauge-covariant determinant regulator. No numerical or analytic claim here identifies $A_\epsilon,D_\epsilon$ with the actual overlap divergences.

For separated $f,g$, $h$ vanishes near zero, $h(0)=h''(0)=0$, and $B_\chi=B$ for every $\chi,a,b$. Thus the positive response of section 4 is completely independent of all these contact choices. Any integral of a local finite-jet density also has zero mixed variation on disjoint profile supports. It cannot cancel $B$.

∎

### Q.0.7.5 Registered Event-Phase Decomposition

<a id="definition-q07e-registered-forward-event-phase-ledger-and-overhead-decomposition"></a>**Definition Q.0.7e (Registered Forward Event-Phase Ledger and Overhead Decomposition).** Let $\phi$ be a concatenated forward history of registered events carrying dimensionless increments $\{\varepsilon_i\}_{i\in\phi}$, and define
$$
\Theta_{\mathrm{evt}}(\phi):=\sum_{i\in\phi}\varepsilon_i,
\qquad
U_{\mathrm{evt}}(\phi):=e^{i\Theta_{\mathrm{evt}}(\phi)}.
$$
If $\phi$ belongs to the calibrated action ensemble, then $\Theta_{\mathrm{evt}}(\phi)=\mathcal S(\phi)/\hbar$. If every registered event is assigned the structural phase reference $\varepsilon_0=\ln2$ and a certified phase overhead $\delta\varepsilon_i:=\varepsilon_i-\ln2\ge0$, then
$$
\Theta_{\mathrm{evt}}(\phi)
=N(\phi)\ln2+\Delta(\phi),
\qquad
\Delta(\phi):=\sum_{i\in\phi}\delta\varepsilon_i\ge0.
\tag{Q.0.7e.1}
$$
These are structural phase weights. Identifying $\varepsilon_i$ with a registered physical reset ledger requires the separate eventwise calibration
$$
\varepsilon_i=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{reset},i}=H_{q_i}(P_i\mid R_i)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{diss},i}.
\tag{Q.0.7e.0}
$$
On the conditionally uniform branch $H_{q_i}(P_i\mid R_i)=\ln2$, this gives $\delta\varepsilon_i=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{diss},i}$. Without (Q.0.7e.0), structural phase overhead, reset entropy, and bath heat remain distinct.

On the joint branch where the action calibration is eventwise additive, (Q.0.7e.0) holds, $H_{q_i}(P_i\mid R_i)=\ln2$, and $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{diss},i}=0$, write $\Delta\mathcal S_i$ for one event's action increment and $T_i$ for its registered reset temperature. That event satisfies
$$
\frac{\Delta\mathcal S_i}{\hbar}
=
\frac{\langle Q_{\mathrm{bath},i}\rangle}{k_BT_i}
=
\varepsilon_i
=\ln2.
$$
These are three calibrated projections of one event. A source-exhaustive cost ledger counts that event once rather than summing the action, reset, and phase readings as independent costs. The equality supplies no calibration or common microscopic mechanism beyond the stated joint branch.

This additive positive ledger is not, by itself, connection holonomy: holonomy inverts under oriented path reversal, whereas entropy production of a physically reversed protocol need not. It becomes a holonomy representation only on a branch carrying the differential character of Theorem Q.0.7d2 and the explicit compatibility certificate
$$
h(\gamma)=e^{i\Theta_{\mathrm{evt}}(\gamma)}
\tag{Q.0.7e.2}
$$
for the admitted oriented loops. The formal inverse phase is distinct from the entropy ledger of a physically reversed process.

<a id="definition-q07e-arithmetic-phase-defect-functionals"></a>**Definition Q.0.7e′ (Arithmetic Phase-Defect Functionals).** For $x\in\mathbb R$, let $\|x\|_{\mathbb Z}:=\inf_{m\in\mathbb Z}|x-m|$. For $N\ge1$, define
$$
\delta_N
:=\min_{k\in\mathbb Z}|N\ln2-2\pi k|
=2\pi\left\|\frac{N\ln2}{2\pi}\right\|_{\mathbb Z}.
$$
For a fixed positive exact-closure integer $k$, define
$$
\Delta_k^*
:=\min_{N\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}}|2\pi k-N\ln2|.
$$
These are arithmetic mismatch functionals. Neither is a topological invariant without an independent differential-character or homotopy certificate.

### Q.0.7.6 Exact-Closure Overhead Principle

<a id="proposition-q07f-registered-exact-phase-closure-identity"></a>**Proposition Q.0.7f (Registered Exact-Phase-Closure Identity).** Let $\gamma$ be a nonempty finite registered forward loop on the nonnegative-overhead branch of Definition Q.0.7e, with $N[\gamma]\ge1$ and $\varepsilon_i=\ln2+\delta\varepsilon_i$, $\delta\varepsilon_i\ge0$, for every event. Assume the exact closure condition
$$
U_{\mathrm{evt}}(\gamma)=1.
$$
Then there is a unique integer lift $k\ge1$ such that
$$
\Theta_{\mathrm{evt}}(\gamma)=2\pi k,
$$
and
$$
\Delta[\gamma]
=2\pi k-N[\gamma]\ln2.
\tag{Q.0.7f.1}
$$
Consequently $\Delta[\gamma]\ge0$ implies $N[\gamma]\ln2\le2\pi k$. The integer $k$ is an exact-phase lift; it is topological only when the separate certificate (Q.0.7e.2) and a homotopy/cohomology identification are supplied.

*Proof.* Equation (Q.0.7e.1) and $U_{\mathrm{evt}}(\gamma)=1$ give $\Theta_{\mathrm{evt}}(\gamma)\in2\pi\mathbb Z$. Nonemptiness and $\varepsilon_i\ge\ln2>0$ make this phase lift positive. Substitution gives (Q.0.7f.1). ∎

<a id="corollary-q07g-strict-overhead-on-a-nonzero-exact-closure-branch"></a>**Corollary Q.0.7g (Strict Overhead on a Nonzero Exact-Closure Branch).** Under Proposition Q.0.7f,
$$
\Delta[\gamma]>0.
$$

*Proof.* If $\Delta[\gamma]=0$, then $N[\gamma]\ln2=2\pi k$ with positive integers $N[\gamma]$ and $k$, contradicting the irrationality of $\ln2/(2\pi)$. ∎

**Registered interpretation.** A nonempty forward event ledger that closes its selected phase exactly has positive structural phase overhead. It is a topological cost only when the differential-character and topological-identification premises are registered, and it is physical entropy production only when the eventwise reset equality (Q.0.7e.0) is certified.

<a id="definition-q07g1-closure-lift-ledger-mathfrak-c_mathrmref"></a>**Definition Q.0.7g.1 (Closure-Lift Ledger $\mathfrak C_{\mathrm{ref}}$).** For a closed retained predictive loop $\gamma$ satisfying Proposition Q.0.7f, define
$$
q_{\mathrm{ref}}(\gamma)
:=\frac{\Theta_{\mathrm{evt}}(\gamma)}{2\pi}
\in\mathbb Z_{>0}.
$$
A closure-lift ledger is the finite record
$$
\mathfrak C_{\mathrm{ref}}
=
(\Gamma_{\mathrm{loop}},q_{\mathrm{ref}},N,\Delta,
\text{exact-closure domain},\text{deformation class},
\text{resolution window},\text{outcome independence}).
$$
The integer is a topological or gauge charge only when the ledger also contains the differential-character compatibility and homotopy/cohomology identification of Definition Q.0.7e.

<a id="proposition-q07g2-closure-lift-constancy-on-continuous-exact-closure-families"></a>**Proposition Q.0.7g.2 (Closure-Lift Constancy on Continuous Exact-Closure Families).** Let a connected continuously parameterized family of loops remain in the exact-closure domain, and let $\Theta_{\mathrm{evt}}$ vary continuously on that family. Then $q_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is constant. A change of $q_{\mathrm{ref}}$ requires loss of exact closure or a discontinuity of the registered phase ledger. This is an integer-lift statement, not a universal local Noether-current law.

*Proof.* On the exact-closure family,
$$
q_{\mathrm{ref}}
=\Theta_{\mathrm{evt}}/(2\pi)
$$
is a continuous integer-valued function on a connected set and is therefore constant. Proposition Q.0.7f supplies the positive structural-overhead identity. A topological or gauge interpretation requires the additional identification certificate in Definition Q.0.7g.1, and a reset-entropy interpretation requires (Q.0.7e.0). ∎

### Q.0.7.7 Sector-Minimal Overhead

<a id="definition-q07h-one-sided-and-symmetric-arithmetic-mismatches"></a>**Definition Q.0.7h (One-Sided and Symmetric Arithmetic Mismatches).** For $k\ge1$, define
$$
\Delta_k^+
:=
\min_{\substack{N\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\\N\ln2\le2\pi k}}
(2\pi k-N\ln2)
=
2\pi k-\left\lfloor\frac{2\pi k}{\ln2}\right\rfloor\ln2
$$
and
$$
\Delta_k^{\mathrm{sym}}
:=
\min_{N\in\mathbb Z}|2\pi k-N\ln2|.
$$
These are arithmetic mismatches. They equal the structural phase overhead of a realized loop only when an admitted exact-closure loop realizes the same pair $(k,N)$ under Definition Q.0.7e and Proposition Q.0.7f. Identifying that value with physical entropy production additionally requires the eventwise reset calibration (Q.0.7e.0).

<a id="proposition-q07i-bounds-and-equidistribution-of-arithmetic-mismatches"></a>**Proposition Q.0.7i (Bounds and Equidistribution of Arithmetic Mismatches).** For every $k\ge1$,
$$
0<\Delta_k^+<\ln2,
\qquad
0<\Delta_k^{\mathrm{sym}}<\frac{\ln2}{2}.
$$
With $\beta_L=2\pi/\ln2$,
$$
\frac{\Delta_k^+}{\ln2}=\{\beta_Lk\}\in(0,1),
$$
and $\{\Delta_k^+/\ln2\}_{k\ge1}$ is equidistributed in $(0,1)$.

*Proof.* The floor and nearest-integer definitions give $\Delta_k^+<\ln2$ and $\Delta_k^{\mathrm{sym}}\le\ln2/2$. Irrationality of $\beta_L$ makes both mismatches nonzero. Equality $\Delta_k^{\mathrm{sym}}=\ln2/2$ would make $\beta_Lk$ a half-integer and hence $\beta_L$ rational, which is impossible; therefore the symmetric upper bound is strict. Weyl's theorem applied to the irrational rotation $k\mapsto\{\beta_Lk\}$ gives equidistribution. ∎

### Q.0.7.8 Beatty Staircase Structure

<a id="proposition-q07j-beatty-staircase-and-the-two-step-lower-approximant-spectrum"></a>**Proposition Q.0.7j (Beatty Staircase and the Two-Step Lower-Approximant Spectrum).** Let
$$
\beta_L=\frac{2\pi}{\ln2}\in(9,10),
\qquad
N_k^*:=\lfloor\beta_Lk\rfloor.
$$
Then:

1. $N_k^*$ is the largest integer $N$ satisfying $N\ln2\le2\pi k$.
2. $N_{k+1}^*-N_k^*\in\{9,10\}$.
3. The limiting frequencies of the $10$- and $9$-steps are $\beta_L-9$ and $10-\beta_L$, respectively.

These are statements about lower integer approximants. A cycle count or exact-closure loop is obtained only if the corresponding registered physical ledger realizes that integer pair.

*Proof.* Item 1 is the floor definition. Since $9<\beta_L<10$, consecutive floors differ by $9$ or $10$. The $10$-step occurs exactly when $\{\beta_Lk\}+\{\beta_L\}\ge1$; equidistribution from Proposition Q.0.7i gives limiting frequency $\{\beta_L\}=\beta_L-9$. ∎

### Q.0.7.9 Continued Fraction Spectrum

<a id="theorem-q07k-continued-fraction-spectrum-of-exceptional-phase-mismatch"></a>**Theorem Q.0.7k (Continued-Fraction Spectrum of Exceptional Phase Mismatch).** Let
$$
\alpha_L=\frac{\ln2}{2\pi}=[0;a_1,a_2,\ldots]
$$
and let $p_n/q_n$ be its convergents. Then:

1. for every $p\in\mathbb Z$ and $1\le q\le q_n$,
   $$
   \left|\alpha_L-\frac{p_n}{q_n}\right|
   \le
   \left|\alpha_L-\frac pq\right|,
   $$
   while the second-kind bound is
   $$
   |q_n\alpha_L-p_n|
   \le|q\alpha_L-p|
   \qquad(1\le q<q_{n+1});
   $$
2. 
   $$
   \left|\alpha_L-\frac{p_n}{q_n}\right|
   <\frac1{q_nq_{n+1}}
   \le\frac1{q_n^2},
   $$
   and therefore
   $$
   |2\pi p_n-q_n\ln2|
   <\frac{2\pi}{q_{n+1}}
   \le\frac{2\pi}{q_n};
   $$
3. if $\gcd(p,q)=1$ and
   $$
   \left|\alpha_L-\frac pq\right|<\frac1{2q^2},
   $$
   then $p/q$ is a convergent.

*Proof.* Write $\alpha=\alpha_L$. Lemma Q.0.7b gives irrationality and an infinite simple continued fraction. The classical approximation criteria are Khinchin (1964, Theorems 16, 17, and 19); the following argument establishes the required inequalities with the present denominator conventions. Since $0<\alpha<1/2$, its simple continued fraction has $a_0=0$ and $a_1\ge2$. Use
$$
p_{-1}=1,\quad p_0=0,\qquad q_{-1}=0,\quad q_0=1,
\qquad
p_{n+1}=a_{n+1}p_n+p_{n-1},\quad
q_{n+1}=a_{n+1}q_n+q_{n-1}.
$$
The positive partial quotients imply $q_{n+1}>q_n\ge1$ and $q_n\to\infty$. The determinant changes sign at each recurrence step, starting from $p_0q_{-1}-p_{-1}q_0=-1$, so
$$
p_nq_{n-1}-p_{n-1}q_n=(-1)^{n-1}.
$$
For the complete quotient $\alpha_{n+1}=[a_{n+1};a_{n+2},\ldots]>a_{n+1}$, start from $\alpha=1/\alpha_1$. Substituting $\alpha_{n+1}=a_{n+1}+1/\alpha_{n+2}$ and collecting numerator and denominator coefficients proves by induction that
$$
\alpha=\frac{p_n\alpha_{n+1}+p_{n-1}}{q_n\alpha_{n+1}+q_{n-1}},
\qquad
e_n:=q_n\alpha-p_n=\frac{(-1)^n}{q_n\alpha_{n+1}+q_{n-1}}.
$$
Thus consecutive errors have opposite signs. Writing $\delta_n=|e_n|$, the denominator identity gives
$$
0<\delta_n<\frac1{q_{n+1}},
\qquad
\left|\alpha-\frac{p_n}{q_n}\right|
=\frac{\delta_n}{q_n}
<\frac1{q_nq_{n+1}}\le\frac1{q_n^2}.
$$
Multiplication by $2\pi q_n$ proves item 2.

For item 1, fix $p\in\mathbb Z$ and $1\le q<q_{n+1}$. The determinant identity makes the two integer vectors $(p_n,q_n)$ and $(p_{n+1},q_{n+1})$ a basis of $\mathbb Z^2$, so write
$$
(p,q)=u(p_n,q_n)+v(p_{n+1},q_{n+1}),\qquad u,v\in\mathbb Z.
$$
If $v=0$, then $u\ge1$ and $|q\alpha-p|=u\delta_n\ge\delta_n$. If $v>0$, the upper bound on $q$ forces $u<0$; if $v<0$, positivity of $q$ forces $u>0$. In either nonzero-$v$ case, $ue_n$ and $ve_{n+1}$ have the same sign, and hence
$$
|q\alpha-p|=|u|\delta_n+|v|\delta_{n+1}>\delta_n.
$$
This proves the second-kind inequality, with equality only at $(p,q)=(p_n,q_n)$. If $q\le q_n$, division additionally gives
$$
\left|\alpha-\frac pq\right|
=\frac{|q\alpha-p|}{q}
\ge\frac{\delta_n}{q}
\ge\frac{\delta_n}{q_n}
=\left|\alpha-\frac{p_n}{q_n}\right|,
$$
which proves the first-kind inequality.

For item 3, take the positive denominator $q$ of the reduced fraction $p/q$ and choose $n$ with $q_n\le q<q_{n+1}$. Put $\delta=|q\alpha-p|<1/(2q)$. The second-kind inequality gives $\delta_n\le\delta$. If $p/q\ne p_n/q_n$, the nonzero integer $pq_n-qp_n$ would satisfy
$$
1\le|pq_n-qp_n|
\le q_n|p-q\alpha|+q|q_n\alpha-p_n|
=q_n\delta+q\delta_n
\le(q_n+q)\delta
\le2q\delta<1,
$$
a contradiction. Therefore $p/q=p_n/q_n$; the determinant identity makes $p_n/q_n$ reduced, and the assumed reduction identifies the numerator and positive denominator. This proves the Legendre criterion. ∎

<a id="corollary-q07k-legendre-criterion-for-a-small-phase-mismatch"></a>**Corollary Q.0.7k′ (Legendre Criterion for a Small Phase Mismatch).** Let $k,N\ge1$, put $d=\gcd(k,N)$, and set $(p,q)=(k/d,N/d)$. If
$$
\left|\alpha_L-\frac{k}{N}\right|<\frac1{2N^2},
$$
equivalently
$$
|N\ln2-2\pi k|<\frac\pi N,
$$
then $p/q$ is a convergent of $\alpha_L$.

*Proof.* Reduction gives
$$
\left|\alpha_L-\frac pq\right|
<\frac1{2N^2}
\le\frac1{2q^2},
$$
so Legendre's theorem applies. ∎

<a id="theorem-q07k1-landauer-arithmetic-index-for-integer-phase-pairs"></a>**Theorem Q.0.7k.1 (Landauer Arithmetic Index for Integer Phase Pairs).** For $(N,k)\in\mathbb Z^2$, define
$$
\mathfrak I_L(N,k):=N\alpha_L-k,
\qquad
\delta_L(N,k):=2\pi|\mathfrak I_L(N,k)|.
$$
Then:

1. $\mathfrak I_L$ is additive under addition of integer pairs:
   $$
   \mathfrak I_L(N_1+N_2,k_1+k_2)
   =
   \mathfrak I_L(N_1,k_1)+\mathfrak I_L(N_2,k_2).
   $$
   It represents loop composition only on a realized additive loop ledger.
2. If $(k_n,N_n)=(p_n,q_n)$ is a convergent pair, then
   $$
   |q_n\alpha_L-p_n|
   \le|N\alpha_L-k|
   \qquad(1\le N<q_{n+1}).
   $$
3. If $N\ge1$, $\gcd(k,N)=1$, and $\delta_L(N,k)<\pi/N$, then $k/N$ is a convergent.

*Proof.* Item 1 is direct algebra. Item 2 is the second-kind approximation theorem. Item 3 is the Legendre criterion in Theorem Q.0.7k. These statements classify integer pairs; physical loop realization is an independent premise. ∎

### Q.0.7.11 Universal Crossover Bounds

<a id="corollary-q07m-arbitrarily-small-positive-arithmetic-mismatches"></a>**Corollary Q.0.7m (Arbitrarily Small Positive Arithmetic Mismatches).** For every $\zeta>0$, there exist integers $N,k\ge1$ such that
$$
0<2\pi k-N\ln2<\zeta.
$$
No loop or physical sector is asserted by this arithmetic existence statement.

*Proof.* Set
$$
\eta:=\min\left\{\frac{\zeta}{2\pi},\frac12\right\}.
$$
Density of $\{N\alpha_L\bmod1:N\ge1\}$ gives an $N$ with
$$
\{N\alpha_L\}\in(1-\eta,1).
$$
With $k=\lceil N\alpha_L\rceil$,
$$
0<2\pi(k-N\alpha_L)<2\pi\eta\le\zeta.
$$
The interval excludes $0$, so $k\ge1$. ∎

<a id="corollary-q07m-universal-arithmetic-crossover-bound"></a>**Corollary Q.0.7m′ (Universal Arithmetic Crossover Bound).** Hurwitz's theorem gives infinitely many integer pairs satisfying
$$
|2\pi k-N\ln2|<\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt5\,N}.
$$
Consequently, along this subsequence, $N>2\pi/(\sqrt5\,\zeta)$ implies mismatch below $\zeta$. The constant $\sqrt5$ is the optimal universal Hurwitz constant; it is not a primitive physical proportion.

### Q.0.7.12 Three-Gap Structure

<a id="proposition-q07n-three-gap-structure-for-finite-arithmetic-phase-sets"></a>**Proposition Q.0.7n (Three-Gap Structure for Finite Arithmetic Phase Sets).** For $N_{\max}\ge1$, the set
$$
\{e^{in\ln2}:0\le n<N_{\max}\}
$$
partitions the circle into arcs of at most three distinct lengths.

*Proof.* Apply the three-gap theorem to the irrational rotation by $\alpha_L$. ∎

**Interpretation.** This is a finite arithmetic phase set. It describes accessible physical phases only on a branch that realizes the corresponding update histories and calibrates their ledger values as phases.

### Q.0.7.13 Finite-Budget Phase-Mismatch Selection

<a id="corollary-q07o-finite-budget-phase-mismatch-selection-rule"></a>**Corollary Q.0.7o (Finite-Budget Phase-Mismatch Selection Rule).** Define
$$
\Delta\theta(n)
:=
\min_{k\in\mathbb Z}|n\ln2-2\pi k|
=2\pi\|n\alpha_L\|_{\mathbb Z}.
$$
If $q_j\le N_{\max}<q_{j+1}$, then
$$
\min_{1\le n\le N_{\max}}\Delta\theta(n)
=\Delta\theta(q_j),
\qquad
\Delta\theta(q_j)<\frac{2\pi}{q_{j+1}}.
$$
If $k$ is a nearest integer to $n\alpha_L$, $\gcd(k,n)=1$, and $\Delta\theta(n)<\pi/n$, then $k/n$ is a convergent. These statements determine arithmetic phase positions. They constrain interference only for independently realized, phase-calibrated histories and do not determine amplitudes.

*Proof.* The second-kind best-approximation property gives
$$
\|q_j\alpha_L\|_{\mathbb Z}
\le\|n\alpha_L\|_{\mathbb Z}
\qquad(1\le n<q_{j+1}),
$$
and Theorem Q.0.7k gives the upper bound. The last statement is Legendre's criterion. ∎

### Q.0.7.14 Decoherence from Overhead Fluctuations

<a id="proposition-q07p-conditional-ensemble-dephasing-from-phase-overhead-fluctuations"></a>**Proposition Q.0.7p (Conditional Ensemble Dephasing from Phase-Overhead Fluctuations).** *Let a family of processes $\phi$ share the same baseline cycle count $N[\phi]=N$, let $\Delta[\phi]$ have probability law $P(\Delta)$, and assume the accepted phase calibration gives $\mathcal S[\phi]/\hbar=N\ln2+\Delta[\phi]$ for every member of the ensemble. Then the ensemble-averaged phase factor factorizes as:*
$$\langle e^{i\mathcal{S}[\phi]/\hbar} \rangle = e^{iN\ln 2} \langle e^{i\Delta[\phi]} \rangle = e^{iN\ln 2} \Phi_\Delta(1)$$

*where $\Phi_\Delta(t):=\langle e^{it\Delta}\rangle$ is the characteristic function of $\Delta$. If a registered coherence observable is multiplied by this ensemble average, its visibility is multiplied by $|\Phi_\Delta(1)|\le1$.*

Because Definition Q.0.7e requires $\Delta\ge0$, a nondegenerate Gaussian law is inadmissible. For example, if $\Delta$ has a $\Gamma$ law with shape $r>0$ and scale $\theta>0$ on $[0,\infty)$, then
$$
\Phi_\Delta(1)=(1-i\theta)^{-r},
\qquad
|\Phi_\Delta(1)|=(1+\theta^2)^{-r/2}.
$$
This is an exact supported-law example. It becomes a dephasing prediction only after the coherence observable, ensemble preparation, and pushforward law of Remark Q.0.7p.1 are registered.

<a id="remark-q07p1-conditional-pce-induced-overhead-distribution"></a>**Remark Q.0.7p.1: Conditional PCE-Induced Overhead Distribution.** Let a specified PCE state process $X_t$ satisfy the hypotheses of the applicable Appendix D stationary-law theorem, and let the overhead be a measurable observable $\Delta=\Delta(X_t)$. The stationary law of $X_t$ then induces a pushforward law $P_\Delta$. Concentration of $P_\Delta$ near zero requires, in addition, that $\Delta$ vanish on the relevant minimizing set and that the Appendix D concentration estimate control excursions into states with $|\Delta|>\epsilon$.

### Q.0.7.15 Modular Structure from Continued Fractions

<a id="remark-q07q-the-modular-itinerary-canonically-induced-by-alpha_l"></a>**Remark Q.0.7q: The Modular Itinerary Canonically Induced by $\alpha_L$.** The continued fraction of $\alpha_L$ canonically produces a sequence of matrices in $GL_2(\mathbb{Z})$ via convergents:
$$M_n := \begin{pmatrix} p_n & p_{n-1} \\ q_n & q_{n-1} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \det(M_n) = (-1)^{n-1}, \qquad M_n(\infty) = \frac{p_n}{q_n}$$

The digit string $[0; 9, 15, 2, 4, 1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, \ldots]$ supplies one-sided continued-fraction data for Farey cutting sequences on the modular surface $\mathcal{H}/PSL_2(\mathbb{Z})$ (Series 1985). To specify a complete oriented geodesic, one must also supply a backward endpoint or equivalent initial geometric data; to encode its cuts as a word in the generators $S: \tau \mapsto -1/\tau$ and $T: \tau \mapsto \tau + 1$, one must declare the initial cut and orientation convention. In particular, the matrices $M_n$ with determinant $-1$ are not themselves elements of $PSL_2(\mathbb Z)$.

With these additional choices, the continued-fraction data yield a $PSL_2(\mathbb Z)$-structured itinerary for the chosen irrational number $\alpha_L=\ln2/(2\pi)$. The arithmetic construction alone supplies no bridge to $M=24$, the Leech lattice, $V^\natural$, the Monster, or a physical modular symmetry.

*Note:* The Klein $j$-invariant is defined on the upper half-plane $\mathcal{H} = \{\tau \in \mathbb{C} : \mathrm{Im}(\tau) > 0\}$; the real axis $\mathbb{R}$ lies on the boundary of $\mathcal{H}$, so expressions like $j(\alpha_L)$ are not defined as holomorphic values. The modular itinerary construction avoids this issue entirely.

### Q.0.7.16 Gauge-Holonomy Interface

<a id="remark-q07r-gauge-holonomy-interface"></a>**Remark Q.0.7r: Gauge-Holonomy Interface.** Appendix G derives a local $U(1)$ redundancy with covariant derivative:
$$D_\mu\Psi = (\partial_\mu + \Omega_\mu + iq A_\mu)\Psi$$

and associated $U(1)$ holonomies $\exp(iq\oint_\gamma A_\mu dx^\mu)$ (Section G.4).

The chosen structural phase increment $\ln2$ gives $g_L=e^{i\ln2}$, and the irrationality of $\ln2/(2\pi)$ makes the cyclic subgroup $G_L=\langle g_L\rangle$ dense in $U(1)$. This is a group-closure statement conditional on assigning that phase increment to the registered event family.

Theorem Q.0.7d2 supplies the separate operational completion: a uniformly continuous isometric $G_L$ action extends uniquely to $U(1)$, while genuine connection holonomy requires its differential-character certificate. On the additional compatibility branch $h(\gamma)=e^{i\Theta_{\mathrm{evt}}(\gamma)}$, the registered event phase represents holonomy; exact trivial phase then gives Proposition Q.0.7f's closure identity. Corollary Q.0.7g gives positive structural phase overhead for a nonzero exact-closure lift. The formal inverse phase is not identified with entropy production of a physically reversed protocol.

Accordingly, the exact finite-cycle object is the integer-indexed subgroup $G_L$; its continuous closure is used only on the registered action/continuity branch, and its local gauge interpretation only on the differential-character/descent branch.

<a id="remark-q07r-conditional-event-phaseconnection-compatibility"></a>**Remark Q.0.7r′ (Conditional Event-Phase/Connection Compatibility).** On the differential-character branch of Theorem Q.0.7d2, let $h$ be the registered holonomy character. If (Q.0.7e.2) is independently certified, then for every admitted oriented loop $\gamma$,
$$
h(\gamma)
=e^{i\Theta_{\mathrm{evt}}(\gamma)}
=e^{i(N(\gamma)\ln2+\Delta(\gamma))}.
$$
If the bundle is trivial over a neighborhood of $\gamma$ and $A$ is a chosen local connection form there, this may be written as
$$
h(\gamma)=e^{iq\oint_\gamma A};
$$
on a nontrivial bundle the transition functions are part of the holonomy. For exact closure, $h(\gamma)=1$ and $N\ln2+\Delta=2\pi k$. The quantity $\Delta$ is structural phase overhead and is physical entropy production only under the separate registered-reset calibration. Local changes of section change the local potential but not $h$.

### Q.0.7.17 Non-Abelian Extension

<a id="theorem-q07s-non-abelian-density-mechanism-from-near-identity-generation"></a>**Theorem Q.0.7s (Non-Abelian Density Mechanism from Near-Identity Generation).** *Let $G$ be a connected semisimple real Lie group with Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$. Then there exists an identity neighborhood $\Omega \subset G$ on which $\log = \exp^{-1}$ is defined such that for any $g_1, \ldots, g_m \in \Omega$, if the Lie algebra generated by $\log(g_1), \ldots, \log(g_m)$ equals $\mathfrak{g}$, then the subgroup $\Gamma := \langle g_1, \ldots, g_m \rangle$ is dense in $G$, i.e., $\overline{\Gamma} = G$.*

*Proof.* This is the near-identity density criterion of Breuillard–Gelander (Breuillard and Gelander 2003, Theorem 2.1). $\square$

<a id="corollary-q07t-su2-case-torus-density-plus-non-normalizer-implies-density"></a>**Corollary Q.0.7t (SU(2) Case: Torus Density Plus Non-Normalizer Implies Density).** *Let $G = SU(2)$ and let $T \subset SU(2)$ be a maximal torus. Suppose $\Gamma$ contains an element $t \in T$ whose rotation angle is an irrational multiple of $\pi$ (so $\overline{\langle t\rangle} = T$). If $\Gamma$ also contains an element $g \notin N_{SU(2)}(T)$ (equivalently, $gTg^{-1} \ne T$), then $\overline{\Gamma} = SU(2)$.*

*For a finite inverse-closed gate set generating this dense $SU(2)$ subgroup, the Solovay–Kitaev theorem (Kitaev, Shen and Vyalyi 2002) gives polylogarithmic word length in the inverse approximation tolerance for single-carrier $SU(2)$ gates. The universal protected computation of Appendix A additionally requires its full gate-realization, error-correction, working-memory, and execution-resource hypotheses.*

*Justification.* Since $\overline{\langle t\rangle} = T$, the closure $\overline{\Gamma}$ contains $T$. The only proper closed subgroups of $SU(2)$ containing a maximal torus are $T$ itself and its normalizer $N_{SU(2)}(T)=T\sqcup jT\cong\operatorname{Pin}(2)$, where $j^2=-I$. Moreover $N_{SU(2)}(T)/T\cong\mathbb Z_2$ and $N_{SU(2)}(T)/\{\pm I\}\cong O(2)$. If $g\notin N_{SU(2)}(T)$, the closed subgroup generated by $T$ and $g$ is therefore all of $SU(2)$.

<a id="remark-q07t1-registered-non-normalizer-requirement"></a>**Remark Q.0.7t.1: Registered Non-Normalizer Requirement.** For the standard diagonal torus,
$$
U_\iota=i\sigma_x
$$
satisfies $U_\iota T U_\iota^{-1}=T$, so $U_\iota\in N_{SU(2)}(T)$ and cannot be the element $g\notin N_{SU(2)}(T)$ required by Corollary Q.0.7t. Indeed a dense torus together with $i\sigma_x$ closes only to $N_{SU(2)}(T)\cong\operatorname{Pin}(2)$. Dense $SU(2)$ requires an additional registered element outside the normalizer, for example
$$
g_\beta=\exp(i\beta\sigma_x),
\qquad
\beta\notin(\pi/2)\mathbb Z,
$$
or near-identity generators whose logarithms are proved to span $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ as in Theorem Q.0.7s. QFI mode availability alone does not construct those retained group elements.

*Proof.* Conjugation by $i\sigma_x$ sends $\sigma_z$ to $-\sigma_z$ and $(i\sigma_x)^2=-I$, proving membership in the nonidentity normalizer component. Conjugation by $g_\beta$ sends $\sigma_z$ to $\cos(2\beta)\sigma_z+\sin(2\beta)\sigma_y$, which lies on the torus axis exactly when $\beta\in(\pi/2)\mathbb Z$. ∎

<a id="theorem-q07t2-minimal-two-control-dense-su2-holonomy-witness"></a>**Theorem Q.0.7t.2 (Minimal Two-Control Dense $SU(2)$ Holonomy Witness).** Choose nonzero $\alpha,\beta$ small enough that
$$
U_x=e^{i\alpha\sigma_x},
\qquad
U_z=e^{i\beta\sigma_z}
$$
belong to the logarithm neighborhood of Theorem Q.0.7s. Then $\log U_x=i\alpha\sigma_x$ and $\log U_z=i\beta\sigma_z$ generate $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ because their bracket is a nonzero multiple of $i\sigma_y$. Hence $\langle U_x,U_z\rangle$ is dense in $SU(2)$. No one-element set can be dense in $SU(2)$, because the closure of a cyclic subgroup is abelian. Thus two is the minimum number of near-identity generators for this carrier.

Let a two-valued control register have basis $|x\rangle,|z\rangle$ and define the controlled update
$$
U_{\mathrm{ctrl}}
=|x\rangle\!\langle x|\otimes U_x
+|z\rangle\!\langle z|\otimes U_z.
\tag{Q.0.7t.2.1}
$$
This is unitary. For forward parallel transport with $D=d+\mathcal A$, use the constant anti-Hermitian connection forms $\mathcal A_x=-i\alpha\sigma_x\,ds$ and $\mathcal A_z=-i\beta\sigma_z\,ds$ on a unit parameter loop. The equation $\dot U=-\mathcal A_sU$, $U(0)=I$, gives holonomies $U_x$ and $U_z$, and finite forward control words realize the positive-word monoid generated by $U_x,U_z$. Exact realization of the full subgroup additionally requires realization of the inverse gates. Parallel logarithms instead generate one torus, while adjoining only a torus-normalizer element gives the proper closed normalizer described in Remark Q.0.7t.1; either failure is a finite falsifier of density.

*Proof.* The Lie-bracket calculation and Theorem Q.0.7s prove density. Every cyclic subgroup is abelian, and closure preserves commutation, whereas $SU(2)$ is nonabelian, proving minimality. Orthogonal control projections make (Q.0.7t.2.1) a block-diagonal unitary. For the stated forward transport convention, the solution is $U(1)=\mathcal P\exp(-\int_0^1\mathcal A_s\,ds)$. Constancy of $\mathcal A_s$ removes path ordering and gives $U_x$ or $U_z$ from the displayed negative connection forms, proving the holonomy statement. The proper-closure alternatives follow from the one-dimensional Lie algebra and Corollary Q.0.7t. ∎

<a id="theorem-q07t3-minimal-dense-generation-for-compact-unitary-type-gauge-groups"></a>**Theorem Q.0.7t.3 (Minimal Dense Generation for Compact Unitary-Type Gauge Groups).** Let
$$
G=\Bigl(\prod_{j=1}^mSU(n_j)\times U(1)^k\Bigr)\Big/D,
\qquad m\ge1,\quad n_j\ge2,\quad k\ge0,
\tag{Q.0.7t.3.1}
$$
with $D$ a finite central subgroup; the class contains $SU(n)$, $U(n)$ and $(SU(3)\times SU(2)\times U(1))/F$ for every finite central $F$. For $n\ge2$ put
$$
X^{(n)}:=i\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n),
\quad
\lambda_a:=2^a-\frac1n\sum_{b=1}^n2^b,
\qquad
Y^{(n)}:=i(J_n-I_n),
\tag{Q.0.7t.3.2}
$$
with $J_n$ the all-ones matrix, and for $t>0$ let $g_1(t),g_2(t)\in G$ be the images of
$$
\Bigl(\bigl(e^{tjX^{(n_j)}}\bigr)_{j=1}^m;\ e^{2\pi i\alpha_L},e^{2\pi i\alpha_L^2},\ldots,e^{2\pi i\alpha_L^k}\Bigr),
\qquad
\Bigl(\bigl(e^{tY^{(n_j)}}\bigr)_{j=1}^m;\ 1,\ldots,1\Bigr).
$$
Then:

1. No single element generates a dense subgroup of $G$.
2. There is $t_0>0$ such that $\langle g_1(t),g_2(t)\rangle$ is dense in $G$ for $0<t\le t_0$. Every group in the class therefore has exactly two as its minimal number of topological generators. The semisimple components of $g_1(t),g_2(t)$ tend to the identity as $t\to0$, and for $k\ge1$ the first abelian component of $g_1$ is the registered Landauer generator $g_L=e^{i\ln2}$. Density persists when the abelian component of $g_1$ is replaced by $(e^{2\pi i\alpha_L^l/q})_{l=1}^k$ for an integer $q\ge1$, so for small $t$ and large $q$ both generators lie in any prescribed identity neighborhood of $G$.
3. For every finite-dimensional unitary representation $\rho$ of $G$, the controlled update $|x\rangle\!\langle x|\otimes\rho(g_1)+|z\rangle\!\langle z|\otimes\rho(g_2)$ is unitary, and the constant connection forms $\mathcal A_i=-iH_i\,ds$, with Hermitian $H_i$ satisfying $e^{iH_i}=\rho(g_i)$, have holonomies $\rho(g_1),\rho(g_2)$ in the transport convention of Theorem Q.0.7t.2.

*Proof.* Item 1: the closure of a cyclic subgroup is abelian, while $G$ contains the nonabelian image of $SU(n_1)$.

Lie algebra. Let $\mathfrak s_j:=\mathfrak{su}(n_j)$, $\mathfrak s:=\bigoplus_j\mathfrak s_j$, $X:=(jX^{(n_j)})_j$, $Y:=(Y^{(n_j)})_j$, and let $\mathfrak h\subseteq\mathfrak s$ be the real Lie algebra generated by $X$ and $Y$. For one factor, the complex span of the algebra generated by $X^{(n)}$ and $Y^{(n)}$ contains $p(\operatorname{ad}_{X^{(n)}})Y^{(n)}$ for every polynomial $p$. Since $\operatorname{ad}_{X^{(n)}}E_{ab}=i(\lambda_a-\lambda_b)E_{ab}$ and the numbers $2^a-2^b$, $a\ne b$, are nonzero and pairwise distinct by uniqueness of binary expansions, Lagrange interpolation isolates $iE_{ab}$ for every $a\ne b$. These matrix units generate $\mathfrak{sl}_n(\mathbb C)$, and $\mathfrak{su}(n)\cap i\,\mathfrak{su}(n)=0$, so the real algebra has dimension $n^2-1$ and equals $\mathfrak{su}(n)$; a positive scalar multiple of $X^{(n)}$ generates the same algebra with $Y^{(n)}$. For the sum, induct on $m$, allowing arbitrary pairwise distinct positive scalars in place of $j$. Each projection $\pi_j(\mathfrak h)$ equals $\mathfrak s_j$, and $\mathfrak h\cap\mathfrak s_1$ is an ideal of the simple algebra $\mathfrak s_1$, because $[h,a]=[\pi_1h,a]$ for $a\in\mathfrak s_1$. The projection $\pi'$ onto $\mathfrak s':=\bigoplus_{j\ge2}\mathfrak s_j$ maps $\mathfrak h$ onto $\mathfrak s'$ by induction. If $\mathfrak h\cap\mathfrak s_1=\mathfrak s_1$, then $\pi'h=h-\pi_1h\in\mathfrak h$ for all $h\in\mathfrak h$, so $\mathfrak h=\mathfrak s$. If $\mathfrak h\cap\mathfrak s_1=0$, then $\pi'|_{\mathfrak h}$ is injective and $\pi_1\circ(\pi'|_{\mathfrak h})^{-1}$ is a surjective homomorphism $\mathfrak s'\to\mathfrak s_1$; its kernel is a sum of simple ideals, so it restricts to an isomorphism $\phi:\mathfrak s_{j_0}\to\mathfrak s_1$ with $\phi(c_{j_0}X^{(n)})=c_1X^{(n)}$, $n=n_1=n_{j_0}$, for the two distinct scalars $c_1,c_{j_0}$. Isomorphisms preserve the Killing form, which is negative definite on $\mathfrak{su}(n)$, so $c_{j_0}^2=c_1^2$, a contradiction. Hence $\mathfrak h=\mathfrak s$.

Density. Choose $t_0$ so that for $t\le t_0$ the components of $g_1(t),g_2(t)$ in $G_{ss}:=\prod_jSU(n_j)$ lie in the neighborhood $\Omega$ of Theorem Q.0.7s and have logarithms $tX,tY$; these generate $\mathfrak s$, so the projection to $G_{ss}$ of $\Gamma:=\langle g_1(t),g_2(t)\rangle$, formed first in $\tilde G:=G_{ss}\times U(1)^k$, is dense. Let $H$ be the closure of $\Gamma$ in $\tilde G$. Its projection to $G_{ss}$ is compact and dense, hence equal to $G_{ss}$. The closed subgroup $S_0:=\{g\in G_{ss}:(g,1)\in H\}$ is normal in $G_{ss}$, because conjugating $(s,1)$ by any $(g,\tau)\in H$ gives $(gsg^{-1},1)$. For $(g_1',\tau_1),(g_2',\tau_2)\in H$ the commutator is $([g_1',g_2'],1)$, so $G_{ss}/S_0$ is an abelian compact connected Lie group; its Lie algebra is an abelian quotient of $\mathfrak s=[\mathfrak s,\mathfrak s]$ and therefore vanishes, whence $S_0=G_{ss}$. The projection of $H$ to $U(1)^k$ is closed and contains the powers of the abelian component $(e^{2\pi i\alpha_L^l/q})_{l=1}^k$ of $g_1$, with $q=1$ for the displayed pair. Since $\alpha_L$ is transcendental (Lemma Q.0.7b), $1,\alpha_L/q,\ldots,\alpha_L^k/q$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb Q$, and Kronecker's theorem makes these powers dense in $U(1)^k$. For $(g,\tau)\in\tilde G$ choose $(g',\tau)\in H$; then $(g,\tau)=(gg'^{-1},1)(g',\tau)\in H$. Thus $H=\tilde G$, and the continuous quotient map onto $G$ preserves density. Item 3: orthogonal control projections make the controlled update block-diagonal unitary, and a constant connection form integrates to its exponential as in Theorem Q.0.7t.2. ∎

<a id="theorem-q07t4-complete-compact-connected-lie-group-control-census"></a>**Theorem Q.0.7t.4 (Complete Compact Connected Lie-Group Control Census).** Let $G$ be a finite-dimensional compact connected Lie group, and let $d_{\mathrm{top}}(G)$ be the least number of elements generating a dense subgroup, with the empty set generating $\{1\}$. Then
$$
d_{\mathrm{top}}(G)=
\begin{cases}
0,&G=\{1\},\\
1,&G\ne\{1\}\text{ is abelian},\\
2,&G\text{ is nonabelian}.
\end{cases}
\tag{Q.0.7t.4.1}
$$
This census includes every compact simple Lie-algebra type, repeated simple factors, torus factors and finite central quotients. The following exact controls approach the identity as their integer parameter $q\to\infty$.

Present $G$ as
$$
\pi:S\times U(1)^k\longrightarrow G\cong(S\times U(1)^k)/D,
\tag{Q.0.7t.4.2}
$$
where $S$ is compact, connected, simply connected and semisimple, $k\ge0$, and $D$ is finite and central. The case $S=\{1\}$ is allowed. This presentation follows from the compact-group structure and compactness of the semisimple universal cover (Knapp 2002, Theorems 4.29 and 4.69). For $S\ne\{1\}$, put $\mathfrak s=\operatorname{Lie}(S)$ and choose a Chevalley basis of $\mathfrak s_{\mathbb C}$ compatible with its compact real form: compact conjugation sends $E_\alpha$ to $-E_{-\alpha}$ and $H_a$ to $-H_a$. Enumerate the simple roots of the entire semisimple root system by $a=1,\ldots,r$, assigning different indices to different factors even when they are isomorphic. Define
$$
E_a:=E_{\alpha_a},\quad F_a:=E_{-\alpha_a},\quad H_a:=[E_a,F_a],
\quad C_{ab}:=\alpha_a(H_b),\quad b_a:=2^a,\quad c:=C^{-1}b,
$$
$$
X:=i\sum_{a=1}^r c_aH_a,
\qquad Y:=\sum_{a=1}^r(E_a-F_a).
\tag{Q.0.7t.4.3}
$$
The displayed row convention fixes the Cartan matrix $C$; it is integral and invertible, so $c\in\mathbb Q^r$ and $X,Y\in\mathfrak s$. The compact Chevalley construction and simple-root generation are given in (Chevalley 1955; Serre 1987, Chapter VI, Sections 4 and 6). For every integer $q\ge1$, put
$$
\tau_q:=\bigl(e^{2\pi i\alpha_L^\ell/q}\bigr)_{\ell=1}^k,
\qquad g_{1,q}:=\pi(e^{X/q},\tau_q),
\qquad g_{2,q}:=\pi(e^{Y/q},1).
\tag{Q.0.7t.4.4}
$$
These two elements generate densely in $G$. For $S=\{1\}$ and $k>0$, the single element $\pi(1,\tau_q)$ generates densely; for $S=\{1\}$ and $k=0$, the empty set suffices. If $k>0$, the first torus coordinate before quotienting at $q=1$ is $g_L=e^{i\ln2}$.

For any continuous finite-dimensional unitary representation $\rho:G\to U(d)$, define
$$
Z_{1,q}:=d\pi\!\left(X/q;\,(2\pi i\alpha_L^\ell/q)_{\ell=1}^k\right),
\qquad Z_{2,q}:=d\pi(Y/q;0),
\tag{Q.0.7t.4.5}
$$
omitting absent semisimple terms in the torus case. Thus $g_{j,q}=\exp_G Z_{j,q}$. On a two-dimensional control register with orthonormal basis $|x\rangle,|z\rangle$, the controlled update
$$
|x\rangle\!\langle x|\otimes\rho(g_{1,q})
+|z\rangle\!\langle z|\otimes\rho(g_{2,q})
$$
is unitary, and the constant connection $\mathcal A_{j,q}=-d\rho(Z_{j,q})\,ds$ on a unit parameter loop has holonomy $\rho(g_{j,q})$ for $D=d+\mathcal A$. The one-control case uses its one unitary block. The minimality assertion concerns $G$ itself; a faithful $\rho$ preserves that assertion in its image.

The group also has an explicit finite separating family of normalized matrix responses. Choose a faithful $\rho$, which exists for compact Lie groups (Knapp 2002, Corollary 4.22), and let $R(g):=1\oplus\rho(g)$ on $\mathbb C|0\rangle\oplus\mathbb C^d$. For $1\le a,j\le d$, set
$$
|\psi_j\rangle:=\frac{|0\rangle+|j\rangle}{\sqrt2},
\quad X_{0a}:=|0\rangle\!\langle a|+|a\rangle\!\langle0|,
\quad Y_{0a}:=-i|0\rangle\!\langle a|+i|a\rangle\!\langle0|,
\quad M_{a,\pm}^{x}:=\frac{I\pm X_{0a}}2,
\quad M_{a,\pm}^{y}:=\frac{I\pm Y_{0a}}2.
$$
Each effect pair is positive and sums to $I$, with probabilities
$$
p_{aj,\pm}^{x}(g)
:=\langle\psi_j|R(g)^*M_{a,\pm}^{x}R(g)|\psi_j\rangle
=\frac{1\pm\operatorname{Re}\rho(g)_{aj}}2,
\qquad
p_{aj,\pm}^{y}(g)
:=\langle\psi_j|R(g)^*M_{a,\pm}^{y}R(g)|\psi_j\rangle
=\frac{1\pm\operatorname{Im}\rho(g)_{aj}}2.
\tag{Q.0.7t.4.6}
$$
Equality of these finite arrays is equivalent to equality in $G$. For control words, the response equivalence is exactly equality of their products in $G$.

*Proof.* Put $U_a=E_a-F_a$ and $V_a=i(E_a+F_a)$. The Cartan relations and $Cc=b$ give
$$
[X,U_a]=2^aV_a,
\qquad [X,V_a]=-2^aU_a,
\qquad (\operatorname{ad}_X)^2U_a=-4^aU_a.
$$
For each $a$, the real polynomial
$$
P_a(z):=\prod_{\substack{1\le b\le r\\b\ne a}}
\frac{z+4^b}{4^b-4^a}
$$
(with empty product $1$) satisfies $P_a(-4^b)=\delta_{ab}$. Hence $\mathfrak l:=\operatorname{Lie}_{\mathbb R}(X,Y)$ contains
$$
P_a\bigl((\operatorname{ad}_X)^2\bigr)Y=U_a,
\qquad 2^{-a}[X,U_a]=V_a.
$$
Its complexification contains $E_a=(U_a-iV_a)/2$, $F_a=-(U_a+iV_a)/2$ and $H_a=[E_a,F_a]$. Every positive root can be written as a sum of simple roots with every partial sum a root, and the associated iterated root-vector bracket is nonzero. Thus the simple positive and negative root vectors generate every root space and the Cartan subalgebra. Therefore $\mathfrak l_{\mathbb C}=\mathfrak s_{\mathbb C}$ and $\mathfrak l=\mathfrak s$. The global indices separate repeated factors without a diagonal identification.

To pass to the specified group elements, note that $\operatorname{ad}_X$ and $\operatorname{ad}_Y$ have algebraic entries in the Chevalley basis: its structure constants are integers and $c$ is rational. Compactness makes these operators skew-adjoint for a positive-definite inner product. For $Z=X$ or $Y$, their eigenvalues are therefore $i\lambda_1,\ldots,i\lambda_N$ with real algebraic $\lambda_\nu$. Diagonalize the operator over $\mathbb C$. An integer character $m\in\mathbb Z^N$ annihilates the cyclic subgroup generated by $(e^{i\lambda_\nu/q})_\nu$ precisely when
$$
q^{-1}\sum_{\nu=1}^N m_\nu\lambda_\nu\in2\pi\mathbb Z.
$$
It annihilates the continuous subgroup $(e^{it\lambda_\nu})_\nu$, $t\in\mathbb R$, precisely when $\sum_\nu m_\nu\lambda_\nu=0$. The conditions agree: the sum is algebraic, while a nonzero integer multiple of $2\pi q$ is transcendental (Lindemann 1882). Closed subgroups of a finite torus are determined by their annihilating integer characters, the subgroup form of Kronecker's theorem (Kronecker 1884). Thus the cyclic and continuous adjoint subgroups have the same closure.

Let $K_q:=\overline{\langle e^{X/q},e^{Y/q}\rangle}\subseteq S$. Its adjoint image is compact and closed, and contains $\operatorname{Ad}(e^{tX})$ and $\operatorname{Ad}(e^{tY})$ for every real $t$. Consequently
$$
\operatorname{ad}X,\operatorname{ad}Y
\in\operatorname{Lie}(\operatorname{Ad}K_q)
=\operatorname{ad}(\operatorname{Lie}K_q).
$$
The adjoint differential is injective on the semisimple algebra $\mathfrak s$, so $X,Y\in\operatorname{Lie}K_q$. The Lie-generation result gives $\operatorname{Lie}K_q=\mathfrak s$. A closed subgroup with the full Lie algebra is open, and connectedness of $S$ gives $K_q=S$. This proves equality in $S$, including its finite center.

Lemma Q.0.7b gives rational independence of $1,\alpha_L/q,\ldots,\alpha_L^k/q$: a rational relation would give a nonzero rational polynomial vanishing at the transcendental $\alpha_L$. Hence $\overline{\langle\tau_q\rangle}=U(1)^k$ by Kronecker's theorem. Let $H_q$ be the closure of the two-generator subgroup in $S\times U(1)^k$ before quotienting. Both projections are surjective, by compactness and the density just proved. The subgroup $N_q:=\{s\in S:(s,1)\in H_q\}$ is closed and normal, since every $s\in S$ has a lift $(s,\tau)\in H_q$. Given arbitrary $s_1,s_2\in S$, their lifts have commutator $([s_1,s_2],1)$, so $S/N_q$ is abelian and connected. Its Lie algebra is an abelian quotient of $\mathfrak s=[\mathfrak s,\mathfrak s]$, hence zero. Thus $S/N_q$ is trivial and $N_q=S$. Surjectivity onto the torus now yields $H_q=S\times U(1)^k$. The continuous surjection $\pi$ preserves density. For $S=\{1\}$ the torus argument alone applies. All displayed controls tend to the identity as $q\to\infty$.

An empty set generates $\{1\}$, and the closure of a cyclic subgroup is abelian because commutation is preserved under limits. These give the required lower bounds, attained by the constructions. A finite central quotient preserves the Lie algebra, so $G$ is nonabelian exactly when $S\ne\{1\}$; otherwise it is a $k$-torus. The low-rank identifications $B_1=C_1=A_1$, $B_2=C_2$, $D_2=A_1\oplus A_1$ and $D_3=A_3$ all therefore have minimum two. In particular, $SO(1)$ has minimum zero, $SO(2)$ minimum one, and $SO(n)$ for $n\ge3$ minimum two. The construction applies without alteration to the remaining classical and exceptional compact forms.

Orthogonal control projections prove unitarity. Forward transport with $\mathcal A=-d\rho(Z)\,ds$ integrates to $e^{d\rho(Z)}=\rho(\exp_G Z)$, giving the holonomies. The eigenvalues of $X_{0a}$ and $Y_{0a}$ lie in $\{-1,0,1\}$, so the effects are positive and normalized. The output state is $(|0\rangle+\sum_a\rho(g)_{aj}|a\rangle)/\sqrt2$; its displayed expectations are the real and imaginary parts of $\rho(g)_{aj}$. Equation (Q.0.7t.4.6) therefore recovers every entry of $\rho(g)$, and faithfulness recovers $g$. The invariant reference turns scalar-center phases into relative phases, retaining distinctions erased by unreferenced conjugation on an irreducible carrier. ∎

<a id="definition-q07t5-finite-spin-source-for-decorated-control-words"></a>**Definition Q.0.7t.5 (Finite-Spin Source for Decorated Control Words).** Fix the finite Hilbert/instrument branch of Definition 27, reuse the local primitive-service contracts and tariff of Definition C.6c.4a, and fix positive units $\tau_*,u_*,\hbar$. Use one fixed two-port graph with one lane of descriptor $1$. Each port has the three labeled register factors of Section 7.1.3. All additional data, detector, controller and archive factors below are individually owned local auxiliaries at port $0$. The other port and the unused lane remain in the allocation and holding ledger. No communication service or initial shared input-dependent state is used.

The source's input is a finite dimension, a finite list of explicitly described Hermitian matrices $L_j$, certified bounds $\|L_j\|\le B_j$, and a finite typed endpoint-protocol tree. The elementary quantum commands are $\exp(-iL_j)$, their inverses, coherent control by the interface register, the preparations and binary instruments specified below, and identity padding. Each matrix has a finite exact description and an explicit Hermiticity and bound certificate. A formal exact matrix-function description is used in the same ideal-service sense as Definition C.6c.4a; a finite-precision description instead carries its error certificate. This source syntax is fixed for all finite dimensions and matrices before a group or a preferred control word is inserted. Its primitive services name no group, group element or measurement probability.

Encode an $r$-dimensional data carrier in the first $r$ computational basis states of $b=\lceil\log_2r\rceil$ local data qubits. Extend every data operation by the identity on its orthogonal complement. For a controlled operation, the two blocks act on the actual interface qubit, not on a measured copy of that qubit. Let $n$ be the total number of allocated quantum bits, including the six port-carrier bits, data, fresh detector and quantum-record bits, all padded or unused bits and any explicitly retained preparation factors. The bare Hamiltonian is zero, exactly as in Definition C.6c.4a:
$$
H_{\rm idle}=0.
\tag{Q.0.7t.5.1}
$$
Each gate occupies one complete slot of duration $\tau_*$. For its full supported Hermitian matrix $L$, choose an integer $m\ge0$ with $2\pi m\ge\|L\|$, and put
$$
K_L=\frac\hbar{\tau_*}(L+2\pi m I),\qquad
H_L(s)=K_L,\quad 0<s<\tau_*.
\tag{Q.0.7t.5.2}
$$
The identity in $K_L$ is the identity on the full allocated quantum carrier. One common $m$ is used across both blocks of a coherently controlled operation. Its $2\pi m$ phase is recorded, not independently removed in the two blocks. The actual local coupling is the following finite spin Hamiltonian, including its scalar part:
$$
H_L(s)=\sum_{P\in\{I,X,Y,Z\}^{\otimes n}}a_P(s)P,
\qquad a_P(s)=2^{-n}\operatorname{Tr}[PH_L(s)]\in\mathbb R.
\tag{Q.0.7t.5.3}
$$
Only the port-$0$ factors occur in its nontrivial control support. All Pauli coefficients are constant during the slot, and the pulse is switched off at its endpoints. The finitely many coefficients, their supports, their entrance and exit switches and their bounds are supplied by the local pulse/controller service. This is a finite explicitly driven spin source. Equation (Q.0.7t.5.3) gives the delivered coupling, rather than only a stored target matrix. It is a prescribed certified local pulse of the already nominated finite local-unitary service. The graph, primitive contracts, tariff and inter-port communication rule are unchanged. The endpoint grammar is the control-word grammar defined here; the passive-payload heat grammar of Definition C.6c.4a and its decoder are separate.

At a slot boundary the source admits arbitrary states on the data and coherent interface carrier, with arbitrary external spectators, independently of its fresh supplier stock conditional on the classical descriptor. Invalid data-code states are not discarded: all gates and effects have the complete extensions specified here. Endpoint arming is the next valid typed command. Each unitary command has one instrument outcome; the perspective kernel is the identity on one nominated perspective. Readout commands have their complete two-outcome instruments. This specifies both clauses of Definition 27.

The fixed preparation of $(|0\rangle+|j\rangle)/\sqrt2$ uses the unitary $V_j$ that is the Hadamard matrix on $\operatorname{span}\{|0\rangle,|j\rangle\}$ and the identity on its complement. Its generator is $L_j^{\rm prep}=\frac\pi2(I-V_j)$, with spectrum in $\{0,\pi\}$. For a Hermitian contraction $A$ on the data, the binary effects are $E_\pm=(I\pm A)/2$. Allocate a fresh detector qubit in $|0\rangle$ and use
$$
\Theta=\arcsin\sqrt{E_-},\qquad
L_E=Y_{\rm det}\otimes\Theta,
\qquad
U_E=e^{-iL_E}=
\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt{E_+}&-\sqrt{E_-}\\ \sqrt{E_-}&\sqrt{E_+}\end{pmatrix}.
\tag{Q.0.7t.5.4}
$$
The source applies the explicit pulse (Q.0.7t.5.2), then the admitted computational-basis record service on that detector, with the detector and every durable outcome copy retained. Thus its selective data map at the complete slot boundary is $\rho\mapsto\sqrt{E_z}\rho\sqrt{E_z}$, accompanied by its detector, outcome and source records. A record service occupies its own complete clock slot. No detector, archive or coherent control is reset or reused as fresh.

The protocol tree has a fixed maximum slot count $S$; short branches use identity slots. Each fresh source preparation, prescribed pulse, record service, classical control evaluation and clock update is listed separately in the emitted finite word. A direct pulse occupies one slot; a binary readout therefore occupies its coupling slot and its separate record slot. Initial installation, coefficient production and checks precede acceptance of the unknown input and have their own finite scheduled slots and costs. The retention deadline is $(S+S_{\rm setup}+1)\tau_*$. It includes every reserved but unused branch stock. The source exposes completed quantum outputs, all selective outcomes, the complete classical word and branch history, the full preparation/driver/clock records and the complete resource ledger. It exposes no extra intrapulse command port and no archive-feedback port.

Use exactly the fixed positive tariff coefficients and counters of Definition C.6c.4a: allocated lanes, their idle time, all nonlane bits and bit-time, local pulse and record calls, link calls, clock slots and actual peak strength; the pulse action remains its separate retained record. The finite descriptions of all $4^n$ Pauli coefficients, including zero coefficients, occupy a certified finite number $B_{\rm desc}$ of controller bits. A supplied external waveform is the declared open control service, not an unlisted autonomous battery. Its required positive peak reserve is bounded by

R_L=1+\left\lceil B+2\pi m\right\rceil
\tag{Q.0.7t.5.5}

units of $\hbar/\tau_*$ for every pulse with certified bound $B$. The actual peak is charged by the inherited peak-strength term; the bound is not charged again as a second copy of that service. The source retains its full signed-work and gross-throughput formulae below, without representing the control reserve as reset heat. Unused branch stock and the common phase/clock service retain their allocated support, calls and intervals. Every counter is obtained from the emitted finite word and its owned intervals. <a id="theorem-q07t6-response-faithful-pu-realization-of-the-compact-group-controls"></a>**Theorem Q.0.7t.6 (Response-Faithful PU Realization of the Compact-Group Controls).** For every group and every $q$ in Theorem Q.0.7t.4, its minimal generating controls, their inverses and their coherently controlled updates have a realization in the source of Definition Q.0.7t.5. Product-equal control words have equal payload transformations; their possibly different durations, programmes, invoices and old records remain distinct in the full source response.

For the exact finite-description mode the construction applies to the canonical compact-Lie presentations and representations with their explicitly described structure and representation matrices. Every compact connected Lie-group isomorphism class admits such a presentation: root and weight lattices, finite central subgroups and torus characters are finite integral data, and the compact highest-weight matrix constructions use finite algebraic operations and square roots.
