### Q.6.4 Experimental Predictions

<a id="prediction-q61-no-leading-lorentz-violating-mdr-at-the-pce-attractor"></a>**Prediction Q.6.1 (No Leading Lorentz-Violating MDR at the PCE Attractor).** Modified dispersion relations (MDRs) are a widely studied candidate signature in quantum-spacetime phenomenology; their presence and form depend on the propagation model and are not implied by a fundamental discretization scale alone (Amelino-Camelia 2013, Sections 2.2.1 and 3.1–3.2; Mattingly 2005, Sections 2–3). On the joint branch consisting of the serialized-frontier calibration of Proposition Q.6.1, the full Corollary 46a/Appendix O Lorentzian-promotion package, and cone sharing by the retained propagation sector with no appended preferred-frame operator, leading-order Lorentz-violating MDR terms written separately in powers of $E$ and $p$ are absent:
$$
E^2-p^2c^2=m^2c^4+\text{Lorentz-invariant corrections}.
$$
On that joint branch, the exact factor
$$
\frac{\delta}{L_P}=\frac{\tau_{\min}}{t_P}=\sqrt{8\ln 2}
$$
fixes the invariant MPU cutoff
$$
\Lambda_{\mathrm{MPU}}:=\frac{\hbar c}{\delta}=\frac{E_P}{\sqrt{8\ln 2}}\approx0.42466\,E_P,
$$
but it is not, by itself, an effective Lorentz-violation energy scale $E_{\mathrm{QG}}$.

*Derivation.* Proposition Q.6.1 calibrates the spatial and temporal scales only after the independent attained-frontier premise is accepted; it does not establish Lorentzian kinematics. The full Corollary 46a/Appendix O package supplies the Lorentzian principal symbol, while cone sharing and the absence of an appended preferred-frame operator exclude a sector-specific leading LIV term. Under those combined hypotheses the displayed dispersion relation is Lorentz invariant. If a non-attractor preferred-frame term is appended, its coefficient is instead governed by Prediction Q.6.2. Thus the null prediction belongs to the stated joint branch, not to Theorem 46 or Proposition Q.6.1 alone. $\square$

<a id="prediction-q62-scale-ledger-bound-for-non-attractor-liv-branches"></a>**Prediction Q.6.2 (Scale-Ledger Bound for Non-Attractor LIV Branches).** If an explicitly appended non-attractor propagation branch introduces a leading photon-speed correction
$$
\frac{\Delta v}{c}=\xi_n\left(\frac{E}{\Lambda_{\mathrm{MPU}}}\right)^n+O\!\left(\left(\frac{E}{\Lambda_{\mathrm{MPU}}}\right)^{n+1}\right),
\qquad n\in\{1,2\},
$$
then, for $\xi_n\ne0$, the energy scale in the photon-dispersion convention of Vasileiou et al. (2013) and LHAASO Collaboration (2024), whose leading speed term is $\Delta v/c=-s(n+1)(E/E_{\mathrm{QG},n})^n/2$ with $s=-\operatorname{sgn}\xi_n$, is
$$
E_{\mathrm{QG},n}=\Lambda_{\mathrm{MPU}}\left(\frac{n+1}{2|\xi_n|}\right)^{1/n}.
$$
Thus an observational lower bound $E_{\mathrm{QG},n}>B_n$ in that convention and for the corresponding sign constrains the non-attractor branch coefficient by
$$
|\xi_n|<\frac{n+1}{2}\left(\frac{\Lambda_{\mathrm{MPU}}}{B_n}\right)^n.
$$
Within the deterministic photon-dispersion and source-emission models of the cited timing analyses, these bounds constrain the appended LIV branch. For $|\xi_1|=1$, the scale $E_{\mathrm{QG},1}=\Lambda_{\mathrm{MPU}}\approx0.42466E_P$ is below their quoted linear lower limits above $E_P$. For $|\xi_2|=1$, the corresponding scale is $E_{\mathrm{QG},2}=\sqrt{3/2}\,\Lambda_{\mathrm{MPU}}\approx0.52010E_P$, which is above their quoted quadratic lower limits and is not excluded by those limits. This comparison retains each analysis's sign, confidence level and source-systematic assumptions.

*Derivation.* Equating the magnitudes of the leading speed coefficients gives $|\xi_n|/\Lambda_{\mathrm{MPU}}^n=(n+1)/(2E_{\mathrm{QG},n}^n)$, which yields the scale and coefficient bound. The sign identity follows from the same coefficient comparison. If $\xi_n=0$, the order-$n$ scale is $E_{\mathrm{QG},n}=\infty$ by convention; any higher-order coefficients remain separate. The Lorentz-invariant attractor branch of Prediction Q.6.1 has no such leading LIV coefficient and is not excluded by finite lower limits on an appended branch's scale. $\square$

<a id="theorem-q62a-finite-rotational-mdr-class-and-coefficient-nonentailment"></a>**Theorem Q.6.2a (Finite Rotational MDR Class and Coefficient Nonentailment).** Let $J\ge2$ be an integer. Consider a real, translation-invariant, spatially rotation- and parity-invariant scalar quadratic propagation equation whose only time-derivative term is the canonically normalized $\partial_t^2$, with no mixed time--space derivatives and a polynomial spatial symbol of order at most $2J$. Register the constant coefficient $\mu^2\ge0$, a positive quadratic coefficient $c^2$, and a scale $\delta>0$. Its Fourier dispersion has the form
$$
\omega^2(k)
:=\mu^2+c^2|k|^2
+c^2\sum_{j=2}^{J}b_j\delta^{2j-2}|k|^{2j},
\tag{Q.6.2a.1}
$$
with real $b_j$. Conversely, every such coefficient vector for which the right-hand side is nonnegative on the retained momentum window defines a second-order equation with no exponentially growing Fourier mode on that window. A zero-frequency mode can still have a solution $A+Bt$, so nonnegativity alone is not boundedness of all solutions. Neither the cutoff length $\delta$ nor these symmetries determines any $b_j$.

On the massless branch, take one registered coefficient vector and let $b_j$ be its first nonzero entry. As $x:=\delta|k|\to0$ along the positive-frequency branch with $|k|>0$,
$$
\frac{v_g(k)}c
:=1+\frac{2j-1}{2}b_j(\delta|k|)^{2j-2}
+O\!\left((\delta|k|)^{2j}\right)
+O\!\left(b_j^2(\delta|k|)^{4j-4}\right).
\tag{Q.6.2a.2}
$$
The remainder constants and the neighborhood where this expansion applies may depend on the full coefficient vector. Smallness of the first displayed correction alone does not control arbitrarily large higher coefficients. If every $b_j=0$, the massless positive-frequency branch has $v_g=c$. The choices $b_2=\cdots=b_J=0$ and $b_2>0$, $b_3=\cdots=b_J=0$, give distinct Fourier symbols with the same cutoff and structural symmetries and no exponentially growing modes. Their responses differ on any retained window containing nonzero momenta.

*Proof.* Translation invariance diagonalizes the operator in Fourier space. Rotation and parity invariance make the real spatial polynomial a polynomial in $|k|^2$. The exact time-derivative premise contributes only $-\omega^2$, giving (Q.6.2a.1) after registering the constant and quadratic terms. For a retained Fourier mode, the equation is $\ddot f+\omega^2(k)f=0$: positive $\omega^2$ gives oscillations, zero gives $A+Bt$, and negative $\omega^2$ gives exponential solutions. This proves the stated modal scope.

For $\mu=0$, put $F(x)=1+\sum_{\ell=2}^Jb_\ell x^{2\ell-2}$. For the registered finite vector, $F(x)>0$ sufficiently near zero and $\omega=c|k|\sqrt{F(x)}$. Therefore
$$
\frac{v_g}c=\sqrt{F(x)}+\frac{xF'(x)}{2\sqrt{F(x)}}.
$$
Taylor expansion at $F(0)=1$ gives (Q.6.2a.2), with constants depending on the full polynomial. The zero and positive-$b_2$ examples prove coefficient nonuniqueness. ∎

<a id="theorem-q62b-rank-six-anisotropy-floor-for-shell-symmetric-symbols"></a>**Theorem Q.6.2b (Rank-Six Anisotropy Floor for Shell-Symmetric Symbols).** Fix $J\ge1$. Let $\ell$ be a real polynomial of order at most $2J$ on the retained momentum window in $\mathbb R^4$ that is invariant under the group $\Gamma^{+}$ of Proposition C.6h; this polynomial premise holds for a registered Taylor truncation of the symbol of a real translation-invariant operator on the $D_4$ lattice whose coupling function is constant on $\Gamma^{+}$-orbits, in particular for equal-weight root-shell couplings, with finite support, or sufficient absolute moment bounds, and a controlled truncation remainder on the registered window as in Theorem Q.6.2a. Then every homogeneous component of $\ell$ of degree at most $5$ is a real multiple of a power of $|k|^2$, and the degree-$6$ component lies in the span of $|k|^6$ and $T_6(k)$ of (C.6h.1). In the normalization of (Q.6.2a.1), in which the degree-$2j$ stratum carries the prefactor $\delta^{2j-2}$ relative to the quadratic term, no coefficient choice within this class produces a rotation-noninvariant term at relative order $(\delta|k|)^0$ or $(\delta|k|)^2$: the lowest-order rotation-noninvariant contribution enters at relative order $(\delta|k|)^4$, is proportional to the single anisotropic pattern of $T_6$, and its two displayed equal-weight shell moments are the Lemma C.6f defects $-1/d_0$ and $+1/M$. Along every fixed direction $\hat k$ the restriction $\ell(|k|\hat k)$ is a polynomial in $|k|^2$ whose coefficients through $|k|^4$ are direction independent, with direction dependence first possible in the $|k|^6$ coefficient. On the joint branch of Prediction Q.6.1 extended by the registered premise that the retained propagation symbol is $\Gamma^{+}$-invariant, rotation-noninvariant dispersion terms at relative orders $(\delta|k|)^0$ and $(\delta|k|)^2$ are therefore absent, the first admissible one is the $T_6$ stratum at relative order $(\delta|k|)^4$. A propagation experiment tests this exclusion after its Lorentzian, polarization, and observable maps identify the measured coefficient with this scalar symbol. This supplies the anisotropic sector of the microscopic coefficient map on this branch: below rank six the anisotropic coefficients are not free parameters but vanish identically, while the isotropic coefficients remain nonentailed exactly as in Theorem Q.6.2a.

*Proof.* For a finite-support real coupling function $c$ constant on $\Gamma^{+}$-orbits of the $D_4$ lattice, the exact trigonometric symbol is $\ell(k)=\sum_xc(x)e^{ik\cdot x}$; the product of the four sign changes lies in $\Gamma^{+}$, so $c$ is even and $\ell(k)=\sum_xc(x)\cos(k\cdot x)$ is real, and for $g\in\Gamma^{+}$ the substitution $x=gy$, which permutes the lattice by Proposition C.6h item 1, gives $\ell(gk)=\sum_yc(gy)\cos\left(gk\cdot gy\right)=\sum_yc(y)\cos(k\cdot y)=\ell(k)$ by orthogonality and orbit constancy. Its registered Taylor truncation inherits this invariance term by term. The action of $\Gamma^{+}$ on polynomials is linear and degree preserving, so every homogeneous component of an invariant polynomial is invariant, and Proposition C.6h items 2 and 3 give the stated component structure through degree $6$. The degree-$2$ and degree-$4$ strata are multiples of $|k|^2$ and $|k|^4$ and hence rotation invariant, so with the (Q.6.2a.1) prefactors the relative orders $(\delta|k|)^0$ and $(\delta|k|)^2$ carry no rotation-noninvariant term, and the degree-$6$ stratum at relative order $(\delta|k|)^4$ is the first that can, its rotation-noninvariant direction being spanned by $T_6$ modulo $|k|^6$; its equal-weight shell moments are the Lemma C.6f defects because $\frac1MT_6$ is the full contraction of the equal-weight sixth-moment tensor, by Proposition C.6h. Evenness makes the ray restriction $\ell(|k|\hat k)$ a polynomial in $|k|^2$; its coefficients through $|k|^4$ come from strata that are multiples of powers of $|k|^2$ and are direction independent, while the $|k|^6$ coefficient acquires the direction-dependent contribution proportional to $T_6(\hat k)$, and $T_6$ is nonconstant on the unit sphere by the values $12$ and $18$ recorded in Proposition C.6h. On the extended joint branch the retained propagation symbol lies in the classified class, so the exclusion at relative orders $(\delta|k|)^0$ and $(\delta|k|)^2$ and the identification of the first admissible pattern follow from the classification, and an observation contradicting the exclusion contradicts membership in the class for every coefficient assignment, falsifying the branch. The classification constrains no isotropic coefficient, so the Theorem Q.6.2a nonentailment statement for them is unchanged, while the anisotropic entries of the microscopic coefficient map are supplied identically zero below rank six on this branch. ∎

<a id="theorem-q62c-exact-d_4-shell-symbols-rank-six-amplitude-and-two-shell-cancellation"></a>**Theorem Q.6.2c (Exact $D_4$ Shell Symbols, Rank-Six Amplitude and Two-Shell Cancellation).** Let $a>0$, let $aD_4$ be the scaled $D_4$ lattice with nearest-neighbour spacing $\delta=\sqrt2\,a$, and for a finitely supported real coupling $w$ on $D_4\setminus\{0\}$ that is constant on $\Gamma^{+}$-orbits define
$$
\ell_w(k):=\sum_{y\in D_4\setminus\{0\}}w(y)\bigl(1-\cos(a\,y\cdot k)\bigr),
\qquad k\in\mathbb R^4.
\tag{Q.6.2c.1}
$$
Write $\Xi_2:=\Xi_{D_4}$ for the root shell and $\Xi_4$ for the $24$ lattice vectors of squared norm $4$, namely $\pm2e_i$ and $(\pm1,\pm1,\pm1,\pm1)$, and put $u:=(1,1,0,0)/\sqrt2$.

1. *Orbit-constant strata.* Every $\Gamma^{+}$-orbit $O$ satisfies $\sum_{y\in O}(y\cdot k)^2=\frac14|O||y|^2|k|^2$, $\sum_{y\in O}(y\cdot k)^4=\frac18|O||y|^4|k|^4$ and $\sum_{y\in O}(y\cdot k)^6=\alpha_O|k|^6+\beta_OT_6(k)$ with
   $$
   \beta_O=\frac16\sum_{y\in O}\bigl[(y\cdot u)^6-(y\cdot e_1)^6\bigr],
   \qquad
   \alpha_O+15\beta_O=\frac5{64}|O||y|^6.
   $$
   Consequently
   $$
   \ell_w(k)=\frac{a^2}2\kappa_2|k|^2-\frac{a^4}{24}\kappa_4|k|^4+\frac{a^6}{720}\bigl(\kappa_6|k|^6+\beta_wT_6(k)\bigr)+R_w(k),
   \tag{Q.6.2c.2}
   $$
   where $w_O$ is the value of $w$ on the orbit $O$, with $\kappa_2=\frac14\sum_yw(y)|y|^2$, $\kappa_4=\frac18\sum_yw(y)|y|^4$, $\kappa_6=\sum_Ow_O\alpha_O$, the rank-six amplitude $\beta_w=\sum_Ow_O\beta_O$, a linear functional of the orbit weights, and $|R_w(k)|\le\frac{a^8}{8!}\sum_y|w(y)||y|^8|k|^8$.
2. *Equal-weight root shell.* For $w=\mathbf 1_{\Xi_2}$, $\ell_{\Xi_2}(k)=24-4\sum_{i<j}\cos(ak_i)\cos(ak_j)\ge0$, with zeros exactly at $ak\in2\pi D_4^{*}$, and $(\kappa_2,\kappa_4,\kappa_6,\beta_w)=(12,12,0,1)$. With the quadratic stratum normalized,
   $$
   \frac{\ell_{\Xi_2}(k)}{3\delta^2}
   =|k|^2-\frac{\delta^2}{24}|k|^4+\frac{\delta^4}{17280}T_6(k)+\hat R(k),
   \qquad
   |\hat R(k)|\le\frac{\delta^6|k|^8}{5040}.
   \tag{Q.6.2c.3}
   $$
   Along a unit direction $\hat k$, $12\le T_6(\hat k)\le18$, with the minimum attained exactly on the directions of $\Xi_4$, the maximum exactly on the root directions, and spherical mean $15$. In the normalization of (Q.6.2a.1), the isotropic quartic coefficient is $b_2=-1/24$, the isotropic sextic coefficient is $15/17280=1/1152$, the rank-six anisotropy ranges over $[-3,3]/17280$ at relative order $(\delta|k|)^4$, and the relative Taylor remainder is at most $(\delta|k|)^6/5040$.
3. *Two-shell cancellation.* $\beta_{\Xi_4}=-8$ and $\alpha_{\Xi_4}=240$. For the positive coupling $w=\mathbf 1_{\Xi_2}+\frac18\mathbf 1_{\Xi_4}$, $\beta_w=0$, $\ell_w\ge0$ with the same zero set, and
   $$
   \frac{4\,\ell_w(k)}{15\delta^2}
   =|k|^2-\frac{\delta^2}{20}|k|^4+\frac{\delta^4}{720}|k|^6+\hat R_w(k),
   \qquad
   |\hat R_w(k)|\le\frac{\delta^6|k|^8}{2100}.
   \tag{Q.6.2c.4}
   $$
   Its degree-eight stratum is not a multiple of $|k|^8$, so its first rotation-noninvariant stratum occurs at relative order $(\delta|k|)^6$.

Within the class of Theorem Q.6.2b, the lattice, the $\Gamma^{+}$ symmetry and nonnegativity of the symbol therefore leave the rank-six amplitude undetermined: the normalized coefficient of $\delta^4T_6(k)$ is $1/17280$ in (Q.6.2c.3) for the equal-weight root shell and $0$ in (Q.6.2c.4) for the positive two-shell coupling. The two-shell coupling enlarges the support of the fixed root shell, so it is compatible with Theorem C.6g.

*Proof.* Item 1. For an orbit $O$, the power sums $\sum_{y\in O}(y\cdot k)^{p}$ are $\Gamma^{+}$-invariant homogeneous polynomials, because $\Gamma^{+}$ is orthogonal and permutes $O$; odd power sums vanish because $-I\in\Gamma^{+}$. By Proposition C.6h they are multiples of $|k|^2$ and $|k|^4$ in degrees $2$ and $4$ and lie in $\operatorname{span}\{|k|^6,T_6\}$ in degree $6$. On $\mathbb R^4$, $\Delta(y\cdot k)^2=2|y|^2$, $\Delta^2(y\cdot k)^4=24|y|^4$, $\Delta|k|^2=8$ and $\Delta^2|k|^4=192$, which fix the degree-two and degree-four constants. The values $T_6(e_1)=12$ and $T_6(u)=18$ of Proposition C.6h give $\beta_O$. The unit-sphere mean of $(y\cdot\hat k)^6$ is $15|y|^6/192$, so the mean of $T_6$ is $24\cdot8\cdot15/192=15$ and the mean of the orbit sum gives $\alpha_O+15\beta_O$. Expanding $1-\cos x=\frac{x^2}2-\frac{x^4}{24}+\frac{x^6}{720}-\cdots$ with Lagrange remainder at most $x^8/8!$ termwise gives (Q.6.2c.2).

Item 2. The identity $\cos(A+B)+\cos(A-B)=2\cos A\cos B$ applied to the four roots $\pm e_i\pm e_j$ of each coordinate pair gives the closed form. Every summand of (Q.6.2c.1) is nonnegative, and $\ell_{\Xi_2}(k)=0$ exactly when $a\xi\cdot k\in2\pi\mathbb Z$ for all roots, that is, $ak\in2\pi D_4^{*}$, because the roots generate $D_4$. Item 1 gives $\sum_\xi(\xi\cdot k)^2=12|k|^2$ and $\sum_\xi(\xi\cdot k)^4=12|k|^4$, in agreement with Lemma C.6f, and (C.6h.1) gives $\sum_\xi(\xi\cdot k)^6=T_6(k)$; substituting $a^2=\delta^2/2$ and dividing by $3\delta^2$ gives (Q.6.2c.3), with remainder constant $24\cdot16/(16\cdot8!\cdot3)=1/5040$. On the unit sphere put $v_i=\hat k_i^2$; then $T_6(\hat k)=60\sum_iv_i^2-48\sum_iv_i^3$ on the simplex $\sum_iv_i=1$, $v_i\ge0$. At an extremum the Lagrange condition on the positive coordinates is $120v_i-144v_i^2=\lambda$, so these coordinates take at most two values, which sum to $5/6$ when both occur. The resulting finitely many candidates give $12$ at $(1,0,0,0)$ and $(\frac14,\frac14,\frac14,\frac14)$, $18$ at $(\frac12,\frac12,0,0)$, $\frac{44}3$ at $(\frac13,\frac13,\frac13,0)$ and $(\frac34,\frac1{12},\frac1{12},\frac1{12})$, and $\frac{46}3$ at $(\frac23,\frac16,\frac16,0)$, which proves $12\le T_6(\hat k)\le18$; since every extremizer is a candidate, the minimizing directions are $\pm e_i$ and $\frac12(\pm1,\pm1,\pm1,\pm1)$, those of $\Xi_4$, and the maximizing directions are those of $\Xi_2$. Division of the degree-six coefficient by the quadratic one gives the stated normalized coefficients.

Item 3. The orbit $\Gamma\cdot2e_1\cup\Gamma\cdot(1,1,1,1)$ is one $\Gamma^{+}$-orbit because $r_v(2e_1)=(1,-1,-1,-1)$. At $e_1$ the sextic power sum of $\Xi_4$ is $2\cdot64+16=144$, and at $u$ it is $4\cdot8+8\cdot8=96$, so $\beta_{\Xi_4}=-8$ and $\alpha_{\Xi_4}=144+96=240$. Hence $T_6+\frac18(240|k|^6-8T_6)=30|k|^6$. Item 1 gives the degree-two and degree-four sums $24|k|^2$ and $48|k|^4$ for $\Xi_4$, so $\kappa_2=15$, $\kappa_4=18$ and $\kappa_6=30$; dividing by $\frac{15}4\delta^2$ gives (Q.6.2c.4), with remainder constant $(384+\frac18\cdot24\cdot256)\cdot4/(16\cdot8!\cdot15)=1/2100$. Positivity and the zero set follow as in item 2, since $\Xi_4\subset D_4$. The octic power sums $\sum_{\Xi_2}(\xi\cdot k)^8+\frac18\sum_{\Xi_4}(y\cdot k)^8$ equal $12+66=78$ at $e_1$ and $33+24=57$ at $u$, two unit vectors, so the degree-eight stratum is not radial. The final assertions compare items 2 and 3. ∎

<a id="theorem-q62d-complete-fixed-root-coupling-fiber-and-response-reconstruction"></a>

**Theorem Q.6.2d (Complete Fixed-Root Coupling Fiber and Response Reconstruction).** Let $a>0$, $\delta=\sqrt2\,a$, and let $\Xi_2$ be the $24$ roots in Theorem Q.6.2c. Consider every real even weighting $w(-\xi)=w(\xi)$ on this fixed support with $\sum_\xi w(\xi)=1$. Define
$$
Q_w:=\sum_{\xi\in\Xi_2}w(\xi)\xi\xi^{\mathsf T},\qquad
M_{j,w}(k):=\sum_{\xi\in\Xi_2}w(\xi)(\xi\cdot k)^j,
\qquad
L_w(k):=\sum_{\xi\in\Xi_2}w(\xi)\bigl(1-\cos(a\xi\cdot k)\bigr).
\tag{Q.6.2d.1}
$$
The corresponding real self-adjoint conservative scalar operator is the finite translation operator with Fourier symbol $L_w$. Nonnegative weights give a nonnegative quadratic form; item 2 also classifies signed weights whose full symbol is nonnegative. The signed domain is an operator-positivity class, whereas nonnegative edge-rate realizations use the simplex in item 1. All moment, reconstruction and uncertainty statements below concern this four-dimensional Euclidean scalar response.

1. *Complete isotropic quadratic fiber.* The condition $Q_w=I_4/2$ holds exactly for the following two-parameter family. Partition the six coordinate pairs into
   $$
   \mathcal M_1=\{12,34\},\quad
   \mathcal M_2=\{13,24\},\quad
   \mathcal M_3=\{14,23\}.
   $$
   There is a unique real triple $p=(p_1,p_2,p_3)$ with $\sum_mp_m=1$ such that
   $$
   w(\pm e_i\pm e_j)=\frac{p_m}{8}\quad(ij\in\mathcal M_m).
   \tag{Q.6.2d.2}
   $$
   Nonnegative couplings are exactly the simplex $p_m\ge0$. Strictly positive couplings are its interior. The equal-weight root shell is $p_*=(1/3,1/3,1/3)$.

2. *Exact symbol and complete nonnegativity domain.* Put $c_i=\cos(ak_i)$ and
   $$
   B_m(c):=\sum_{ij\in\mathcal M_m}c_ic_j.
   $$
   Then
   $$
   L_p(k)=1-\frac12\sum_{m=1}^3p_mB_m(c),\qquad
   L_p(k)\ge0\ \hbox{for every }k\in\mathbb R^4
   \iff p_m\le1\ \hbox{for every }m.
   \tag{Q.6.2d.3}
   $$
   Thus the complete stable-symbol domain in this isotropic fiber is the triangle with vertices $(-1,1,1)$, $(1,-1,1)$ and $(1,1,-1)$; the positive-coupling simplex is a proper subset. If every $p_m<1$, the zero set is exactly $ak\in2\pi D_4^*$, including for signed weights in this interior. On its boundary the following interpolation formula gives the complete zero set:
   $$
   L_p(c)=\sum_{s\in\{-1,1\}^4}\lambda_s(c)L_p(s),\qquad
   \lambda_s(c):=\prod_{i=1}^4\frac{1+s_ic_i}{2}.
   \tag{Q.6.2d.4}
   $$
   Here $L_p(s)=0$ when all four signs agree, $L_p(s)=1$ when one or three signs are negative, and $L_p(s)=2(1-p_m)$ when the two negative indices form one pair of $\mathcal M_m$. For a nonnegative symbol, $L_p(c)=0$ exactly when $\lambda_s(c)=0$ for every vertex with $L_p(s)>0$.

3. *Complete fourth-moment defect and its sharp size.* For $\alpha_m:=p_m-1/3$ and
   $$
   H_m(k):=\sum_{ij\in\mathcal M_m}k_i^2k_j^2,
   \qquad
   J_m(k):=\sum_{ij\in\mathcal M_m}(k_i^4k_j^2+k_i^2k_j^4),
   $$
   the exact moments are
   $$
   \begin{aligned}
   M_{2,p}(k)&=\tfrac12|k|^2,\\
   M_{4,p}(k)&=\tfrac12|k|^4+3\sum_m\alpha_mH_m(k),\\
   M_{6,p}(k)&=\tfrac12\sum_i k_i^6+\tfrac{15}{2}\sum_mp_mJ_m(k).
   \end{aligned}
   \tag{Q.6.2d.5}
   $$
   In particular, fourth-moment isotropy holds exactly at $p=p_*$. Every other point of the isotropic quadratic fiber has its first nonradial even moment in degree four, while $p_*$ has its first such moment in degree six by Lemma C.6f. Set $D_{4,p}(u):=M_{4,p}(u)-1/2$ for $|u|=1$, and let $d\sigma$ be normalized spherical measure. Its exact directional extrema and mean-square size are
   $$
   \min_{|u|=1}D_{4,p}(u)=\frac34\min_m\alpha_m,
   \quad
   \max_{|u|=1}D_{4,p}(u)=\frac34\max_m\alpha_m,
   \quad
   \int_{S^3}D_{4,p}(u)^2\,d\sigma(u)=\frac3{80}\sum_m\alpha_m^2.
   \tag{Q.6.2d.6}
   $$
   The normalized full symbol has the controlled expansion
   $$
   \frac{8L_p(k)}{\delta^2}
   =|k|^2-\frac{\delta^2}{24}|k|^4
   -\frac{\delta^2}{4}\sum_m\alpha_mH_m(k)
   +\frac{\delta^4}{720}M_{6,p}(k)+R_p(k),
   \qquad
   |R_p(k)|\le\frac{\delta^6|k|^8}{5040}\sum_m|p_m|.
   \tag{Q.6.2d.7}
   $$
   For nonnegative couplings the last sum is one. At $p_*$, (Q.6.2d.7) is exactly the normalized root-shell expansion (Q.6.2c.3).

4. *Finite-window reconstruction and deterministic uncertainty.* Choose the three unit root directions $u_1=(e_1+e_2)/\sqrt2$, $u_2=(e_1+e_3)/\sqrt2$ and $u_3=(e_1+e_4)/\sqrt2$. For any $r>0$ such that $A(r):=1-\cos(\delta r/2)>0$,
   $$
   M_{4,p}(u_m)=\frac{1+3p_m}{4},\qquad
   L_p(ru_m)=A(r)-\frac{p_m}{2}A(r)^2,
   \qquad
   p_m=\frac{2\bigl(A(r)-L_p(ru_m)\bigr)}{A(r)^2}.
   \tag{Q.6.2d.8}
   $$
   Thus three scalar Fourier responses at any such radius determine the entire root-supported operator. The compatible readings satisfy $\sum_mL_p(ru_m)=3A(r)-A(r)^2/2$; two readings suffice if the quadratic normalization is known exactly. If readings $\widetilde L_m$ have deterministic absolute errors at most $\epsilon_m$, define
   $$
   I_m:=\left[
   \frac{2(A-\widetilde L_m-\epsilon_m)}{A^2},
   \frac{2(A-\widetilde L_m+\epsilon_m)}{A^2}
   \right].
   \tag{Q.6.2d.9}
   $$
   The exact compatible coupling set is $\{p:\sum_mp_m=1,\ p_m\in I_m\}$ intersected with $p_m\ge0$ if nonnegative couplings are required, or with $p_m\le1$ if full-symbol nonnegativity is required. These intervals are necessary and sufficient under the stated independent deterministic error bounds. The componentwise inverse error factor is exactly $2/A(r)^2$, asymptotic to $128/(\delta r)^4$ as $r\to0$. For any two normalized triples,
   $$
   \sup_{k\in\mathbb R^4}|L_p(k)-L_{p'}(k)|
   =2\|p-p'\|_\infty.
   \tag{Q.6.2d.10}
   $$
   The reconstruction fixes $\delta$ and the response normalization. Errors in those calibrations require their own propagated intervals.

5. *Exact pullback of the local PCE tensor objective.* On every weighting in item 1, Theorem C.6e's tensor objective at $C_\Sigma=2$ takes the same minimum value $-\log\det(I_4/2)=4\log2$. Consequently its pullback to the declared nonnegative root-coupling class has the entire simplex as its minimizer set, although its minimizing tensor is unique. For example $p_*$ and $(1/2,1/3,1/6)$ have the same normalized quadratic tensor, objective, fixed root support and reciprocal zero set, but distinct symbols and distinct fourth moments. Fourth-moment isotropy singles out $p_*$ within this class; its physical admission or selection requires a coupling-level law in addition to the tensor objective. C.6e specifies feasible tensors and supplies no physical admission rule for every weighting in this pullback.

*Proof.* For a coordinate pair $i<j$, let $x_{ij}$ be the common weight of $\pm(e_i+e_j)$ and $y_{ij}$ the common weight of $\pm(e_i-e_j)$. The off-diagonal entry $(Q_w)_{ij}$ is $2(x_{ij}-y_{ij})$, so isotropy gives $x_{ij}=y_{ij}=:b_{ij}$. The diagonal entries give $4\sum_{j\ne i}b_{ij}=1/2$, hence all four weighted degrees equal $1/8$. Subtracting pairs of these equations yields $b_{12}=b_{34}$, $b_{13}=b_{24}$ and $b_{14}=b_{23}$. The remaining equation is $b_{12}+b_{13}+b_{14}=1/8$. Setting these values equal to $p_1/8,p_2/8,p_3/8$ proves necessity, uniqueness and sufficiency in item 1; their signs give its simplex assertions. This argument exhausts the twelve independent even weights rather than assuming coordinate-pair symmetry.

The four roots on a pair have cosine sum $4c_ic_j$. Each matching carries eight roots, so (Q.6.2d.2) gives (Q.6.2d.3)'s symbol formula. It is affine separately in each $c_i$. Repeated one-dimensional interpolation therefore gives (Q.6.2d.4). Its coefficients are nonnegative and sum to one on $[-1,1]^4$. Direct substitution gives the stated vertex values. Each cosine variable ranges independently over $[-1,1]$, so nonnegativity of every vertex is necessary and sufficient for nonnegativity at every momentum. The vertex values impose exactly $p_m\le1$. The three intersections of two of these boundary lines with $\sum_mp_m=1$ give the stated stable triangle. The interpolation also proves the zero-set test.

If all $p_m<1$, the only zero vertices are $(1,1,1,1)$ and $(-1,-1,-1,-1)$. If some $c_i$ is strictly between $-1$ and $1$, the interpolation support contains two vertices differing only at that coordinate. At least one is a positive vertex, because the two zero vertices differ in all four coordinates. Thus every zero has all $c_i\in\{-1,1\}$ and all signs equal. This says $ak\in2\pi\mathbb Z^4$ or $ak\in\pi(1,1,1,1)+2\pi\mathbb Z^4$, precisely $2\pi D_4^*$. This proves item 2 including the signed case.

Summing $(\pm k_i\pm k_j)^n$ over the four sign choices gives, for $n=4$, $4(k_i^4+6k_i^2k_j^2+k_j^4)$, and for $n=6$, $4(k_i^6+15k_i^4k_j^2+15k_i^2k_j^4+k_j^6)$. Multiplying by $p_m/8$ and using $\sum_mp_m=1$ proves (Q.6.2d.5). Every coefficient of $k_i^4$ is $1/2$. If the fourth moment is radial, its radial coefficient must therefore be $1/2$. Its mixed coefficient on a pair of $\mathcal M_m$ is $3p_m$ and the radial coefficient is one, forcing every $p_m=1/3$. Conversely these equalities give the radial fourth moment. The odd moments vanish by evenness; the second moment is radial throughout the fiber. Lemma C.6f supplies the nonradial sixth moment at its center.

For the extrema, put $v_i=u_i^2$ so $v_i\ge0$ and $\sum_iv_i=1$, and write $S(v)=\sum_m\alpha_m\sum_{ij\in\mathcal M_m}v_iv_j$. The symmetric matrix representing $S$ has zero diagonal, off-diagonal entries $\alpha_m/2$, and row sums zero. Its eigenvalues on the sum-zero subspace are $\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3$, using the three orthogonal sign vectors associated with the matchings. When $\alpha\ne0$, their sum zero forces both a positive and a negative eigenvalue, so there is no interior simplex maximum or minimum. On a triangular face, after permuting indices, its restriction is
$$
\alpha_1v_1v_2+\alpha_2v_1(1-v_1-v_2)+\alpha_3v_2(1-v_1-v_2).
$$
The Hessian determinant is $4\alpha_2\alpha_3-4\alpha_1^2<0$: indeed $\alpha_2\alpha_3\le\alpha_1^2/4$ since $\alpha_2+\alpha_3=-\alpha_1$, with strict negativity also when $\alpha_1=0$ and $\alpha\ne0$. Thus no relative face interior is an extremum. On an edge associated with $\mathcal M_m$, $S=\alpha_m t(1-t)$, giving extrema $\min_m\alpha_m/4$ and $\max_m\alpha_m/4$. Multiplication by three proves the first two assertions in (Q.6.2d.6); $\alpha=0$ is immediate.

The normalized spherical even-moment formula in four dimensions gives
$$
\int H_m^2\,d\sigma=\frac1{96},\qquad
\int H_mH_n\,d\sigma=\frac1{160}\quad(m\ne n).
$$
For completeness, the required eighth moments are $\int u_i^4u_j^4\,d\sigma=9/1920$, $\int u_i^4u_j^2u_l^2\,d\sigma=3/1920$ for distinct indices, and $\int u_1^2u_2^2u_3^2u_4^2\,d\sigma=1/1920$. These follow by pairing the eight coordinates and dividing by $4\cdot6\cdot8\cdot10$. Expanding $9\int(\sum_m\alpha_mH_m)^2d\sigma$ and using $\sum_m\alpha_m=0$ gives $9(1/96-1/160)\sum_m\alpha_m^2=3\sum_m\alpha_m^2/80$.

Taylor's theorem bounds the remainder in $1-\cos x=x^2/2-x^4/24+x^6/720+\text{remainder}$ by $|x|^8/8!$. Here $\sum_\xi|w(\xi)|=\sum_m|p_m|$ and $|\xi\cdot k|^8\le16|k|^8$. Multiplication by $8/\delta^2$ and $a^8=\delta^8/16$ yields the bound in (Q.6.2d.7). Substitution of (Q.6.2d.5) gives its other terms. At $p_*$, $M_{6,p}=T_6/24$ by its definition, giving (Q.6.2c.3).

On $k=ru_m$ the two cosine coordinates belonging to the nominated pair equal $C=\cos(\delta r/2)$ and the other two equal one. Consequently $B_m=C^2+1$ and the other two $B$ values are $2C$. Substitution in (Q.6.2d.3) gives $L_p=1-C-p_m(1-C)^2/2$, proving the exact inversion. The fourth-moment probe formula follows either from (Q.6.2d.5) or from the same ray expansion. The inversion is affine in its reading, so the independent error intervals give exactly (Q.6.2d.9) and their intersection with the chosen domain. Since $A(r)=\delta^2r^2/8+O(\delta^4r^4)$, its inverse factor has the stated asymptotic.

The difference $L_p-L_{p'}$ is again multiaffine in $c$. At the vertices its values are zero or $-2(p_m-p'_m)$. Interpolation bounds its absolute value by $2\|p-p'\|_\infty$, and a vertex associated with a maximizing component attains that value. Every such vertex is a cosine image of a momentum, proving (Q.6.2d.10). Finally, the constant tensor and its determinant establish item 5. The two displayed triples lie in the interior of the positive simplex and have all components below one. Item 2 gives their identical zero set; item 4 gives distinct responses, for example $L_{p_*}=4/3$ and $L_{(1/2,1/3,1/6)}=1$ at $ak=(\pi,\pi,0,0)$. This completes the proof. $\square$

<a id="proposition-q62e-parity-correct-gaussian-d4-transfer-and-conditional-source-causal-obstruction"></a>**Proposition Q.6.2e (Parity-correct Gaussian D4 transfer and conditional-source causal obstruction).**

**Hypotheses.** The coupling lies in the fixed-support scalar p-fiber of Theorem Q.6.2d. A Gaussian Euclidean action, a preferred coordinate time and its canonical positive-transfer continuation are added as assumptions; the tensor objective of Theorem C.6e is constant on the fiber (Theorem Q.6.2d, item 5).

**1. Parity of the time slices.**

Write $D_4=\{n\in\mathbb{Z}^4:\sum n_i\ \text{even}\}$, with physical lattice coordinates $an$. Designate coordinate 0 as time. Its $t=n$ slice has spatial parity $\sum x_i\equiv n\bmod 2$. The spatial translation lattice is $D_3$, not $\mathbb{Z}^3$. Pure time translation by $a$ and reflection $n\to 1-n$ do NOT preserve $D_4$. Pure time translation by $2a$ and site reflection $n\to -n$ do.

Spatial momenta satisfy $k\sim k+(\pi/a)(1,1,1)$. Under that identification the temporal Fourier variable shifts by $\pi$. Therefore the sign of a nearest-slice coefficient is not an obstruction to a positive *two-step* transfer, and reflection positivity on $D_4$ is tested with the site reflection $n\to -n$.

**2. Exact Gaussian covariance from the retained scalar symbol.**

Number the matching parameters so that $(01,23)$ has $p_1$, $(02,13)$ $p_2$, and $(03,12)$ $p_3$; $\sum p=1$. Put $c_i=\cos(ak_i)$, $i=1,2,3$, and

$$
\begin{aligned}
A&=\mu+1-(p_1 c_2 c_3+p_2 c_1 c_3+p_3 c_1 c_2)/2, \\
B&=(p_1 c_1+p_2 c_2+p_3 c_3)/2.
\end{aligned}
$$

The Gaussian action has multiplier $K(\omega,k)=A-B\cos\omega$, namely exactly $\mu+L_p(\omega/a,k)$, not a fitted polynomial. Assume $p_{m}\le 1$ (the exact full-symbol-positive domain) and $\mu>0$. Then $A-|B|\ge\mu$ and $A>0$. Fourier inversion gives, with $D=\sqrt{A^{2}-B^{2}}$,

$$
G_n(k)=r(k)^{|n|}/D(k),\qquad r=B/(A+D),\qquad |r|<1.
$$

At $B=0$ this is read as $G_0=1/A$, $G_n=0$ for $n\ne 0$. This formula follows by solving the covariance recurrence $AG_n-(B/2)(G_{n-1}+G_{n+1})=\delta_{n0}$, including its normalization. Fourier measure is normalized consistently on the parity quotient; a doubled full-zone representation has the same result after the parity constraint is imposed.

For finite linear test functions supported at times $n\ge 0$, reflection covariance is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{nm} \int dk\, \overline{f_n(k)}\, G_{n+m}(k) f_m(k) \\
&=\int dk\, D^{-1} |\sum_n r^n f_n(k)|^2 \ge 0.
\end{aligned}
$$

The allowed slice transforms obey $f_n(k+\pi\mathbf{1}/a)=(-1)^n f_n(k)$; $r$ changes sign under the same shift, so the integrand descends to the quotient. Gaussian reflection positivity for polynomial/Weyl observables follows from the positive reflected covariance by Gaussian Wick expansion (equivalently symmetric tensor powers). This establishes **site reflection positivity**.

For the following logarithmic Hamiltonian claim, restrict to infinite spatial volume with its ordinary $L^2$ momentum space. On the one-particle reconstruction, pure two-step temporal transfer is multiplication by $r^{2}$. It is positive and contractive. $B$ is a nonzero real-analytic trigonometric polynomial ($\sum p=1$), so its zero set has spatial measure zero; multiplication by $r^{2}$ is injective on the ordinary $L^2$ one-particle space. Its logarithm defines a densely defined positive self-adjoint generator. The full free-field generator is its bosonic second quantization. This is a Gaussian transfer construction on the stated action and slicing in infinite spatial volume. On a finite torus it fails: a sampled $B=0$ momentum has $G_0=1/A>0$ but all nonzero-time covariances zero. Its nonzero reflection-plane OS vector is annihilated by the two-step transfer. No densely defined self-adjoint $H$ can have $\exp(-\Delta t\,H/\hbar)$ annihilate a nonzero vector. Removing that sector would discard a source-active contact mode. For example, the spatial quotient $D_3/4\mathbb{Z}^3$ admits $k=(\pi/(2a))(1,1,1)$, with $G_0=1/(1+\mu)$ at equal weights. The logarithmic Hamiltonian is therefore asserted on infinite spatial $L^2$ only.

**3. Physical time, source, and dispersion.**

Choose an independent clock calibration $c>0$ so that the two-step elapsed physical time is $\Delta t=2a/c$. The reconstructed one-particle energy and angular frequency are

$$
\begin{aligned}
E(k) &= \hbar\, \Omega(k), \\
\Omega(k) &= (c/a) \operatorname{arcosh}[A(k)/|B(k)|].
\end{aligned}
$$

The formula follows from $r^{2}=\exp(-\Delta t\,\Omega)$. Near the origin $B>0$ it agrees with the appropriate analytic-continuation pole. The $B<0$ sector has an alternating one-slice sign; ignoring it loses a branch of the Euclidean source. The two-step expression and energy are invariant under the true spatial reciprocal identification.

A retained linear Euclidean source $J$ couples to the original scalar field: $Z[J]/Z[0]=\exp(\langle J,GJ\rangle/2)$. Its full slice-to-canonical-source interface is not trivial. Away from $B=0$ put $s(k)=\operatorname{sgn}B(k)$. Then $r^{|n-m|}=s^{n+m}\exp[-a\Omega|n-m|/c]$, so the original source at slice $n$ maps to $\tilde{J}_n(k)=s(k)^nJ_n(k)$. This is invariant under the spatial reciprocal parity identification because both $s$ and the odd-slice $J_{n}$ change sign. Even slices use the canonical field; odd slices require the $s$ multiplier, generally spatially nonlocal, rather than the bare canonical field at time $na/c$. This sign multiplier is part of the source map. The $B=0$ source-active finite-volume contact sectors remain excluded as stated above.

Fix canonical field normalization by $\langle\Phi(t,k)\Phi(0,-k)\rangle=D(k)^{-1}\exp[-i\Omega(k)t]$. For the source-Hamiltonian convention $H_J=H-\int J\Phi$, its linear retarded response is $\chi_R(t,k)=(2/[\hbar D(k)])\,\theta(t)\sin[\Omega(k)t]$, since $\chi_R=(i/\hbar)\theta(t)\langle[\Phi(t),\Phi(0)]\rangle$. Original odd-slice source/readout legs additionally carry the stated $s$ factors. This field carries one scalar polarization. Transverse polarizations, a gauge constraint and detector couplings for the selected equal-weight coupling are constructed in Theorem Q.6.2g.

For $\mu>0$ the rest frequency is $\Omega(0)=(c/a)\operatorname{arcosh}(1+2\mu)$. A rest energy $mc^{2}$ corresponds to $\mu=[\cosh(amc/\hbar)-1]/2$ under the clock calibration.

The $\mu\downarrow 0$ formulas hold pointwise away from all zero-frequency/$D=0$ sectors. For the full stable domain $p_{m}\le 1$, boundary parameters can have additional zero modes or zero sets; they are not exhausted by the constant mode. For example $p_1=1$ and $p_2+p_3=0$ gives $K(0,(0,\pi/a,\pi/a))=0$. The massless statements below are restricted to equal weights near the origin in infinite spatial volume.

**4. Equal-weight physical spatial asymptotic, distinct from the Euclidean defect.**

At $p_1=p_2=p_3=1/3$ and $\mu=0$, define $s_2=k_1^{2}+k_2^{2}+k_3^{2}$. On the low-momentum positive-$B$ branch,

$$
\Omega(k)^{2}/c^{2}=s_2+(a^{4}/90)[s_2^{3}-(k_1^{6}+k_2^{6}+k_3^{6})]+O(a^{6}|k|^{8}).
$$

Derivation: with $q=(i\Omega/c,k)$, $L(q)=a^{2}q^{2}/4-a^{4}(q^{2})^{2}/48+a^{6}M_6(q)/720+O(a^{8}|q|^{8})$. The quartic term vanishes to the needed order on the null cone. At $q^{2}=0$, $M_6(q)=-2\sum_\alpha q_\alpha^{6}=2[s_2^{3}-\sum_i k_i^{6}]$. Solving the leading quadratic equation gives the coefficient 1/90. The implicit analytic equation for $\Omega^{2}$ has nonzero derivative at the origin after removing the overall $a^{2}$ factor, so the displayed local series exists. The remainder is a local asymptotic.

The leading sixth-degree correction vanishes on spatial coordinate axes and is largest for equal absolute spatial components at fixed $|k|$, since $\sum_i k_i^{6}$ ranges from $s_2^{3}/9$ to $s_2^{3}$. The maximum bracket is $8s_2^{3}/9$. This is a three-dimensional statement on the chosen slice, distinct from the four-dimensional Euclidean defect of Theorem Q.6.2d. Equivalently $a^{4}/90=\delta^{4}/360$. Along an axis the exact check is $\cosh(a\Omega/c)=(5-2\cos ak)/(2+\cos ak)$; its difference from $\cosh(ak)$ begins $-(ak)^8/6048$, corroborating the absence of a sixth-order axial correction.

**5. Ultraviolet obstruction of this canonical completion.**

For equal weights, $k^*=(\pi/(2a),\pi/(2a),\pi/(2a))$ has $B=0$ and $A=1+\mu>0$, with $\nabla B=-(a/6)(1,1,1)\ne 0$. Both representatives of this point of the $D_3$ reciprocal quotient have $B=0$.

As a regular $B=0$ surface is approached,

$$
\begin{gathered}
\Omega=(c/a)[\log(2A/|B|)+O(B^{2}/A^{2})], \\
\nabla\Omega=(c/a)[\nabla A/A-\nabla B/B+O(B)]
\end{gathered}
$$

along smooth transverse paths with $A$ bounded away from zero. Consequently the group velocity is unbounded. The generator's Fourier multiplier also has a logarithmic singularity, hence is not finite-range in spatial lattice coordinates. Thus this particular canonical continuous-time completion cannot have a finite global signal cone of relativistic type; in particular no finite universal velocity bound can be inferred from its infrared speed $c$. There is also a direct strict-cone proof: at any fixed positive real time the retarded multiplier $D^{-1}\sin(\Omega t)$ oscillates without a limit on approach to a regular $B=0$ surface. It has no continuous representative there. A spatial kernel supported in a finite-radius lattice ball would have a trigonometric-polynomial Fourier transform, necessarily continuous. Hence this retarded response has no exact finite-radius support at that time. The unbounded wavepacket velocities separately rule out a finite global group-velocity bound.

The obstruction concerns this canonical completion with all lattice momenta retained.

**6. Exact conditioning and outstanding uncertainty joins.**

Away from $B=0$ and $D=0$, the dimensionless $\varepsilon=\operatorname{arcosh}(A/|B|)$ obeys

$$
d\varepsilon=[dA-(A/B)dB]/D.
$$

Thus the local deterministic bound is $|d\varepsilon|\le(|dA|+|A/B|\,|dB|)/D$. Derivatives of $A$ and $B$ are explicit linear functions of $dp$, $d\mu$ and trigonometric functions of $a,k$. Correlated coefficient uncertainty is propagated by this signed Jacobian (or exact interval image of $\operatorname{arcosh}(A/|B|)$), not by adding independent error bars without a covariance model. For $\Omega=c\varepsilon/a$,

$$
d\Omega=(c/a)d\varepsilon+(\varepsilon/a)dc-(c\varepsilon/a^{2})da,
$$

where $d\varepsilon$ includes the dependence of $ak$ on $a$ and $k$. Conditioning diverges at the $B=0$ surfaces, and also at the massless zero mode in these coordinates. A finite bound requires a stated compact experimental momentum window with lower bounds on $|B|$ and $D$. Inside this model the exact symbol has no polynomial truncation error.

<a id="theorem-q62f-six-shell-scalar-isotropy-cone-and-gaussian-reflection-boundary"></a>

**Theorem Q.6.2f (Six-Shell Scalar Isotropy Cone and Gaussian Reflection Boundary).**

Let $D_4=\{x\in\mathbb{Z}^4:\sum x_i\ \text{even}\}$, let $X_R=\{x\in D_4:|x|^{2}=R\}$, and restrict to the six squared radii $R=(2,4,6,8,10,12)$. Put $N_R=|X_R|=(24,24,96,24,144,96)$. Give each vector of $X_{R}$ the same nonnegative rate $w_{R}$, and define

$$
L_w(k)=\sum_R w_R \sum_{x\in X_R} [1-\cos(a\, x\cdot k)],\quad a>0.
$$

No probability or kinetic normalization is imposed unless explicitly stated. The zero vector of rates is excluded from minimal-support assertions. “Isotropic through order m” means every homogeneous Taylor term up to m is radial in four-dimensional **Euclidean** k. “Support size” below means number of used shells, not number of vectors.

1. The full nonnegative cone isotropic through order eight has exactly four extreme rays, in the displayed radius order:

   $$
   \begin{aligned}
   v_1&=(224,48,8,1,0,0), \\
   v_2&=(256,60,0,5,0,1), \\
   v_3&=(0,2640,1560,405,112,0), \\
   v_4&=(0,4020,0,1215,128,195).
   \end{aligned}
   $$

   Every such rate vector is a nonnegative linear combination of these rays. Exactly four shells are necessary and sufficient at minimum.

2. The full real solution space isotropic through order ten is one-dimensional. Its nonnegative part is the ray

   $$
   w=t(2736,780,200,45,8,1),\quad t\ge 0.
   $$

   Every nonzero member uses all six shells. No nonzero member is isotropic at order twelve, hence this restricted support class has no nonzero nonnegative solution isotropic through order twelve.

3. For $t=1$, $Q=\sum_x w_x\,xx^{\mathsf T}=85680\,I_4$, total rate mass is 105912, and $\sum_x w_x|x|^{2}=342720$. The normalization $Q=I_4/2$ is $t=1/171360$, **not** $t=1/105912$. Under the former normalization the total mass is $1471/2380<1$; under probability normalization $Q=(1190/1471)I_4$, not $I_4/2$.

4. For the order-ten rate vector at $t=1$, the massive scalar Gaussian precision $K_\mu=\mu+L_w$ with $\mu=1$ fails site-reflection positivity, even on strictly positive even-time slices of the actual $D_4$ lattice. The failure has finite spatial-support tests in infinite spatial volume. It is invariant under the correct spatial parity alias and persists under simultaneous positive scaling of rates and the additive precision parameter. It therefore obstructs the extension of Proposition Q.6.2e's canonical positive two-step construction to this stencil.

The classification concerns shell-constant rates on these six shells.

**Proof. I. Exact harmonic decomposition.**

For $P_{R,m}(k)=\sum_{x\in X_R}(x\cdot k)^m$, let $h_6$ and $h_8$ be the top harmonic projections of $P_{2,6}$, $P_{2,8}$, respectively. With $s_2=|k|^{2}$, the degree-six polynomial is

$$
h_6=-3[\sum_i k_i^6-5 \sum_{i\ne j} k_i^4 k_j^2+30 \sum_{i<j<l}k_i^2k_j^2k_l^2].
$$

Explicitly,

$$
h_8=(3/2)\sum_i k_i^8-14 \sum_{i\ne j}k_i^6k_j^2+49 \sum_{i<j}k_i^4k_j^4-42 \sum_i \sum_{j<l;\, j,l\ne i}k_i^4k_j^2k_l^2+756 \prod_i k_i^2.
$$

The shell moments are W(F4)-invariant. Fischer decomposition together with the invariant ring of degrees 2,6,8,12 gives one invariant harmonic at degrees six and eight, none at degree ten, and two at degree twelve. In particular, for $m\le 10$ only the radial part and the indicated h6/h8 descendants occur. The harmonic coefficients are

| $R$ | $N_R$ | $a_R$ (degree six) | $b_R$ (degree eight) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
|2|24|1|1|
|4|24|−8|16|
|6|96|12|−156|
|8|24|64|256|
|10|144|−210|870|
|12|96|−96|−2496|

For a homogeneous polynomial P of degree m in dimension four its top harmonic is

$$
H_m(P)=\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor m/2\rfloor} [(-1)^j (m-j)!/(4^j j!\, m!)]\, s_2^j \Delta^jP.
$$

Applying $\Delta$ proves this formula by pairwise cancellation. The complete shells are the signed coordinate permutations of the following representatives, with duplicates removed:

| R | Representatives and orbit cardinalities |
|---|---|
|2|(1,1,0,0): 24|
|4|(2,0,0,0): 8; (1,1,1,1): 16|
|6|(2,1,1,0): 96|
|8|(2,2,0,0): 24|
|10|(3,1,0,0): 48; (2,2,1,1): 96|
|12|(3,1,1,1): 64; (2,2,2,0): 32|

These lists exhaust all even-sum integer vectors of the indicated squared norms: each coordinate has magnitude at most three and the partitions of $R$ into four integer squares give exactly the listed cases. For any multi-index $\alpha$ of total degree $m$, the coefficient of $k^\alpha$ in $P_{R,m}$ is

$$
[m!/\prod_i\alpha_i!]\sum_{\xi\in X_R}\prod_i\xi_i^{\alpha_i}.
$$

The sum vanishes if any $\alpha_{i}$ is odd. Applying this coefficient formula to the displayed finite orbit lists and applying the harmonic projection gives every entry in the table. This is also a direct coefficient derivation of the polynomial identities below, independent of the invariant-ring description. More generally $\Delta P_{R,m}=m(m-1)R\,P_{R,m-2}$, and

$$
\Delta(s_2^j h_l)=2j(2l+4+2j-2)s_2^{j-1}h_l.
$$

Thus the **full**, not just top-harmonic, formulas are

$$
P_{R,6}=a_R h_6+(5/64)N_R R^3 s_2^3,
$$

$$
P_{R,8}=b_R h_8+(7/4)R a_R s_2 h_6+(7/128)N_R R^4 s_2^4,
$$

$$
P_{R,10}=(9/4)R b_R s_2 h_8+(35/16)R^2 a_R s_2^2 h_6+(21/512)N_R R^5 s_2^5.
$$

The radial coefficients follow by spherical averaging: $\mathbb{E}_{u\in S^3}(x\cdot u)^{2j}=|x|^{2j}(2j-1)!!/[4\cdot 6\cdots(2j+2)]$. Lower moments are $P_{R,2}=N_RRs_2/4$ and $P_{R,4}=N_RR^{2}s_2^{2}/8$. For completeness, the displayed finite-orbit coefficient formula yields the right-hand sides at every even multi-index of total degree six, eight and ten, on each of the six shells; direct differentiation gives $\Delta h_6=\Delta h_8=0$. Thus the finite statement does not require importing the invariant-ring classification. Sign symmetry kills all coefficients with an odd coordinate exponent.

Distinct Fischer harmonic summands are linearly independent. Consequently the order-eight equations are exactly

$$
\sum w_R a_R=0,\quad \sum w_R b_R=0,\quad \sum w_R R a_R=0.
\tag{A}
$$

The order-ten equations add exactly

$$
\sum w_R R b_R=0,\quad \sum w_R R^2 a_R=0.
\tag{B}
$$

This establishes necessity and sufficiency, including all lower-harmonic descendant constraints.

**II. Full cone and minimal support at order eight.**

The matrix of (A), with row order a,b,Ra, is

[1, −8, 12, 64, −210, −96;
 1, 16, −156, 256, 870, −2496;
 2, −32, 72, 512, −2100, −1152].

Its first three columns have determinant −1536; exact elimination gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
w_2&=224 w_8-810 w_{10}-864 w_{12}, \\
w_4&=48 w_8-150 w_{10}-180 w_{12}, \\
w_6&=8 w_8-15 w_{10}-40 w_{12}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{C}
$$

A nonzero nonnegative solution has $w_8>0$: if $w_8=0$, the first equality forces $w_{10}=w_{12}=0$ and all other entries vanish. Set $y=w_{10}/w_8$ and $z=w_{12}/w_8$. The feasible section is

$$
y,z\ge 0,\quad 810y+864z\le 224,\quad 15y+40z\le 8.
$$

The $w_4$ inequality is redundant. Indeed $(55/324)$ times the first displayed upper bound plus $(5/6)$ times the second bounds $150y+180z$ by $3620/81<48$; hence $w_4/w_8\ge268/81>0$.

The polygon's four vertices are

$$
(y,z)=(0,0),\ (0,1/5),\ (112/405,0),\ (128/1215,13/81).
$$

Substitution in (C) gives exactly v1–v4, each up to positive scale. A convex polygon is the convex hull of its vertices, so the original cone is exactly their positive hull; vertices give precisely the extreme rays. Each listed ray has four nonzero entries. Since nonnegative summation cannot cancel a positive entry, every nonzero cone element has support containing the support of at least one extreme ray; therefore fewer than four shells is impossible, and the four rays attain the minimum.

**III. Order ten and the order-twelve obstruction.**

Appending (B) and reducing gives the exact reduced row-echelon matrix

[1,0,0,0,0,−2736;
 0,1,0,0,0,−780;
 0,0,1,0,0,−200;
 0,0,0,1,0,−45;
 0,0,0,0,1,−8].

Its rank is five and its real nullspace is the line spanned by (2736,780,200,45,8,1); its nonnegative part is the stated positive ray. Thus all six shells are necessary, even before imposing nonnegativity on nonzero solutions.

At $t=1$, substitution of the rate vector into the proved moment formulas gives the radial coefficients

$$
\begin{aligned}
P_{w,2}&=85680\, s_2, \\
P_{w,4}&=181440\, s_2^2, \\
P_{w,6}&=604800\, s_2^3, \\
P_{w,8}&=2661120\, s_2^4, \\
P_{w,10}&=14152320\, s_2^5.
\end{aligned}
$$

At degree twelve the two unit directions e1 and (e1+e2)/sqrt(2) have moments 89510400 and 86123520, differing by 3386880. Their norms are equal, so this disproves radiality; the spherical average is 86961600. As an independent structural check, the surviving descendant coefficient sums are

$$
\sum w_R R^3 a_R=-230400,\qquad \sum w_R R^2 b_R=161280.
$$

The corresponding degree-twelve descendants are $(77/32)s_2^{3}h_6$ and $(27/8)s_2^{2}h_8$ times those sums, alongside the degree-twelve top harmonic; their nonzero values already prevent radiality by Fischer uniqueness. Since every through-twelve solution must first solve (A),(B), the one-dimensional nullspace and this failure exclude every nonzero through-twelve solution within the six-shell class.

**IV. Exact-symbol positivity, asymptotics and normalization.**

At $t=1$ the symbol has radial expansion through order ten

$$
L_w(k)=42840\, a^2s_2-7560\, a^4s_2^2+840\, a^6s_2^3-66\, a^8s_2^4+(39/10)a^{10}s_2^5+R_{12}(k).
$$

Taylor's theorem for cosine gives the global finite bound

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lvert R_{12}(k)\rvert&\le(a\lvert k\rvert)^{12}[\sum_R N_Rw_RR^{6}]/12!\\
&=(3904/693)(a\lvert k\rvert)^{12},
\end{aligned}
$$

since the numerator is 2698444800. This bounds the first omitted term together with the tail. The leading order-twelve difference between the two unit rays, evaluated at $k=\rho u$, is $-(7/990)(a\rho)^{12}$. Its higher remainder is $O((a\rho)^{14})$; a uniform one-ray bound for the remainder after degree twelve is $(2368/9009)(a\rho)^{14}$. All displayed expansions and bounds multiply by $t$ for a general nonnegative scaling.

Each cosine summand is nonnegative, so the **exact** symbol is nonnegative for all $k$, despite the alternating signs of its truncated Taylor polynomial. For $t>0$ all six shell rates are positive. Because the root shell generates $D_4$, the exact zero set is precisely $ak\in 2\pi D_4^*$ (dual-lattice convention $D_4^*=\{y:y\cdot x\in\mathbb{Z}\ \text{for all}\ x\in D_4\}$).

The rate and second-moment normalizations are different constraints. For any nonnegative stencil on shells with $R\ge 2$, probability mass one implies $\operatorname{tr}Q=\sum_R N_Rw_RR\ge 2$, with equality only if every positive rate is on $R=2$. Thus any strictly positive higher-shell mass makes probability normalization and $Q=I_4/2$ incompatible at fixed coordinates. For the order-ten ray, $Q=I_4/2$ gives total mass $1471/2380$. A zero-jump mass $909/2380$ completes a probability measure without changing the symbol; it enlarges the support by the zero displacement. Changing a rate clock or the lattice scale is a separate normalization.

**V. Gaussian precision and the actual D4 parity quotient.**

Let $D_4=\{(n,x)\in\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}^3:n+\sum x_i\ \text{is even}\}$, with physical coordinate spacing $a>0$. Let $X_{R}$ be its full shell of squared radius $R$. Use the scalar Gaussian precision

$$
K_\mu(\theta,k)=\mu+\sum_R w_R \sum_{\xi\in X_R}[1-\cos(\xi_0 \theta+a\, \xi_{\mathrm{sp}}\cdot k)],
$$

where $\theta=a\omega$ is dimensionless temporal frequency. The action normalization is one-half times this positive quadratic form; the covariance multiplier is $K_\mu^{-1}$. All rates are positive, so $K_\mu\ge\mu$ on real momenta. We fix $\mu=1$ in these raw rate units throughout the proof.

Every even-time slice has spatial lattice $D_3=\{x\in\mathbb{Z}^3:\sum x_i\ \text{even}\}$. Pure time translation by $2a$ and site reflection $n\mapsto -n$ preserve $D_4$; pure time translation by $a$ and the $\mathbb{Z}^4$ link reflection $n\mapsto 1-n$ do not. This proof uses only the former valid operations.

Choose a representative for each $D_3$ spatial character. The alternative representative $k+(\pi/a)(1,1,1)$ satisfies

$$
K_\mu(\theta,k+\pi\mathbf{1}/a)=K_\mu(\theta+\pi,k),
$$

because $\sum\xi_{\mathrm{sp}}\equiv\xi_0\bmod 2$. With

$$
G_n(k)=(1/2\pi)\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \exp(in\theta)/K_\mu(\theta,k)\, d\theta,
$$

it follows that $G_n(k+\pi\mathbf{1}/a)=(-1)^nG_n(k)$. In particular **every even-time covariance is representative-independent**. The even-time tests used below are legitimate functions on the actual spatial reciprocal quotient. A full-zone parity representation or a normalized quotient representation gives the same sign; a possible common positive Fourier-measure normalization cannot remove the obstruction.

**VI. Temporal polynomial and exact root brackets.**

At spatial momentum $k=0$ the total per-vector rates with a given absolute temporal jump are

| Absolute temporal jump $j$ | Weighted count $A_j$ |
|---:|---:|
|0|43052|
|1|55440|
|2|7308|
|3|112|

$A_{j}$ includes both signs of the temporal coordinate. The $j=0$ vectors make no contribution to $K_\mu(\theta,0)$. Using $\cos(2\theta)=2x^{2}-1$ and $\cos(3\theta)=4x^{3}-3x$, $x=\cos\theta$,

$$
K_\mu(x)=\mu+55440(1-x)+7308(1-(2x^{2}-1))+112(1-(4x^{3}-3x))=\mu+70168-55104x-14616x^{2}-448x^{3}.
$$

At $\mu=1$ its exact endpoint values are

$$
\begin{aligned}
K(-29)&=302401,\quad K(-27)=-279103, \\
K(-6)&=-28615,\quad K(-5)=36289, \\
K(1)&=1,\quad K(2)=-102087.
\end{aligned}
$$

The intermediate value theorem gives roots $r_1\in(-29,-27)$, $r_2\in(-6,-5)$, $r_3\in(1,2)$. These are three distinct roots of a cubic and therefore exhaust its roots and are simple. All lie outside $[-1,1]$, as also required by $K(\cos\theta)\ge 1$. Factoring

$$
K(x)=-448(x-r_1)(x-r_2)(x-r_3)
$$

gives $K'(r_1)<0$, $K'(r_2)>0$, $K'(r_3)<0$ exactly, without numerical root approximations.

**VII. Signed covariance atoms.**

For each real root r outside [−1,1], define

$$
q(r)=r-\operatorname{sgn}(r)\sqrt{r^2-1},\qquad |q(r)|<1.
$$

The elementary Poisson/geometric-series identity is

$$
1/(r-\cos\theta)=[\operatorname{sgn}(r)/\sqrt{r^2-1}] \sum_{n\in \mathbb{Z}} q(r)^{|n|} \exp(in\theta).
$$

It follows either by summing the two geometric series or by multiplying through by $r-\cos\theta$. Partial fractions, valid because all roots are simple, give

$$
1/K(x)=\sum_i [1/K'(r_i)]/(x-r_i).
$$

Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}
G_n(0)&=\sum_{i=1}^3 c_i q_i^{|n|}, \\
q_i&=q(r_i), \\
c_i&=-\operatorname{sgn}(r_i)/[K'(r_i)\sqrt{r_i^2-1}].
\end{aligned}
$$

The preceding exact root and derivative signs imply

$$
c_1<0,\quad c_2>0,\quad c_3>0.
$$

Set $\lambda_i=q_i^{2}$. Since $|r_1|>|r_2|>|r_3|>1$ and $u-\sqrt{u^{2}-1}$ is strictly decreasing on $u>1$,

$$
0<\lambda_1<\lambda_2<\lambda_3<1.
$$

The parity change of spatial representative sends $q_{i}$ to $-q_i$ but leaves $c_i$, $\lambda_i$ and every $G_{2n}$ unchanged. In particular the negative atom is not the odd-slice sign of the nearest-slice case of Proposition Q.6.2e.

**VIII. Failure on strictly positive even-time slices.**

For the times $0,2,4$, the reflected covariance matrix is $H_{ij}=G_{2(i+j)}(0)$, $i,j=0,1,2$. Writing $V_{ij}=\lambda_j^i$ gives

$$
H=V \operatorname{diag}(c_1,c_2,c_3) V^{\mathsf T},
$$

$$
\det H=c_1c_2c_3 \prod_{i<j}(\lambda_j-\lambda_i)^2<0.
$$

A negative determinant for this real symmetric matrix rules out positive semidefiniteness. More strongly, no reflection-plane/contact ambiguity is needed. On strictly positive times 2,4,6, choose real coefficients

$$
\alpha_1=\lambda_2\lambda_3,\quad \alpha_2=-(\lambda_2+\lambda_3),\quad \alpha_3=1.
$$

Their time polynomial is $p(\lambda)=\alpha_1\lambda+\alpha_2\lambda^{2}+\alpha_3\lambda^{3}=\lambda(\lambda-\lambda_2)(\lambda-\lambda_3)$. Consequently the reflected quadratic form is exactly

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i,j=1}^3 \alpha_i G_{2(i+j)}(0) \alpha_j \\
&=\sum_j c_j p(\lambda_j)^2 \\
&=c_1 \lambda_1^2(\lambda_1-\lambda_2)^2(\lambda_1-\lambda_3)^2<0.
\end{aligned}
$$

All these time slices exist on $D_4$ and are exchanged with their negative counterparts by the actual site reflection. Equivalently the strictly-positive-time Hankel determinant equals the preceding determinant times $\prod_i\lambda_i^{2}$ and remains negative.

The result excludes reflection positivity of the Gaussian measure already for a linear field observable.

**IX. Finite spatial-support witnesses.**

At $k=0$ the preceding form is strictly negative. Because $K_1(\theta,k)\ge 1$ and the precision is a finite trigonometric polynomial, each fixed $G_n(k)$ is continuous in $k$ by dominated convergence. Keep the $\alpha_{i}$ fixed at the $k=0$ values. Then

$$
F(k)=\sum_{i,j=1}^3 \alpha_i G_{2(i+j)}(k) \alpha_j
$$

is strictly negative on an open neighborhood $U$ of zero in the $D_3$ reciprocal torus. Choose a nonzero spatial Fourier test $g$ supported in $U$, with the even-slice parity identification. Its reflected norm is $\int|g(k)|^{2}F(k)\,dk<0$. One may choose $U$ and $g$ inversion-symmetric to obtain real field tests.

This gives a valid infinite-volume $L^2$ source, not a single nonnormalizable plane wave. If the test algebra is restricted to finite spatial support, trigonometric polynomials for $D_3$ are dense in the reciprocal-torus $L^2$ space. Since the covariance is bounded ($K_1^{-1}\le 1$), the reflected form is continuous under such approximation. A sufficiently close finite-support approximation therefore still has negative reflected norm. Alternatively, a finite periodic spatial quotient $D_3/(2M\mathbb{Z}^3)$, $M\ge 1$ an integer, contains the zero character as an actual finite-dimensional mode and directly admits the displayed constant-spatial test.

**X. Scaling and the continuation boundary.**

The stencil's kinetic normalization $Q=I_4/2$ scales its raw rates by $t=1/171360$. To retain the same dimensionless Gaussian precision up to overall scale, also scale the additive mass parameter from $\mu=1$ to $\mu'=t$. Then

$$
K'=tK_1,\qquad G'=t^{-1}G,
$$

so all reflected quadratic-form signs are unchanged. Scaling only the rates at fixed $\mu=1$ is a different mass-to-rate model. The parameter $\mu$ is an additive precision parameter.

Proposition Q.6.2e is a conditional Gaussian same-symbol construction on the fixed-root scalar $p$-fiber, where $K=A-B\cos\theta$ yields one covariance atom, whose even-step weight is nonnegative. The present longer-temporal-range precision has three atoms, one negative. Positive Euclidean Fourier multiplier and nonnegative jump rates are therefore insufficient for that canonical positive two-step reconstruction. The failure persists after restricting to strictly positive even slices and after the correct $D_4$ spatial alias quotient.

This proves the theorem. ∎

<a id="theorem-q62g-stationary-selected-root-propagation-source"></a>

**Theorem Q.6.2g (Stationary-Selected Root Propagation Source).** Let $a>0$, let $D_4=\{x\in\mathbb Z^4:\sum_ix_i\ \text{even}\}$ carry coordinate spacing $a$, let $\Xi_2$ be its $24$ roots, and let $T_r$ be translation by $r$. Fix a cell gap $\epsilon>0$, a length unit $u_L>0$ and a time unit $u_T>0$. The source of this theorem is an explicitly appended non-attractor propagation branch in the sense of Prediction Q.6.2. It consists of a code controller, a port array, a transverse gauge-field module whose matrices one fixed interpreter computes from the controller's stationary law, finitely many exchange ports, clock references and retained records, specified in items 1–6.

1. *Stationary selection of the coupling.* The controller states are the codes $r\in D_4\setminus\{0\}$, with excitation energy $\epsilon\lVert r\rVert^2$ carried by unary cells (cell $j$ of a coordinate has energy $(2j-1)\epsilon$). At each step a root $s\in\Xi_2$ is drawn uniformly and recorded; the code moves to $r+s$ if $r+s\ne0$ and $\lVert r+s\rVert^2\le\lVert r\rVert^2$, and otherwise stays, and any released energy is transferred to a fresh ground-state register that is retained. This chain has the unique stationary probability
$$
q_r=\tfrac1{24}\quad(r\in\Xi_2),\qquad q_r=0\quad(r\notin\Xi_2)
\tag{Q.6.2g.1}
$$
on all of $D_4\setminus\{0\}$; every initial law converges to $q$, and the controller restricted to an energy ball $\lVert r\rVert^2\le M$ has the same stationary law. If the initial law gives probability at most $\delta_M$ to $\lVert r\rVert^2>M$, then after $m+3b$ steps
$$
\operatorname{TV}\bigl(\operatorname{law}(r_{m+3b}),q\bigr)\le\min\Bigl\{1,\ \delta_M+B(m,N)+\bigl(\tfrac{575}{576}\bigr)^{b}\Bigr\},\qquad N=\max\bigl\{0,\lfloor(M-2)/2\rfloor\bigr\},
\tag{Q.6.2g.2}
$$
where $B(m,N)=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\binom mj24^{-j}(23/24)^{m-j}$ for $m\ge N$, $B(m,0)=0$, and $B(m,N)=1$ for $m<N$.

2. *Port form of the selected coupling.* The interpreter sets the port amplitudes from $q$, $W_qf=\bigoplus_r\sqrt{12q_r}\,(T_r-I)f$. Then
$$
W_q^*W_q=L_q=24I-\sum_{r\in\Xi_2}T_r,\qquad
\ell_q(k)=24-4\sum_{1\le i<j\le4}\cos(ak_i)\cos(ak_j)=24\,L_{p_*}(k),
\tag{Q.6.2g.3}
$$
where $L_{p_*}$ is the equal-weight symbol of Theorem Q.6.2d.

3. *Census of translation-invariant operators.* Let $m\ge1$. A closed densely defined operator on $\ell^2(D_4;\mathbb C^m)$ whose graph is invariant under every translation is, after Fourier transform, multiplication by a measurable, almost everywhere finite matrix field $M(k)$ on the dual torus, with domain $\{f:M\hat f\in L^2\}$; the field is unique up to null sets, and every such field defines such an operator. The operator is bounded, self-adjoint, nonnegative, real or covariant under a lattice symmetry $g$ exactly when, almost everywhere, $M$ is essentially bounded, Hermitian, positive semidefinite, satisfies $M(-k)=\overline{M(k)}$, or satisfies $M(gk)=U_gM(k)U_g^*$. The orbit-constant couplings of Theorem Q.6.2c are the scalar fields with $M(gk)=M(k)$ for every $g\in\Gamma^+$; every other field lies outside the orbit-constant class. With the fourth coordinate as Euclidean time, a bounded stationary matrix sequence with $C_{-n}=C_n=C_n^*$ at fixed spatial momentum satisfies $\sum_{i,j\ge0}v_i^*C_{i+j}v_j\ge0$ for every finite vector list exactly when
$$
C_n=\int_{[-1,1]}r^{|n|}\,d\mu(r)
\tag{Q.6.2g.4}
$$
for a unique finite positive matrix measure $\mu$; the inequalities with $C_{i+j+1}$ in place of $C_{i+j}$ hold in addition exactly when $\mu$ is supported in $[0,1]$.

4. *Transfer, gauge carrier and dispersion.* For spatial momentum $k\in\mathbb R^3$ put $c_i=\cos(ak_i)$, $S=\sum_ic_i$, $A=24-4\sum_{i<j\le3}c_ic_j$, $B=4S$ and $D=\sqrt{A^2-B^2}$. Then $\ell_q=A-B\cos(ak_4)$ and $A\ge|B|$, with equality exactly when $c_1=c_2=c_3=\pm1$. Where $D>0$ and $B\ne0$,
$$
E=a^{-1}\operatorname{arcosh}(A/|B|),\qquad
C_n=\frac{\bigl(\operatorname{sgn}(B)\,e^{-aE}\bigr)^{|n|}}{D},\qquad
Z=\frac{2E}{D},
\tag{Q.6.2g.5}
$$
and $C_n$ is the Fourier inverse of $1/\ell_q$ in $k_4$. Let $\mathcal B$ be the spatial Brillouin torus of $D_3=\{x\in\mathbb Z^3:\sum_ix_i\ \text{even}\}$ with normalized Haar measure, let $b_1=(1,1,0)$, $b_2=(1,0,1)$, $b_3=(0,1,1)$ be the columns of $B_{\mathrm{sp}}$, and let $d(k)=a^{-1}B_{\mathrm{sp}}^{-\mathsf T}\bigl(\sin(ab_1\cdot k),\sin(ab_2\cdot k),\sin(ab_3\cdot k)\bigr)^{\mathsf T}$. The gauge module has the action
$$
S_L=\frac12\int dt\int_{\mathcal B}\Bigl(\bigl\lvert\dot A-i\,d\,A_0\bigr\rvert^2-\frac{E^2}{\lvert d\rvert^2}\bigl\lvert i\,d\times A\bigr\rvert^2\Bigr)dk .
\tag{Q.6.2g.6}
$$
Outside the null set $\{S=0\}\cup\{D=0\}\cup\{d=0\}$, Gauss reduction leaves two transverse oscillators of frequency $E(k)$, and with $P_T=I-dd^{\mathsf T}/\lvert d\rvert^2$ and $A_E=\sqrt Z\,A$ the vacuum Schwinger function is
$$
\bigl\langle\mathcal T_E\,A_E(k,2an)\,A_E(-k,0)\bigr\rangle=P_T(k)\,C_{2n}(k).
\tag{Q.6.2g.7}
$$
Real time is generated by $e^{-itH}$ with $H=d\Gamma(E)$ on the transverse Fock space. The dispersion has the expansion
$$
E(k)^2=\lvert k\rvert^2+\frac{a^4}{90}\Bigl(\lvert k\rvert^6-\sum_{i=1}^3k_i^6\Bigr)+O\bigl(a^6\lvert k\rvert^8\bigr),
\tag{Q.6.2g.8}
$$
with no term of order $a^2\lvert k\rvert^4$; the sextic term equals $a^4(k_1^2+k_2^2)(k_1^2+k_3^2)(k_2^2+k_3^2)/30$. Physical units are $x_{\mathrm{phys}}=u_Lx$, $t_{\mathrm{phys}}=u_Tt$, $\nu=E/u_T$ and $H_{\mathrm{phys}}=(\hbar/u_T)H$, and the field and current gains are $\sqrt{Z/(\hbar u_T)}$.

5. *Observables.* An exchange port $b$ of frequency $\omega$, coupled to a normalized transverse wave packet $f$ by the driven Hamiltonian $H_c(t)=\hbar\sum_j\bigl[\gamma_j(t)\,b^\dagger a_j+\overline{\gamma_j(t)}\,a_j^\dagger b\bigr]$ with $\gamma_j(t)=g\,\overline{f_j}\,e^{-i(\omega-\nu_j)t}$, generates exactly the interaction-picture exchange $\hbar g\,[b^\dagger a(f)+a(f)^\dagger b]$ and conserves the total excitation number. Pulses of area $\pi/2$ swap a field mode with a fresh port, which prepares the vacuum, or a one-photon packet when the port is excited. On the one-excitation sector a detector pulse of area $\theta$ registers a photon in $f$ with probability $\sin^2\theta\,\operatorname{Tr}[\rho\,a(f)^\dagger a(f)]$, a polarization analyzer $f$ applied to a one-photon state $\psi$ gives $\lvert\langle f,\psi\rangle\rvert^2$, and the Ramsey readout against a reference port of frequency $\omega$, with the phase of each pulse referenced to its own start time (or with impulsive pulses), gives
$$
p_\pm(T,\phi)=\tfrac12\bigl[1\pm\cos\bigl((\nu_j-\omega)T+\phi\bigr)\bigr].
\tag{Q.6.2g.9}
$$
Every finite adaptive protocol built from these operations, the clock references and the controller has a normalized history law $p(h\mid\theta)=\operatorname{Tr}[K_h\rho_0K_h^\dagger]$.

6. *One uncertainty law.* For one compact parameter set $\Theta$ covering the source constants, the selector history, the units, the controls, the clock records and the readouts, the predictions form the single image $\{(p(h\mid\theta))_h:\theta\in\Theta\}$. For two parameter records with initial trace distance $\delta_\rho$, per-step unitary discrepancies $\delta_l$ and instrument discrepancies $\epsilon_l$ (half the diamond distance),
$$
\operatorname{TV}(p,p')\le\min\Bigl\{1,\ \delta_\rho+\sum_l(\delta_l+\epsilon_l)\Bigr\},
\tag{Q.6.2g.10}
$$
without any independence assumption. The selector discrepancy (Q.6.2g.2), the window and energy-mesh error $Q\,T\,\Delta$ of a finite realization with excitation budget $Q$, duration $T$ and mesh $\Delta$, the clock errors and the gate errors enter this one bound.

For $a=1$, $N=11$, $h=\pi/11$ and the finite device whose field consists of the transverse modes at the six momenta $\pm he_1$, $\pm h(e_1+e_2)$, $\pm h(e_1+e_2+e_3)$ of the spatial quotient $D_3/(2N\mathbb Z^3)$, all of which have $S>0$, $D>0$ and $d\ne0$, the readout (Q.6.2g.9) at $T=8$, $\omega=1/4$ and $\phi=0$ gives $p_+=0.979859711848672\ldots$, $0.666390743130177\ldots$ and $0.310944412632953\ldots$ for the three directions.

*Proof.* Item 1. Accepted moves never increase $\lVert r\rVert^2$. If $r\notin\Xi_2$ has two nonzero coordinates $r_i,r_j$, the root $s=-\operatorname{sgn}(r_i)e_i-\operatorname{sgn}(r_j)e_j$ gives $\lVert r+s\rVert^2-\lVert r\rVert^2=2-2(\lvert r_i\rvert+\lvert r_j\rvert)\le-2$, and $r+s\ne0$ because $r$ is not a root. If $r$ has one nonzero coordinate, parity gives $\lvert r_i\rvert\ge2$, and $s=-\operatorname{sgn}(r_i)e_i+e_j$ lowers $\lVert r\rVert^2$ by $2\lvert r_i\rvert-2\ge2$. Hence every nonroot code has a strictly descending move of probability at least $1/24$, and at most $N$ strict descents occur from $\lVert r\rVert^2\le M$. Coupling the descents with independent Bernoulli$(1/24)$ trials until absorption shows that the probability of not reaching $\Xi_2$ within $m$ steps is at most $B(m,N)$. On $\Xi_2$ an accepted move goes from $r$ to $r+s$ with $r\cdot s=-1$, which is again a root; each root has eight such moves and stays with probability $16/24$. The resulting graph is symmetric and connected with diameter $3$, so the transition matrix on $\Xi_2$ is symmetric, hence doubly stochastic, irreducible and aperiodic, and the uniform law is its unique stationary law. A path of length at most three, padded by holding steps, gives $P^3(x,y)\ge24^{-3}$ for all roots $x,y$, a Doeblin minorization with constant $24\cdot24^{-3}=1/576$ against the uniform law, whence the factor $(575/576)^b$ after $3b$ further steps (Levin and Peres 2017). A stationary law gives constant mass to the nonroot codes; almost-sure absorption makes that mass tend to zero, so the law is carried by $\Xi_2$ and equals $q$. The same arguments apply inside every energy ball, which accepted moves never leave. One step with orthogonal records $\lvert\mathrm{tag}(r,s)\rangle$ of energy $\epsilon(\lVert r\rVert^2-\lVert F(r,s)\rVert^2)$, where $F(r,s)$ is the accepted or retained code, is the isometry $\lvert r\rangle\mapsto24^{-1/2}\sum_s\lvert F(r,s)\rangle\lvert\mathrm{tag}(r,s)\rangle$; it conserves energy, extends to a unitary on each finite energy sector, and its controller marginal is the chain above.

Item 2. $(T_r-I)^*(T_r-I)=2I-T_r-T_r^*$ and $\Xi_2=-\Xi_2$; summing with the weights $12q_r=\frac12$ gives $L_q$. The four roots $\pm e_i\pm e_j$ contribute $4\cos(ak_i)\cos(ak_j)$ to $\sum_r\cos(ar\cdot k)$, which gives $\ell_q$, and comparison with (Q.6.2d.3) at $p_*$ gives $\ell_q=24L_{p_*}$.

Item 3. The Fourier transform carries translations to multiplication by characters. The orthogonal projection onto the closed graph commutes with them, hence with all bounded measurable multiplications, and is therefore a measurable field of projections on $\mathbb C^m\oplus\mathbb C^m$. A vector $(0,v)\ne0$ in the fibres on a set of positive measure would give a nonzero element $(0,g)$ of the graph, and a defect of the first projection on a set of positive measure would give a nonzero vector orthogonal to the domain; so almost every fibre is the graph of a matrix $M(k)$, and the domain is maximal. Conversely, the graph of a measurable field is closed and translation invariant, and its domain is dense because it contains the functions supported where $\lVert M\rVert$ is bounded. Boundedness, adjoints, positivity, reality and covariance are pointwise statements under the unitary Fourier transform (Reed and Simon 1980). For (Q.6.2g.4), positivity gives a semidefinite form on vector polynomials with $\langle z^iv,z^jw\rangle=v^*C_{i+j}w$. Multiplication by $z$ is a symmetric operator $X$ on its quotient, and boundedness of $(C_n)$ together with $\lVert Xp\rVert\le\lVert p\rVert^{1-2^{-j}}\lVert X^{2^j}p\rVert^{2^{-j}}$ gives $\lVert Xp\rVert\le\lVert p\rVert$. The closure of $X$ is a self-adjoint contraction, and its spectral measure compressed to the constant vectors is $\mu$; uniqueness follows from density of polynomials in $C([-1,1])$, and the converse from $\sum_{i,j}v_i^*C_{i+j}v_j=\int p(r)^*\,d\mu(r)\,p(r)$ with $p(r)=\sum_iv_ir^i$. The inequalities with $C_{i+j+1}$ state $X\ge0$, that is $\operatorname{supp}\mu\subset[0,1]$.

Item 4. With $k_4$ as time, $\sum_{r\in\Xi_2}\cos(ar\cdot k)=4\sum_{i<j\le3}c_ic_j+4c_4S$, so $\ell_q=A-B\cos(ak_4)$. For $\varepsilon=\pm1$ the multiaffine function $6-\sum_{i<j\le3}c_ic_j-\varepsilon S$ on $[-1,1]^3$ has nonnegative values at the eight vertices and vanishes only at $c=(\varepsilon,\varepsilon,\varepsilon)$, which gives $A\ge|B|$ and the equality case. For $D>0$ and $B\ne0$ put $r=(A-D)/B=\operatorname{sgn}(B)e^{-aE}$; then $\lvert r\rvert<1$, and $r^{|n|}/D$ solves $AC_n-\frac B2(C_{n-1}+C_{n+1})=\delta_{n0}$ and is summable, so it is the Fourier inverse of $(A-B\cos\theta)^{-1}$. The identities $d\times d=0$ and $(i\,d\times)^2=\lvert d\rvert^2P_T$ make (Q.6.2g.6) invariant under $A\mapsto A+i\,d\,\chi$, $A_0\mapsto A_0+\dot\chi$; varying $A_0$ gives the constraint $d\cdot\Pi=0$, and on the transverse quotient the Hamiltonian is $\frac12(\Pi_T^2+E^2A_T^2)$. Each $b_i$ lies in $D_3$, so $d$ is periodic on $\mathcal B$; it is odd and $d(k)=k+O(a^2\lvert k\rvert^3)$. The oscillator Schwinger function $e^{-E\lvert\tau\rvert}/(2E)$ multiplied by $Z$ is $e^{-E\lvert\tau\rvert}/D$, which at $\tau=2an$ equals $C_{2n}$, and the transverse projection gives (Q.6.2g.7). The sets $\{S=0\}$, $\{D=0\}$ and $\{d=0\}$ are zero sets of nonzero trigonometric polynomials, hence Haar-null; multiplication by $E$ is self-adjoint on $\{f\in L^2(\mathcal B;\mathbb C^3):P_Tf=f\}$, and $H=d\Gamma(E)$. For (Q.6.2g.8) put $s_2=\lvert k\rvert^2$; on the branch $S>0$ near $k=0$,
$$
\frac AB=1+\frac{a^2s_2}{2}+\frac{a^4s_2^2}{24}+a^6\Bigl(\frac{s_2^3}{720}+\frac{s_2^3-\sum_ik_i^6}{180}\Bigr)+O\bigl(a^8\lvert k\rvert^8\bigr),
$$
and comparison with $\cosh(aE)=\sum_n(aE)^{2n}/(2n)!$ order by order gives (Q.6.2g.8); the sextic form follows from $s_2^3-\sum_ik_i^6=3(k_1^2+k_2^2)(k_1^2+k_3^2)(k_2^2+k_3^2)$. The unit map rescales the canonical pairs by $\sqrt{\hbar u_T}$ and $\sqrt{\hbar/u_T}$.

Item 5. With $H_0$ the free Hamiltonian, $H_c(t)=e^{-iH_0t/\hbar}\,\hbar g[b^\dagger a(f)+a(f)^\dagger b]\,e^{iH_0t/\hbar}$, so the interaction-picture generator is the exchange exactly, and both commute with $\sum_ja_j^\dagger a_j+\sum_lb_l^\dagger b_l$. On the one-excitation sector a pulse of area $\theta$ maps $\lvert f\rangle\mapsto\cos\theta\lvert f\rangle-i\sin\theta\lvert b\rangle$ and $\lvert b\rangle\mapsto\cos\theta\lvert b\rangle-i\sin\theta\lvert f\rangle$ and fixes the modes orthogonal to $f$; this gives the preparation, counting and analyzer probabilities, and two pulses of area $\pi/4$ separated by free evolution for time $T$ give (Q.6.2g.9). The instrument identities $\sum_xM_x^\dagger M_x=I$ and backward induction on the finite protocol tree give $\sum_hK_h^\dagger K_h=I$. The one-particle Hamiltonian of field and port, $\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}E&gf\\ \bar g f^*&\omega\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$, is nonnegative when $\lvert g\rvert^2\lVert E^{-1/2}f\rVert^2\le\omega$ by the Schur complement, so every admitted profile allows a nonzero coupling.

Item 6. Replace one step at a time: unitary conjugation changes the trace distance by at most $\lVert U-U'\rVert$, an instrument changes it by at most half its diamond distance, and the final readout contracts trace distance; summing gives (Q.6.2g.10). Duhamel's formula bounds $\lVert U-U'\rVert$ by $\hbar^{-1}\int\lVert H-H'\rVert\,dt$, and on excitation number at most $Q$ one has $\lVert d\Gamma(h)-d\Gamma(h')\rVert\le Q\lVert h-h'\rVert$. For a finite realization choose a compact window $K$ on which $E$, $D$, $\lvert S\rvert$ and $\lvert d\rvert$ are bounded away from $0$ and $\infty$, count the profile mass outside $K$ as initial-state error, and replace $E$ on $K$ by a cellwise constant $E_\Delta$ with $\lVert(E-E_\Delta)1_K\rVert\le\Delta$; then $\lVert(e^{-itE}-e^{-itE_\Delta})1_K\rVert\le\lvert t\rvert\Delta$, and on excitation number at most $Q$ the free evolutions differ by at most $Q\lvert t\rvert\Delta$ on the same Fock space. The approximating one-particle space is finite-dimensional and invariant under $E_\Delta$, so every gate is a finite matrix with a finite two-level decomposition (Nielsen and Chuang 2010). The example values follow from (Q.6.2g.5) and (Q.6.2g.9) by direct evaluation. ∎

### Q.6.5 Summary

The branch fixes a spatial resolution of a little more than two Planck lengths. The same numerical time scale follows under the propagation calibration; capacity and geometry have their separately stated branch inputs.
